Regarding the point that says, as the Philosopher says in the <term>Ethics</term> <gloss>Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics</gloss>, that all things whose value can be measured by coin or is accustomed to being bought are given and accepted in exchange. And therefore, those acts that are performed for the relief of another's misery, even though they are received as gifts, are nonetheless expended with a final intention <note>meaning: the intention of the giver</note>. Regarding the second, he says that habits are distinguished by acts, and acts by their objects. Therefore, sometimes names are shared between habits, acts, and objects. As is evident in the case of faith, which can signify the habit of faith, or the act of faith, or the very thing believed. Similarly, the name "alms" sometimes signifies the very thing given, and in that sense, it is not defined here. Sometimes it signifies the very act of giving, and in that sense, the aforementioned definition is accepted. Regarding the third, I say that even if clerics themselves do not have need of alms, they are given to them as ministers of the poor and dispensers of alms. And therefore, what is given to them as alms is transmitted by them to the poor. Regarding the fourth, he says that, as was stated in the fourth book, distinction 26, the names of sensible passions are sometimes transferred by a certain similarity to acts of the will that are without passion. And thus, compassion properly imports a passion of sadness regarding the misery of another, and also the act of the will by which something is displeasing to someone regarding another's misery, and alms must never be given without such compassion. For no one would relieve another's misery unless he willed that he should not be miserable. And such compassion is also in God, because our evils are displeasing to Him from a preceding will, and sometimes also from an antecedent one. In us, however, sometimes a passion properly so called is added, because the superior appetite is born to move the inferior appetite. Whence it happens that there is a strong impression in the superior, and there will also be one in the inferior unless something resists it. And according to this, mercy and modesty and certain other passions are praiseworthy insofar as they proceed from a due election of the good. Regarding the fifth, he says that although one does not give the alms for the sake of God with respect to its primary being, he nevertheless gives it to himself as the ultimate complement, which is meritorious. And therefore, it is placed last in the definition of alms itself. Regarding the second question, I say that to desist from sin is not of the essence of satisfaction, as is evident from the aforesaid. This is a preamble to satisfaction, that a foundation for it be made. Whence, when someone sins again by not doing what he is held to do, it is not of the essence of satisfaction, but a preamble to it. Whence, when someone is bound to the distribution of alms and someone is not, as will appear later, it stands that the distribution of those alms to which one is bound is not a part of satisfaction, but a preamble to it. Those alms, however, to which one is not bound, can be satisfactory when they are good and penal works, which was required for a satisfactory work. For they are imposed upon one not only from the affliction of the body, but from the subtraction of things. And through this, the solution to the first is evident. Some, however, say that even the first are satisfactory from the largesse of divine mercy. Regarding the second, he says that that reasoning proceeds from an integral part. Alms, however, is not such a part of satisfaction, but rather it is subjective, and therefore, even without it, satisfaction completes its own work by itself, or otherwise in each of its species. Regarding the third, he says that penalty is called evil insofar as it subtracts some good, by which nature is harmed. Whence, there is a diverse ratio of the good in riches, which the lust of the eyes desires; and in delights, which the lust of the flesh desires; and in honors, toward which the pride of life tends. Thus, there is a diverse ratio of penalty in alms, which subtracts riches; and in fasting, which subtracts delights; and in prayer, which depresses the height of the proud spirit through humility. And because of this, they are diverse parts of satisfaction. Nor does it differ regarding the aforesaid goods whether they are simply good or esteemed good, as much regarding the ratio of penalty as regarding the ratio of appetite. For penalty is contrary to the will, as Anselm says. Regarding the fourth, he says that alms does not consist only in the bestowal of money, but also in other services performed for neighbors for the sake of God, as has been said. Whence, even if this wealth is lacking, the faculty of giving alms is not absent. And if the faculty were entirely absent regarding corporal alms on account of the scarcity of things and the weakness of the body, the faculty would not be lacking regarding spiritual alms, because one could at least either advise another or pray. And if even that faculty were entirely lacking, a complete will would suffice. Regarding the third question, it must be said that, since a virtue is a habit by which we are directed toward operating well, it is necessary that every act that imports rectitude in itself be reduced to some virtue, even if in its definition it does not express everything that is required for the perfection of virtue. For example, to give when it is to be given is called an act of liberality, although in this not all the due circumstances that are required for the act of liberality are expressed. We, therefore, wishing to obviate such precautions and frauds, desire that the very same thing be done in this kind of case as is done in other cases in which there is no such free collusion and the truth can be known from many indications. That is to say, if the heirs or others who are called to the succession do not wish to proceed, or wish to desist after the suit has been contested, or even appear to be acting through collusion, then another of those heirs should be admitted to such prosecution or defense. But if none of the heirs or others who are called to the succession wish to prosecute such a suit, then it is necessary for an investigation to be made by the office of the judge so that the truth may be elicited from other reasons and indications, and truly [for] the judgment of those who, for the fraud and collusion in the inconvenience and loss of the heirs or others who are called to the succession, have secretly or openly caused themselves to be accused, or have caused themselves to be accused in fraud or to the detriment of those who are called to the succession.

In this manner, we also desire in other cases in which there is no such free collusion and the truth can be known from many indications. VIII. Diabolical and superstitious Magic is a certain method or art of working wonders through signs by the aid of demons. Just as natural Magic uses natural causes, so superstitious Magic uses signs which are moral causes; for by these, through a compact, the demon is enticed to do what the Magician requests, and thus the signs themselves appear to accomplish something, as St. Augustine suggests in Book 12 of *The City of God*, chapter 6, where he also records that these signs and the entire discipline were first instituted by demons, who nevertheless do not take pleasure in the signs viewed in themselves, but insofar as they are honored by them, or insofar as they depend upon their institution. But who among men was the first author and the first instrument through whom the devil infused this plague into the world? Gregory of Tours, in Book 1 of *History of the Franks*, chapter 6, says that Cush, the firstborn of Ham, with the devil instilling it, was the inventor of the entire Magical art; the Persians called him Zoroaster (as if a living star) when he came to them, and they regarded him as a god because he was struck by lightning. St. Clement, in Book 2 of the *Recognitions*, thinks that Magic also flourished before the flood and was handed down after the flood by Ham to his son Mizraim, from whom came the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Persians, who were most devoted to these arts.

IX. Furthermore, as certain as it is to Christian philosophers that demons exist, it is just as certain that Magic is demonic, which relies neither on the industry or craft of men, nor on purely natural causes, but is supported by a certain immaterial and separate power or action—that is, it proceeds from immaterial and separate substances—and this is demonstrated above all by experience. For the ability to give answers about the most hidden things, to suddenly acquire knowledge without any labor of learning, to remove bodies from the eyes of those looking on, etc., can be reduced to no cause other than some intellectual and separate nature; this, however, is not God, nor any good genius (who do not involve themselves in vain things), and therefore it is only a <term>Cacodæmon</term> <gloss>evil spirit/demon</gloss>, as Delrio rightly proves in Book 2, question 2. From this you may learn that, aside from the natural Magic exposed above, there is no "White" and licit Magic that flows down to us immediately from God alone, or mediately from Him through good angels, but every other kind is "Black" and illicit, being handed down by malignant spirits and resting upon their explicit or implicit compact.

Secondly, the study and public treatment of Magic can justly be prohibited in a Republic if it is feared that, once published among the common people, it might provide many (such is the inclination of the human mind toward evil) with an opportunity to abuse it for the ruin and destruction of others. And although physicians could also abuse Medicine, which for the same reason would also seem to be prohibited, yet the rationale of Medicine is one thing, that of Magic another; since Medicine and its use are in themselves necessary to mortals, and its abuse is more manifest than that it could be entirely hidden, and therefore it is easier to punish and correct. However, the use of Magic is not in itself necessary to human society, and its abuse is occult, for it lies hidden by what things and in what manner Magic operates. For which reason it can be greatly feared that, the more occult it is in its operation, the more, through the confidence of impunity, it becomes prone to doing harm, says Pererius, chapter 14.

VIII. Diabolical and superstitious Magic is a certain method or art of performing wonders through signs with the help of demons. Just as natural Magic uses natural causes, so superstitious Magic uses signs that are moral causes; for by these, through a pact, the demon is enticed to do what the Magician requests, and thus the signs themselves appear to accomplish something, as St. Augustine suggests in his *City of God*, book 12, chapter 6, where he also records that these signs and the whole discipline were first instituted by demons, who nevertheless are not pleased by the signs when viewed in themselves, but only insofar as they are honored by them, or insofar as they depend on their institution. But who among men was the first author, and the first instrument through whom the devil poured this plague into the world? Gregory of Tours, in his *History of the Franks*, book 1, chapter 6, says that Cush, the firstborn of Ham, with the devil instilling it, was the inventor of the entire Magical art; the Persians named him Zoroaster (as if to say "living star") when he came, and because he was struck by lightning, they held him for a God. St. Clement, in *Recognitions*, book 2, also thinks that Magic flourished even before the flood, and after the flood was handed down by Ham to his son Mizraim, from whom came the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Persians, who were most devoted to these arts.

IX. Furthermore, as certain as it is to Christian philosophers that demons exist, it is just as certain that there is demonic Magic, which relies neither on the industry or artifice of men, nor on merely natural causes, but on a certain immaterial and separate power or action—that is, one proceeding from immaterial and separate substances—and this is demonstrated primarily by experience. <margin>In mineral waters, spiritual tinctures are not present.</margin>
The opinion of those who can attribute nothing to mineral waters, such as acidulous ones, etc., except spiritual mixtures and immature "nurseries" or first entities, which are assumed by the waters before they coagulate and acquire form, is refuted by such a generation. It must be admitted that this can indeed happen; but it should not be considered a universal rule, since art itself not infrequently elicits these juices from mineral waters by coagulating them, perfect in their own substance. To claim that such waters do not exist in minerals is quite narrow-minded and shows a spirit too enamored of its own ideas. But who can name and point out a metallic water which carries with it the first matter of metals before it is formed, and which, not yet having form, also lacks the virtues of a perfect metal? How will they call this water "serrated" <note>likely referring to harsh or jagged water</note> or "aerated" if they have never known the qualities of the first matter of individual metals? Everything can be reduced into <term>hydrargyrum</term> <gloss>mercury</gloss>; from all things salt and <term>calcanthum</term> <gloss>vitriol</gloss> are elicited—who could distinguish these in their beginnings and crudity? The opinion of our Philosopher is more likely, namely that things of this kind occur through resolution either into spirits, of which we spoke above, or into soluble juices or calxes, since art testifies that calcined metals are dissolved into liquids, and other juices are elicited from them and washed away through filtered elementary waters: indeed, they are corroded by acrid substances (sharp waters, cements, colorants, etc.), and this corrosion is so mixed with the waters that they do not appear at all until after coagulation; in this way, such a quantity exists in the clearest wine, the juices of boiled things in purified decoctions, metallic shavings in <term>aqua fortis</term> <gloss>nitric acid</gloss>, and soluble juices in solutions.

# CAP. XII.
## Analogues of Minerals.

**T**hose waters which acquire nothing at all in the mineral, or rather in the caverns of the earth, but bring with them a virtue already created by mixing in the outer parts of the earth, can also be recalled to this class of corpulent mixtures. Thus, if the sea were to enter a chasm of the earth and burst forth again at another point, it could be held for a mineral spring: thus, if rainwater, river water, stagnant water, or swamp water, etc., having received force from the juices of plants, the excrement of animals, or other things, were to descend to some depth and then emerge again affected in the same way, or at least changed to some extent by that principle. It is known that where flocks of animals are stabled, the places soaked with excrement receive the beginnings of <term>kalinitrum</term> <gloss>potassium nitrate/saltpeter</gloss>. If this is then absorbed by a stream winding through the area and eventually emerging from a single spring, the water will end up being called almost mineral. It is also known that various things can putrefy in stagnant waters, especially animal and vegetable matter. From there, too, will come an origin representing a mineral.

# CAP. XIII.
## The Opinion of Paracelsus.

<margin>The first matter of metals.</margin>
**P**aracelsus was taught this also by his preceptors and by the evidence of experience. For although he sometimes attributes to mineral waters a proper and primordial nature from the creation of the world, and says that mineral waters were one and the same with simple waters, but were separated for the health of animals and plants and later flow separately; yet he can be seen either to have corrected his opinion, or to have varied later according to the habit of his inconsistency or of Sceptical and Socratic uncertainty, when he left it written that cold mineral waters arise either from alum, salt, or vitriol, immature and unmixed in their vein: so that no elementary water is added, but those very immature, uncongealed things, existing in the form of a liquid, emerge purely and constitute a mineral spring by a perennial flow? If this is so, it is necessary that an immense force be collected in receptacles and a vast space, so that the flow might suffice for a long time, or that nature in that place fails in its effort and emits nothing but imperfect abortions into the light; or else from the three principles of the seven metals before they consist, if the water runs through them and corrupts them so that they cannot be perfected, or at least from the first matter of these three in each metal, both simply and mixed: (as if the influx of elementary water anticipated nature's operation and dissipated the salt, sulfur, and mercury of gold, silver, tin, lead, iron, copper, and mercury, which are about to be coagulated—although that thing cannot be called first matter, since it is nothing other than dissolved salt, uncongealed sulfur, and unconcreted mercury: for the true first matter of these is either a seminal vapor and breath having the power for those things, or a viscous principle fecundated by such a spirit, which, if it is snatched away before its maturity and diluted by waters, can by no means imprint a metallic nature upon the waters, since it has it not in act but in potency, just as one who, when a chicken's liquor is disturbed and mixed with water, does not endow this with the nature and powers of a hen, so that it cannot yet be recognized. It is ridiculous, however, that such a principle could flow simply, since it is certain that it is enclosed in the ore and matures in the manner of the fruits of plants and animals: which if it flows together, it is only that it is not, or has already received form in the ore, lacking proper coagulation, which it finally acquires in its pool. It is certainly easier to invent such a thing than to show it. It cannot be denied, however, that from immature metallic beginnings, whether they be spirits or liquids, through the mixing of wild waters, metallic waters emerge in some way. But if you also add that those three principles are to be understood separately, so that thus <margin>Doubt regarding metallic beginnings.</margin> a twenty-one-fold mineral flux could exist from them, you will rave even more. For they do not exist separately, nor are metals made by composition from those separate things, but are produced as if from a seed, in which those principles were together in potency, if indeed they are to be held as true principles and not rather as Chymical masteries, elicited by art from differently affected metals, in which way we can make from them vitriol, flowers, calxes, liquors, etc., which nevertheless are not held for true beginnings, etc.) or from the spirits of the three metallic principles: (The same is said: For it matters nothing whether they appear as spirits or liquids on the outside, if they are imperfect on the inside. We can, however, also understand the breath of resolved things, and take these principles catachrestically <note>using words in a forced or metaphorical sense</note> for salt, sulfur, and mercury, not those which are the beginnings of the composition or generation of things, but which are things perfect in themselves, just as we consider the elements in themselves, insofar as they are simple bodies...

Like a bramble, it has thorns, curved into a hook, leaves like a quince, fruit like an olive; when this splits open, a white flower bursts forth, and when this falls, an oblong nut grows together, which finally unfolding itself, represents red grains, such as are seen in the pomegranate, with large, spriggy roots. The stalks, leaves, flowers, seeds, and nuts seasoned with salt are brought to us in this appearance and shape which we have described. France now nourishes the shrub. Much caper grows in Cyprus. It offers little nourishment to those eating it, because it excels in the thinness of its parts, being born for medicine rather than food. The fruit is preserved sprinkled with salt, otherwise it quickly experiences corruption. Fresh, not having experienced salt, it nourishes more than when aged in it, yet it moves the bowels more. When washed and macerated for a while until it puts aside all the nature of salt, it does not nourish at all, but invites a languishing appetite. It dispels disgust for food, casts down the phlegm that had gathered in the stomach, and clears away the obstructive infarctions of the spleen and liver. But to perform these uses, it must be preferred to other dishes with honeyed vinegar, or oil and vinegar. While the tender buds are green, they are eaten with vinegar and salt, and stored for use. They say that those who eat them daily are not in danger of the dissolution of the nerves, nor of pains of the spleen. The root removes white vitiligo <note>a skin condition causing loss of pigment</note> if rubbed on when ground in the sun. It is useful to the splenetic when drunk in wine, two drachms of the bark of the root, with the use of baths omitted. And they say that in thirty-five days the whole spleen is sent out through the urine and the bowels. It is drunk for pains of the loins and paralysis. The seed ground and boiled in vinegar, or the chewed root, sedates toothaches. A decoction is poured into the ear for pain with oil. Leaves and fresh root with honey heal ulcers which they call phagedena <note>rapidly spreading, gangrenous ulcers</note>. Thus the root also dispels glandular swellings and parotids. Boiled in vinegar, it removes ulcerations of the mouth; it also heals evils of the liver and kills small worms in the ears. They give it in vinegar and honey for ringworm. It is agreed among authors that they are useless to the stomach. The stalk and fruit are seasoned for the sake of food. It disturbs the bowels, harms the stomach, and creates thirst. Yet it is more useful to the stomach cooked than raw. The seed itself, taken in wine in the amount of two drachms for forty days, consumes the spleen. It draws out urine and expels bloody strippings. It is useful in pains of the hips and resolution of the nerves; likewise for ruptures and convulsions. It moves the menses and elicits phlegm from the head. Seed boiled in vinegar sedates toothaches if the mouth is rinsed. The dried bark of the root has the same effects. It cleanses all old and filthy ulcers and those that have calloused. For those with splenic troubles, it is applied with barley flour. The root, seized bitingly by the tooth, relieves that evil. It removes white vitiligo when ground with vinegar. The root and leaves ground together dispel glandular swellings and hardnesses. The juice is poured in against worms of the ears. The foreign caper, which is carried from Marmarica in Libya, excites great inflations. The Apulian causes vomiting. The African is most harsh, as is that which is carried from the Red Sea; indeed it raises pustules in the mouth, an enemy to the gums, for it eats them away to the bone, wherefore it is condemned as food.

### Lepidium. Chapter CV

The appearance of *lepidium* <note>pepperwort</note> is not represented by Dioscorides. *Lepidium* was once foreign, now it is sown in many places by Favonius; then when it has become shrubby, it is cut down near the ground, and mown like cut leek, but more rarely. ## XII.

It is therefore established that the fanatical opinions of the Paracelsians, Weigelians, Mystics, Quakers, and others, who are commonly called by the name of the illuminated, agree on this point: that besides the body and the rational soul, there is in man a certain substantial part granted to him by God, and, as most do not deny, derived from the very essence of God. The same doctrine regarding the three parts of man is explained quite prolixly by Felgenhawer in *The Forecourt, in the Holy and Most Holy Place of the Temple of God* <note>original: "Vorhoff/ im heiligen und Allerheiligsten am Tempel GOttes"</note>. The individual readings in this fanatical booklet sufficiently declare the reasons for each part and the dreams the fanatics hold concerning them. It is also worth consulting Bartholomew Sclei's *Decent General Doctrine of God* <note>original: "anständige allgemeine GOttes Lehre"</note>, as well as *The Book of Testimony of the Hidden Field-Treasure* <note>original: "Buch des Zeugnisses des verborgenen Ackerschatzes"</note>, whose author calls himself HIEL, *The One-Essence Life of God* <note>original: "einwesige Leben GOttes"</note>, as well as the *Thorough Instruction* <note>original: "gründlicher Unterricht"</note> of Matthes Weyer, who was highly illuminated by God, and similar monstrosities of books written by those furies—truly unworthy things upon which one might waste good and irrevocable hours reading.

## XIII.

Furthermore, this doctrine of the threefold part of man holds the leading place in their own <term>mataeologia</term> <gloss>vain or empty discourse</gloss>. For the author of *The Forecourt* claims, most ineptly in Chapter XII, that it contains the foundation not only of the whole of Christianity, but of all wisdom in general that exists in heaven and on earth. But if by chance someone does not know that he has five senses, or what the nature of sight, hearing, or the rest might be, must it therefore be established that they are unable to perform their duty? I certainly do not think so. very certain, for the city of Gubbio, where it finally began to lift its head and flourish again, it was necessary to labor greatly to compose the scattered members of its territory and to recover what had been lost. This was the first care of the people of Gubbio after the form of a republic was introduced into the city, in the eleventh century, in my opinion. From that time, the rural counts and other noble men, who had built camps <note>original: "castra"</note>, fortresses, towers, and fortifications on their own lands and estates, or who had occupied those built in ancient times, began to migrate into the city and be counted among the citizens, with the surrender of their camps and fortresses made on equal terms. If any, however, resisted more obstinately, they were conquered by arms; the castles and rights of many were also purchased by the commune at a just price. This was also done with the bishop and the abbots, for whom, after grave disputes, it was necessary to abdicate the lordship of the camps which they possessed in the territory of Gubbio, and to concede them to the community of the people of Gubbio, regarding which matter some things will be said in their proper place in the chronology of the bishops, and even more in the second book of the Avellanan antiquities.

II. In this manner, by the example of other cities <margin>(a)</margin>, the Eugubine state was gradually restored, the number of citizens was increased, the strength of the treasury was augmented, and the city appeared to flourish most greatly. Under the reign of Frederick I, the people of Gubbio held a not insignificant part of their territory by best right, in which these places and camps were contained, some of which, however, still appear to have pertained to the bishopric and the monasteries of Saint Peter and Saint Donat, namely: Mons Episcopi, otherwise known as the camp of the Episcopal Mount; Agnanum; Mons Ranaldi; Mons Lulianus; Monticellius; Sanvictorinum, otherwise known as the Mount of Saint Victorinus; Mons Fragarius; Turris; Collis Palumbi; Glomifcium; Mons Saint Mary; Clefium; Petrorium; and Sclizza, or Schiggia; and Collis Casalis, all of which are enumerated in the diploma of Frederick, indicated in the previous chapter. The diploma of Frederick was given, as I have said, in the year 1163. But in another diploma of Henry VI, given in the year 1191, besides those camps, we have two more: Castilio Ildebrandi and Vallis Marcula, which appear to have been acquired by the people of Gubbio in that interval of time. Many more were acquired thereafter, but it does not appear that the entire ancient county had returned to the jurisdiction of the people of Gubbio at the beginning of the fourteenth century, as is evident from the sentence of Deoticherius of Lorano, who asserted the lordship of the people of Gubbio over the camps of the territory of Gubbio in a legitimate judgment, but nevertheless declared that the camps of Saint Christina, Colcellus, Carpianus, Febinus, Portulae, and all others should be excepted.

# Of Lettuce. Ch. XXII.
Lettuce, as Isidore says, is named from the exuberance of its milky humor, or because it fills nursing women with milk. It restrains the movement of <term>venus</term> <gloss>sexual desire</gloss> in men. There are two species of it: the domestic, and the wild, which we call feral because its back has thorns hard in the manner of iron, as Isidore says in book XVII, last chapter. Regarding it, Pliny says in the *Dietaries*: "Wild lettuce is similar in form to the domestic, but it has longer, finer, rougher, and less green leaves on account of the scarcity of its moisture; and for that reason, it has much bitterness and sharpness in comparison to the domestic, because it is of greater heat and dryness." And therefore, many say that it induces menstruation and expels raw humors, as Dioscorides says. Lettuce for domestic use is cold and moist according to the degree, and in neither quality does it exceed measure. And therefore its use is a serious medicine. When it is subtle and fresh, it is quickly digested and calms the burning and biting of the stomach and red bile. It cools the boiling of the blood, quiets sleeplessness, and heals headache and choleric vapor. It increases milk in women and generates and augments semen in men. This happens because of the goodness of the blood it generates in perfect quantity and at a perfect age. But when it ages and hardens, its moisture is diminished and it becomes bitter, and through its use, very bad blood is generated. The vital power then fails and is weakened; the cause of this is the mortification of the animal sense, which, with its sharpness, suffocates the natural [vitality]. And therefore such lettuce is especially harmful to those wishing to procreate, for it congeals the material and coagulates the seminal fluid, and especially its seed if it is often taken in food or drink. [Thus] Isaac in the *Dietaries*. But Pliny, in book XX, chapter VIII, says about lettuce: "There is a species of lettuce that grows spontaneously which they call goat-lettuce; when it is placed in the sea, it kills nearby fish. Its stalk and leaves, when obtuse, heal cut nerves with coarse salt." There is another species of lettuce that grows in fields, whose leaves, when crushed with polenta and applied, heal ulcers; the Greeks call this *ysopon*. The third species is that which grows in woods, which they call *steraton*; its leaves, crushed with pear-juice, heal wounds. With the root and leaves, they mitigate the holy fire <note>a term for erysipelas</note>. There is also another species of this lettuce, round and short, which many call *beratia*, whose juice hawks take by scratching the herb out of

It also breaks up and suppresses every swelling. # Of Burdock. Ch. XXIII.
Burdock is an herb having broad and thick leaves around the ground, having at the tops of the stems certain prickly and aculeated little heads that are nevertheless curved, which are accustomed to adhere to the clothes of passersby. Hence Isidore says in book XVII: "Burdock <note>Latin: Lappa</note> is so called because it has a stalk disposed toward the earth, and the Greeks call it *philatropos* because it adheres to the clothes of men on account of its roughness." And it grows next to walls, and because of *philatropos*, that is, "loving man," because with a certain affection it seems to adhere to the clothes of a man. There are two species of burdock: the sharp and the round, disposed in the likeness of a horse's foot, as it is called by many "horse-hoof" <note>Latin: vngula caballina</note>. The leaves of both are of a horrible odor and taste, as Dioscorides says. But Pliny says in book XXVI: "There are many species of burdock and all are medicinal. For they treat the stings of scorpions, and they do not strike a man if he has been anointed with its juice." The decoction of its root helps the teeth and also confirms them if held warm in the mouth. Its seed taken internally cures stomach ailments; it is beneficial for those coughing up blood and aids against dysentery, for its root with wine stops the bowels. But when given alone, it helps those with stones. The whole herb crushed with lard is good for swellings <note>Latin: strumae</note>. Thus Pliny, according to Platearius: "Burdock or dock is a hot and dry herb having the power of dissolving, relaxing, opening, and attenuating. And therefore it is good against scabies, itching, herpes, and impetigo, and it draws out humors under the skin. It dissolves the hardness and swelling of abscesses. It is good against cold dropsy and obstruction of the spleen." Its juice mixed with rue purges the brain and rheumatic flow if in a small quantity.

# HENRICI CANNEGIETERI

The prologue of the first book, and many other things, argue that Phaedrus did not write these fables for a few, but for everyone; and not only to alleviate private grief, but also to publicly hunt for fame. For to what end are those anxious <margin>ears</margin> addressed to the reader, not only in the beginning and end, but also in the middle of the books, if there was no need for them among friends? What? When in the prologue of book III he complains peevishly about being received into the assembly, and in the prologue of book V he declares his desire to go forth to the applause of literature, and says of Particulone:

> *A name that will live for his papers,*
> *As long as there is value in Latin letters.*

Do we think he hoped for this immortality of glory from the silent praises of friends, or from the public votes of the most learned men? And indeed, when he names the assembly, he surely defines it as the one we have learned existed in Rome, consisting of those men whose writings were approved by the calculations of critics. Furthermore, how do those things fit together, unless we believe these little books of Phaedrus were handled by everyone’s hands, from the prologue of book III:

> *If anyone errs through his own suspicion,*
> *And snatches for himself what is common to all,*
> *He will foolishly reveal the conscience of his own mind.*
> *I would like to be excused by him nonetheless.*
> *For it is not my intention to censure individuals,*
> *But to show life itself and the character of men.*

It is tiresome to bring forth more, for there is no prologue, no epilogue at the end of the books, that does not teach that the fables were published publicly by him. However, I wonder how those who feel differently than we do were led into the opinion that Phaedrus shows a fear of Sejanus in the prologue of book III, as if Aelius Sejanus himself is understood by this name, and not rather a man not dissimilar to his character. For if you understand Sejanus himself, who, I ask, dared as a freedman to censure him so bitterly in a public poem while he was ruling cruelly under a most savage Prince? ### §. 665.

<margin>How dissent is gathered from an action.</margin>
*If someone does what he could not do unless he willed that something else should not happen, he dissents regarding this very thing.* This is evident in a manner not unlike that which we demonstrated previously (§. 663), where we showed that if someone does what he could not do unless he willed that something else should happen, he consents to that very thing.

The truth of this proposition, by the definition of dissent provided (§. 659), is so manifest that it is rightly ascribed to the number of axioms (§. 273 *Log.*), and therefore we need not be very concerned with demonstrating it (§. 267 *Log.*). A seller who takes away and replaces merchandise upon the price being offered by a buyer serves as an example. Indeed, if he did not want to hand over the merchandise for that price, he could not take it away and replace it, since he wishes to sell the merchandise. By this very action, he sufficiently indicates that he does not want to hand over the merchandise for that price; indeed, he declares his dissent more clearly than if he had said in open words that he could not hand it over for that price. He indicates quite clearly at the same time that he despairs of the buyer offering a just price, and furthermore, that he takes it ill that a higher price is not offered by the buyer.

### §. 666.

<margin>How dissent is gathered from an omission.</margin>
*If someone does not do what he ought to do unless he willed that something else should not happen, he dissents regarding this very thing.* This is evident in a manner not unlike that by which we showed, just a little before (§. 664), that if someone does not do what he ought to do unless he willed something else to happen, he consents.

What we noted regarding the preceding proposition must also be held for the present one. The truth of the proposition is made manifest by an example. If a buyer, who had already seen the merchandise before, returns and offers a price slightly higher than what he had offered before, but the seller does not bring out the merchandise, it is understood abundantly from the fact that he does not do this, that he does not want to hand over the merchandise for that price, and consequently that he still dissents regarding the same (§. 659), even if he does not say a single word.

### §. 665.

<margin>How dissent is gathered from an action.</margin>
*If someone does what he could not do unless he did not want something else to happen, he dissents regarding this very thing.* This is clear in a way not unlike that by which we showed before (§. 663) that if someone does what he could not do unless he wanted something else to happen, he consents to this very thing.

The truth of this proposition, by the definition of dissent provided (§. 659), is so manifest that it is rightfully added to the number of axioms (§. 273 *Logic*), and therefore we need not be very concerned with proving it (§. 267 *Logic*). An example is a seller who, upon an offer of price by a buyer, takes the merchandise away and puts it back. For if he did not want to hand over the merchandise for that price, he could not have taken it away and put it back, since he intends to sell the merchandise. By this very action, he sufficiently indicates that he does not want to hand over the merchandise for that price; indeed, he declares his dissent more clearly than if he had said in plain words that he could not hand it over for that price. He shows quite clearly at the same time that he despairs of the buyer offering a just price, and indeed that he takes it ill that a higher price is not offered by the buyer.

### §. 666.

<margin>How dissent is gathered from an omission.</margin>
*If someone does not do what he ought to do unless he did not want something to happen, he dissents regarding this very thing.* This is clear in a way not unlike that by which we showed a little earlier (§. 664) that if someone does not do what he ought to do unless he wanted something else to happen, he consents.

The notes we made concerning the preceding proposition are also to be held for the present one. The truth of the proposition becomes manifest through an example. If a buyer, who had already seen the merchandise before, returns and offers a slightly higher price than he had offered before, but the seller does not bring out the merchandise, it is abundantly understood from the fact that he does not do this that he does not want to hand over the merchandise for that price, and consequently that he still dissents regarding it (§. 659), even if he does not say a single word.

### Chapter Eight: On the nature and admixture of gold

**S**hould we raise an objection regarding the nature of gold, which alone, according to <term>Hermes</term> <gloss>Hermes Trismegistus</gloss>, is that in which no disease appears? For neither part of its material is infected or intemperate. Since, like other things, it is composed of <term>sulfur</term> <gloss>a combustive principle</gloss> and <term>quicksilver</term> <gloss>mercury</gloss>, its sulfur is most lucid and most clean, and through the most powerful washings, it is brought to a purity that has no combustible oiliness at all, nor any phlegmatic, evaporable watery moisture. And perhaps in concave places, where the solid surface is often sublimated and digested by a temperate heat, it undergoes a digestion called <term>pepasis</term> <gloss>ripening</gloss>. And the earthy substance, which is incorporated into the sulfur, is clean and most subtle, suspended vaporously throughout the entire substance of the radical moisture of that sulfur. Because of this, it remains that the heat of that sulfur is complexionally temperate, departing from it in no way. And this is like the masculine virtue in the composition of gold. Similarly, its quicksilver has two substances purified to their extremes. For the third, which is in the heat itself, is subtilized, not only materially divided, but vaporously; it is most subtle earth, often sublimated in the cavities of the earth by the lifegiving heat of the sun and stars. Similarly, also, the watery part is subtilized through the same mode of repeated subtilization; and when it is thus within the glass <note>referring to the alchemical vessel</note>, it is subtly subtilized. It is clear that, mixed together by heat and the disposition of the place that traps and reflects the vapor back into itself, they are bound by the strongest bond of mixture. 

However, sulfur does not enter into the composition of gold only by quality, but by substance, and since it is a subtle substance, it will penetrate everywhere through the quicksilver, and by coagulating, it colors it. And since both are brought by sublimation to the form of the superior elements, which arrive at a state of perpetual transparency in the nature of the body, both will possess the fullness of purity. And when many parts of the matter are thickened, they will consist together. This is a property of a subtle substance: that, by consisting through coagulation, it will have many parts in a very small space. Therefore, the contracted transparency will make a lemon-yellow color, and the subtlety makes for maximum solidness. And the consistency of many parts together in a small place and position makes for weight, as is proven from those things that have been reasonably demonstrated in the *Metaphysics* and the *Physics* <note>referring to Aristotle's works</note>. It remains, then, from the solidness and the temperance combined, that gold is little evaporable, or not at all; therefore, it is almost odorless. For though an odor is not essentially a smoky evaporation, nonetheless, a strong odor is frequently accompanied by a smoky evaporation. Because of this, it follows further that gold is more incorruptible than any metal and better sustains fire due to the strongest mixture of its parts. For a smoky evaporation indicates a certain corruption of bodies, which is less in silver and more in copper. From these, one has the cause why certain things burn silver that do not burn gold, such as sulfur, arsenic, and certain others. The cause of this-

<margin>Reply to the first point</margin>
**THEOLOGIAN.** To the first, I say: He was a martyr, so to speak, in the knowledge of infused science, but not in the sense of pain and experience. For from the instant of His conception, He had knowledge of all future things in the higher powers of His blessed soul, where He saw the Word most clearly and through infused science. However, foreknowing these future events did not move His sensuality to sentiments of sadness and pain, except as the time of the Passion drew near.

<margin>Thomas in 3, dist. 17, q. final, ad 5</margin>
The holy doctor <note>referring to Thomas Aquinas</note> means this when he says in 3, dist. 17, final question: Although death was foreseen from the beginning of His conception, it was not foreseen as imminent; therefore, it did not cause the agitation, that is, the fear of the affect, but only when it was already impending. For thus we experience fear or pain in ourselves.

<margin>Aristotle, Book 3 of the Ethics, ch. 6</margin>
For a student knows the life of a young man, that death is the end of all terrible things, as the philosopher says in his 3rd Ethics, and that he will die. But because he does not imagine it as near, but as distant, it moves him little or nothing toward sadness. It does, however, move a sensible person if being old and the end being near is considered in this way.

<margin>To the second point</margin>

§. XIV. In place of an appendix, I shall here transcribe what the illustrious Sebastian Schmid commented upon in this passage. Because I had not consulted these works until after these things were already sent to the press, I had previously warned that I would add them at a less convenient place in the Disputations from which I have now formed this booklet. For although he himself does not embrace this interpretation of ours, but prefers to take these words as spoken of Christ himself—understanding that <term>ἀγενεαλόγητον</term> <gloss>without genealogy</gloss> in terms of the mode of production by which diverse essences constitute diverse persons and are numbered among them (whether this is well or poorly founded, I do not now inquire)—he nevertheless writes ingenuously: *This opinion seems the best of all those that the Interpreters have, not so much because it is Epiphanius’s (whose it is, as Justinian also writes in this place, and as we have already noted in §. XI), but because it is the most convenient for our passage, and can be supported by good arguments.* Nor does it weary me to affix them here, since they contribute greatly to the elucidation and confirmation of what we have discussed in the preceding sections. For, he says, 1. *The Apostle does not wish to deny simply that Melchizedek had any kin or genealogy; but he speaks relatively, that his kin is not described when he is called a Priest.* And we do not doubt 2. *that an opposition is made between the priest Melchizedek and the Levitical priests, which opposition the Apostle soon explains at greater length. The status of the Levitical priests was thus arranged, that all were required to demonstrate their priestly lineage and to be* <term>γενεαλογητοί</term> <gloss>recorded in a genealogy</gloss>, *that is, to have their genealogy ready at hand. If they did not have it, they were removed from the altar (Ezra 2:62, 63).* Therefore, a <term>ἱερεὺς γενεαλογητός</term> <gloss>priest with a recorded genealogy</gloss> was one who could exhibit his priestly lineage; but an <term>ἀγενεαλόγητος</term> <gloss>one without a recorded genealogy</gloss> was one who did not have a priestly genealogy. 3. *It is clearly explained in our chapter in this way, both when in verse 6 Melchizedek is said to be* <term>μὴ ἀγενεαλόγητον ἐξ αὐτῶν</term> <gloss>not without descent from them</gloss>, *not tracing his genealogy from them—namely, the sons of Levi—just as all Levitical priests were of the sons of Levi; and also because in verse 13 it is expressly said that Christ is from another tribe, from which no one has offered at the altar; and in verse 14 he is clearly ascribed to the tribe of Judah. Here the comparison of type and antitype will be clear: just as Melchizedek was an* <term>ἀγενεαλόγητος</term> <gloss>un-genealogized</gloss> *Priest, who did not have a priestly lineage, or to whom the priestly office did not descend through race and blood; so the priesthood to Christ ought not to have descended through race and blood, but was conferred upon him from a more sublime principle.* Whence it also follows *that Christ ought not to have been born of the tribe of Levi, but of the tribe of Judah, lest he be a* <term>γενεαλογητός</term> <gloss>genealogized</gloss> *Priest, obtaining the priesthood from his lineage.* Thus far Schmid, with reasoning, as you see, Reader, which is most accurate in every respect, and especially remarkable through this final observation, by which he concludes not only that Christ did not necessarily need to have a genealogy from the tribe of Levi in order to be a Priest, which I also showed quite broadly in §. XIII, but that he even ought not to have had one. For thus Paul demonstrated not obscurely to the attentive Hebrews that it is so far from the case that the priesthood of Jesus should become suspicious to them because he lacks the priestly genealogy they desire in him, that on the contrary, if he possessed it, he could not be a Priest, as he warns later in clear words regarding the earthly priestly dwelling (Hebrews 8:4). Yet, he says that Christ ought not to have been born of Levi, or that the priesthood ought not to have descended to him through race and blood, not because this was necessary by the nature of the thing, or *a priori*, as they say. For why, if it had so pleased God, could Christ not have come from the line of his typical predecessors?

So long as He remained entrenched in the heart of the populace, the temporal and ecclesiastical authorities dared not attack Him without a popular uprising of no mean proportions. But now that they had managed to wean away His public from Him they pressed Him harder and harder with their persecutions and complaints. They forced Him away from the larger towns, and now He was wandering among the less populous regions of the country, and even there the spies and agents of the authorities hunted Him down, seeking to further entrap and compromise Him.

had not been seen climbing the water pipe in the back garden, but she had evidently done something of the kind, for the pipe had parted from the wall, and was occupying a collapsed position in middle air, where it was much disturbed by the wind. She had probably been sketching on the roof.

"Then it was a dream after all," said the Gadfly; and a violent debate followed.

"It was indisputably a collective hallucination," affirmed the Oxford Slouch; "and, indeed, I can demonstrate my point."

Pressed for an explanation, he responded: "I am without aspiration and without hope; I know that only evil can befall me. I do mischief every day. I perceive that all my life is slowly culminating towards some grand, final, colossal blunder which will involve all my friends in ruin, and will extinguish myself. I am also without pains and without pleasures, nor can I be said to be alive. How is it possible for such a being to have entered Fairyland? At this point it will be well if I give a short apology for my existence."

There was great consternation in the company, and they begged him not to trouble himself, with the sole exception of the Dormouse, who was peacefully asleep upon her cushion, and would have been undisturbed by the periods of Tertullian.

->THE BORROWED DAYS.<-

THERE is a singular old proverb preserved in Ray's Collection: "April borrows three days of March, and they are ill."

April is pronounced with an emphasis on the last syllable, so as to make a kind of jingling rhyme with "ill," the last word in the line.

IV. Men who bring forth no fruit to God, yet in suffering destruction may be useful. Although they be not useful
actively, or by any thing which they do; yet they may be useful in what they may suffer; just as a barren tree, which is
no way useful standing in the vineyard, yet may be good fuel,
and be very useful in the fire. God can find use for the most
wicked men; He hath his use for vessels of wrath as well as
for vessels of mercy; as in an house there is use for vessels
of dishonor, as well as for vessels unto honor. 2 Tim. ii.
20. " In a great house there are not only vessels of gold, and
of silver, but also of wood and of earth; and some to honor,
and some to dishonor." Prov. xvi. 4. " The Lord hath made
all things for himself; yea, even the wicked for the day of
evil." I shall briefly take notice of what ends God accomplishes by it.

1. Unfruitful persons are of use in their destruction for
the glory of God's justice. It was the will of God to glorify
his justice, as well as his mercy, on his creatures. The vindictive justice of God is a glorious attribute, as well as his

angels in heaven. Hence we have an account, that they sing

> “In broad-built and stocky persons it causes this part of the temples to widen and bulge out, but in tall, long-headed persons it spreads out upon them, and hence shows to be less than it really is.”

It is directly below <term>Ideality</term> and in front of <term>Acquisitiveness</term>.

*Hamzah’s Precepts:—* The first precept of <term>Ḥamzah</term> enjoins veracity in speech; the second, protection and mutual aid to the brethren in faith; the third, renunciation of all forms of former worship and false belief; the fourth, repudiation of the devil (<term>Iblīs</term>) and all forces of evil; the fifth, confession of the unity of the <term>Ḥākim</term>-God; the sixth, acquiescence in his acts no matter what they be; and the seventh, absolute submission and resignation to his divine will in both secret and public.¹

*Sources and Operation:—* The first two precepts enunciated by the founder of <term>Druzism</term> are ethical in their nature and therefore difficult to trace back to their origin. The genealogy of the third and fourth is likewise difficult to ascertain. The fifth is the dogma we treated before, and the rest are corollaries from that dogma. The operation of the first precept is, of course, circumscribed by the already established law of <term>dissimulation</term>.

Of these principles the second has perhaps been the most potent force in the life and history of the <term>Druze</term> people. It has made of the <term>Druze</term> community one compact social body, presenting more the aspects of a religious fraternal order than a sect. This fraternal feature is one of the distinctive characteristics of the <term>Druze</term> people and has, in a large measure, contributed to their survival to the present day. It has enabled them at the time of crisis to act in unison and as one body moved primarily by motives of self-interest and by the instinct of self-preservation.

->AESAR INTELLECTUAL FIRE OR LOGH.—CHAP. V. SECT. XII.<-

The first, beginning at the bottom of the series, is Aesar.* He is called God; or fire intelligent, Dia or Logh: Mr. Vallencey says, the word Logh means the spiritual flame, and identifies itself with the Λογος of the Greeks. In a vast number of languages the word Logh, standing for some idea relating to fire, is to be found. The word Aesar, in Irish, literally means to kindle a fire. In Chaldean, אזה aza, to illuminate, אשא asa, fire. Sanscrit Osch,† fire or heat. By many of the ancient philosophers fire was considered as the primitive element, and it is unnecessary to say any thing of the fire of the Magi, or of the numerous examples of the appearance of God as a fire to Moses, the sacred fire of the Israelites, &c.

Mr. Selden says, “Although you may truly say with Origen that, before our Saviour’s time, Britain acknowledged not one true God, yet it came as near to what they should have done, or rather nearer than most of others, either Greek or Roman, as by notions in Cæsar, Strabo, Lucan, and the like discoursing of them, you may be satisfied. For although Apollo, Mars, Mercury, were worshiped among the vulgar Gauls, yet it appears that the Druids’ invocation was to one all-healing or all-saving Power.”‡ <margin>the Sun.</margin>

As fire was supposed to be the first principle of all things, it was also supposed, by a peculiar refinement, to be the destroyer, whence, probably, first arose the idea of the Creator and the Destroyer being identified. The primitive fire was supposed to have an insatiable appetite for devouring all things. According to Maximus Tyrius, the ancient Persians threw into the fire combustible matters, crying, Devour, O Lord!§ It is remarkable, that in Irish, easam or asam signifies to make or create. Aesar, then, would be the creator. Aesar was also connected with the power of magic, and he was called a magician. The word אָסַר asr, in Hebrew, has the meaning of ligavit, obligavit, with the signification of incantare. According to Schelling,|| the Eastern words which have the signification of binding, have generally the signification of incantation. He attempts to explain the meaning of the word Osiris by אָסַר asr, ais, ¶ incantator ignis. He founds this interpretation on the Samaritan text of the 18th chapter and 11th verse of Deuteronomy, which renders חבר חבר hbr, hbr, ligans, ligationem, by אָסַר asr, asr, which puts out of doubt the signification of magic. Aesar, considered as the

### HYMN CXXXIV. Indra.

As, like the Morning, thou hast filled, O Indra, both the earth and heaven,
So as the Mighty One, great King of all the mighty world of men, the Goddess Mother brought thee forth, the Blessèd Mother gave thee life.

2 Relax that mortal's stubborn strength whose heart is bent on wickedness.
Trample him down beneath thy feet who watches for and aims at us: The Goddess Mother brought thee forth, etc.

3 Shake down, O Slayer of the foe, those great all-splendid energies.
With all thy powers, O Śakra, all thine helps, O Indra, shake them down;

4 As thou, O Śatakratu, thou, O Indra, shakest all things down
As wealth for him who sheds the juice, with thine assistance thousandfold.

5 Around, on every side like drops of sweat let lightning-flashes fall.
Let all malevolence pass away from us like threads of Dûrvâ grass.

6 Thou bearest in thine hand a lance like a long hook, great Counsellor!
As with his foremost foot a goat, draw down the branch, O Maghavan.

7 Never, O Gods, do we offend, nor are we ever obstinate: we walk as holy texts command.
Closely we clasp and cling to you, cling to your sides, beneath your arms.

Mercury digested two times its weight with mica, is capable of 'killing' the eight metals. It (juice of *khecarī*) can calcine sulphur, orpiment and gold. It also 'fixes' mercury. All metals on being calcined with this, lose their 'essences' (*sattva*).
->127-128<-

It (juice of *khecarī*) can also calcine coral, liquefy mica, and 'kill' diamond. There is no doubt about that.
->129<-

<margin></margin>
'Killing' of mercury (vss. 130-131).
</margin>
O Beautiful-faced! I shall now tell another means by which the *Sādhaka* (performer) attains *siddhi*. Mercury and the juice of *harindarī* kept in the hole of the cow's horn, is to be deposited in heaps of paddy. Mercury is thus 'killed'.
->130-131 (line 1)<-

<margin></margin>
Increase of transmutation power of mercury (vss. 131-133).
</margin>
O God-praised! mercury, which is 'killed' with the juice of this plant being digested with equal weight of gold, can attain the power of transmuting ten hundred thousand times its weight of base metals into noble metals. If digested (with gold) four times of its own weight, it (mercury) is endowed with the capacity of transforming hundred million times its weight of base metals into noble metals. When digested with (gold) six times of its own weight, it (mercury) acquires the capacity of transmuting base metals into noble metals by its 'touch' only.
->131 (line 2)-132<-

When digested seven times its weight with gold, it (mercury) can reach the stage of transmuting base metals into noble metals by its 'smoke'. Thus digested eight times its weight with gold, the transmutation is performed by the 'sight' of mercury only (*avalokita*).
->133 (line 1)<-

One, having no knowledge of the *kulauṣadhīs*, moves in a bewildered state.
->133 (line 2)<-

<margin></margin>
*Kulauṣadhīs* and *tṛṇauṣadhīs* (vss. 133-135).
</margin>
With the juice of *tṛṇauṣadhī* nothing can be achieved (in the pursuit of alchemical preparations). Hence the knowledge of *kulauṣadhī* is to be attained with great care.
->134<-

There are sixty-four groups of *divyauṣadhī* plants. The foolish and the one allured by the illusion of Śiva, are not acquainted with them.
->135<-

<margin></margin>
Inefficacy of *tṛṇauṣadhīs* in mercurial operations (vss. 136-138).
</margin>
The *tṛṇauṣadhīs* are not heavenly (*adivya*, i.e. non-medicinal plant). They grow in the hollow of caves. Mercury is never 'fixed' with the juice of *tṛṇauṣadhī*.
->136<-

O Beautiful lady! mercury, treated with the juice of *tṛṇauṣadhī*, undergoes no loss of weight, i.e. elimination of its impurities (*akṣaya*). It cannot endure the heat of fire. The gold (produced from base metals) on being treated with this mercury can never stand equal to gold (either natural or perfectly transmuted gold) in matter of leaves (i.e. constituting layers), in roasting (i.e. showing unusual colour by being roasted), in emitting brilliance, and in (showing unusual colour when) cutting into two.
->137<-

The gold, yielded as a result of the treatment of any metal with mercury thus prepared with the juice of this plant, can reach a stage, which is up to the half way level as attained in the case of a total (perfect) conversion. O my dear wife! as it is not perfectly 'fixed' the gold prepared from it should never be used for the attainment of *dharma*, *artha*, *kāma* and *mokṣa*.
->138<-

Devī asked:

How mercury being 'killed', gives life to others? How lifeless plant enlivens mercury which has been 'killed'?
->139<-

Śiva said:

<margin></margin>
Efficacy of *kulauṣadhīs* in mercurial operations (vss. 139-142).
</margin>
O Pārvatī! mercury when 'swooned' (*mūrchita*) by the application of medicinal plant (*divyauṣadhī*) becomes devoid of its *kālikā* impurity, and is enlivened.
->140<-

This mercury, being free from impurities, also removes the impurities of others. By the application of this (mercury), all metals become devoid of their impurities.
->141<-

Who can say the perfectly 'swooned' mercury as 'killed'? Mercury loses its own existence by the application of juice of medicinal plants.
->142<-

<margin></margin>
Power of mercury that has been 'killed' with the aid of diamond and gold calces (vss. 143-147).
</margin>
O Goddess! I shall now tell another plant for the 'fixation' of mercury. Diamond is to be 'killed' with the aid of *kṣmāpālana*; likewise gold is to be 'killed' with this.
->143<-

The ashes of diamond and gold are to be tied perfectly (i.e. mixed together). This (compound) product, on being calcined with the juice of *niśācara*, is to be calcined with mercury (*narajīva*).
->144<-

Mercury thus calcined with the aid of this calx becomes 'killed'. This mercury is to undergo quick-exhaustion with the aid of this plant-substance. With this mercury, taken with the juice of *niśācara*, one is blessed with the strength like that of Śiva.
->145<-

, build for the soul and for permanent growth but sympathy builds for nothing.

The world loves the person who will sympathize with its ailments, but those sympathetic ones have never done the world any good. Sympathy breeds into the soul self-pity and the world is filled with people who are sorry for themselves and who feel that for some unknown reason that they are having a hard time which they do not deserve. This is a false concept and those who breed it in the minds of others breed falseness.

Man must be inspired in his efforts instead of being sympathized with in his ailments. The philosopher of old never sympathized with the crying child but sought to teach him the lesson of his fall. There is seldom if ever a time when sympathy really answers the question. It is a false narcotic, which, while it eases the pain for the moment, leaves the ultimate as far off as before.

Occult students want to learn to stop sympathizing with people for into the sympathetic ears of the world are poured all its woes by individuals who live only to tell their troubles to a sympathetic listener, said listener in turn consoling them and saying how sorry he is that it is so, how sad it must be to suffer so, and so forth and on and on into nothingness. This brings into the mind of the other person the belief that they really are terribly abused, badly off, and hopelessly mistreated. This course of procedure destroys the work of the Wisdom-Religion which is seeking to prove to man that he is responsible for his own troubles and suffering and that he must labor himself for the repair of his own temple, digging out of the debris the ruins of his own dreams. But he will never attain with the assistance of those who sympathize with him for they build in nothing but negative and willy-nilly things. The one who is truly the friend is not the one who says he is sorry and how terrible it must be but is the one who instructs and enlightens and takes the suffering of a life to show the workings of the divine powers.

There are two kinds of people in the world: one is the kind who are always bewailing, the other is the group that is eternally trying to find a real reason for the ever-changing conditions of life. The first group sympathize with everyone and everything, telling the

<column-break/>

world how sorry they are and making the rest of the world sorry too; the other group are called heartless because they have no word of sympathy to offer, and yet in their heartlessness they are humanity's truest friends. Instead of singing the emotional lullaby of the soul this second group takes the weak-kneed person who is crying for sympathy and with firmness, yet mercy and compassion, shows them the way and tells them to walk it, to forget that they are abused and march straight on to the path of light. They are the strong characters and man will never grow strong while he seeks to justify his mistakes and soothe his conscience with the sympathetic words of others. The greatest mercy in the world is to tell the truth for while it may hurt today, in eternity it brings its blessing. While today it may be harsh, tomorrow it will be appreciated. Those who spend their lives trying to justify the thing that is not as it should be and who weep with you in your infirmities go down forgotten in history's pages. The friend who raises you is the true friend; the one who weeps with you is just another fool. The more sympathy we get the more we want until all the uncertainty and unbalance of the ages rests upon our shoulders, placed there by our friends whose sympathizing kills out our own incentive to do better. Our worst enemies weep with us while our true friends weep for us as they see us nursing our meanest temperaments and greatest weaknesses with friends around to weep and wail with us.

When a great prince of Egypt died they hired mourners to weep at the tombs and great processions of white-clad figures howled and wailed behind the funeral cortege for so many pieces of silver a day. The richer the family of the departed, the more weepers were hired so that when a great dignitary died the streets literally ran with tears which were paid for at so much per. A pair of lachrymal glands, capable of overflowing at the slightest pretext, was worth a great deal of money in the days of Egypt's glory. ### CHAPTER IX

#### THE MONASTERY ARCHITECTURALLY CONSIDERED

The disposition of the monastic buildings naturally varies according as the site is an open or a restricted one, but certain governing principles are constant. The notable difference between the Eastern and Western monastery plans is the position of the church. Whereas our monastic churches usually occupy one side of a court, the Orthodox make it, where conditions allow, the central building of the whole: it normally stands free in the court, and in a cramped site it is always the court, never the church, which is curtailed, though the actual size of the church is small by Gothic standards. The typical monastery plan (Fig. 1) may then be regarded as a four-sided court, more or less rectangular, and generally enclosed completely by ranges of buildings, with the main church (<term>καθολικὸν</term>) in the centre, various chapels and other buildings

But that which is useless to them, and beneficial to us, will be the reward which we receive from them [of our attention to their concerns]. In sacrifices, therefore, we should abstain from animals. For, though all things are in reality the property of the Gods, yet plants appear to be our property; since we sow and cultivate them, and nourish them by other attentions which we pay to them. We ought to sacrifice, therefore, from our own property, and not from the property of others; since that which may be procured at a small expense, and which may easily be obtained, is more holy, more acceptable to the Gods, and better adapted to the purposes of sacrifice, and to the exercise of continual piety. Hence, that which is neither holy, nor to be obtained at a small expense, is not to be offered in sacrifice, even though it should be present.

14. But that animals do not rank among things which may be procured easily, and at a small expense, may be seen by directing our view to the greater part of our race: for we are not now to consider that some men abound in sheep, and others in oxen. In the first place, therefore, there are many nations that do not possess any of those animals which are offered in sacrifice, some ignoble animals, perhaps, excepted. And, in the second place, most of those that dwell in cities themselves, possess these but rarely. But if some one should say that the inhabitants of cities have not mild fruits in abundance; yet, though this should be admitted, they are not in want of the other vegetable productions of the earth; nor is it so difficult to procure fruits as it is to procure animals. Hence an abundance of fruits, and other vegetables, is more easily obtained than that of animals. But that which is obtained with facility, and at a small expense, contributes to incessant and universal piety.

### THE WAY OF BELIEF

50 Here shall I close my trustworthy speech and thought about the truth. Henceforward learn the beliefs of mortals, giving ear to the deceptive ordering of my words.

Mortals have made up their minds to name two forms, one of which they should not name, and that is where they go astray 55 from the truth. They have distinguished them as opposite in form, and have assigned to them marks distinct from one another. To the one they allot the fire of heaven, gentle, very light, in every direction the same as itself, but not the same as the other. The other is just the opposite to it, dark night, a compact and 60 heavy body. Of these I tell thee the whole arrangement as it seems likely; for so no thought of mortals will ever outstrip thee. R. P. 121.

The liberal mind naturally experiences a difficulty in disbelieving where, a possibility being granted, the testimony in support of a matter is fair and honourable. And though sensible evidence and more than this sometimes is required to silence negative assertion; yet reason, supported by her witnesses, may enervate it, and induce that strict investigation and thought which should always precede experiment, but which the multitude have never yet been found willing to undertake; and are consequently led astray in progress, and learn as it were by chance. It is said that Lord Bacon instituted certain experiments with a view to the discovery of the philosopher's stone, and in the *Advancement of Learning* he faithfully recognises the possibility, as does also Sir Isaac Newton in his works; while Leibnitz devoted his early life to the pursuit: nor did either of these great men, though they were practically unsuccessful themselves, condemn the ancient tradition or deny its validity. Yet it would seem to be more ordinarily natural to the human mind to reject those things, which it has neither been early imbued in the belief of, nor instructed to understand; besides individual research into mere possibilities, and because facts only are alleged, is too hopeless and arduous for this short life, which requires a definite assurance of success, and fruit even from the smallest labour.

# CAPVT IIII.

### Recognition of Puncture Wounds, Arrow Wounds, Falls, and Bruises.

<margin>A</margin>Now further regarding other types of wounds, such as puncture, arrow wounds, falls, and the like. Between these and common wounds, there is no difference in their essence, other than in the fact that such a puncture or arrow, due to its narrowness, cannot provide a place for the <term>Anfall</term> <gloss>an onset or morbid influx/inflammation</gloss>, wherefore it travels further into the flesh and veins than an open wound. For it is the nature of every <term>Anfall</term> that it desires to have much space and breadth around itself. Therefore, open wounds that are not stitched are burdened with less <term>Anfall</term> and concern than stitched ones. And the more a wound is drawn together at the surface, the more concerning it is at the base. Thus it is with punctures and arrow wounds: if they swell on the outside, the <term>Anfall</term> pushes inward, following the same <term>Lacerten</term> <gloss>muscles</gloss>, <term>meatibus</term> <gloss>passages</gloss>, and veins. Therefore, they are closer to death and more dangerous than open wounds, which are wide on the outside.

It is also to be noted in such cases that a puncture or arrow should be withdrawn at once, before the swelling and <term>Anfall</term> close in. Where this does not happen, it tends more toward death than life. And where such a concern is evident, with sufficient signs, the instrument should remain within and be left to come out through the <term>Mumia</term> <gloss>healing essence/balsam</gloss>. For its healing has a different method, and that in two ways: the one, that a wound be cut beside the arrow, or drawn out through the <term>Mumia</term> that is mixed to be attractive, and not by hand. What the medicine thus draws out is not harmful to life. Likewise, it is also with bruises or falls: wounds should be made in that same place so that the <term>Anfall</term> has an exit and does not travel inward toward the life, or it should be quieted and dispersed outwardly through the <term>Mumia</term>. For upon every impact or bruise, be it as hard and severe as it may, blue or black, the <term>Mumia</term> can bring it back to its original state, without cutting or suppuration. For such <term>inflationes</term> <gloss>inflammations/swellings</gloss> are not a destruction or from a broken nature, but a swelling of good things. <margin>B</margin> Therefore they pass away without further complication.

However, should it happen that a fall, puncture, or similar injury has entered the internal <term>regiones</term> <gloss>regions/organs</gloss>, or has broken veins, or has caused a foreign guest to fall into the regions: in that same place, you should be diligent to disperse it, as is written regarding such incidents. But if such an iron has snagged or hooked, know that it will not come out backward, but should be pushed through: or otherwise brought into an abscess and filed out, provided that this location is not harmful to life. But if such a procedure is undertaken, bind it with <term>Mumia attractiva</term> <gloss>a drawing/attracting healing balsam</gloss>, which lowers the swelling to such an extent and removes the <term>Anfall</term> that the hook goes back along the same way it entered. You should also be warned that you must in no way attempt to do anything with tongs or instruments. For you irritate the limb. This would only be acceptable if it were so close to the skin or in a flat place where it could be handled without concern. Although, without <term>Mumia</term>, this is rarely possible. The same also happens often, that bullets are shot into the body and are drawn out again through the <term>Mumia attractiva</term> by its art and nature: unless the bullet has fallen into another <term>region</term>. In this, note that the <term>Mumia</term> has no power in foreign <term>regiones</term>. Therefore, if a bullet is shot into the body and falls down between the <term>Intestina</term> <gloss>intestines</gloss>, or comes outside or below the <term>Diaphragma</term> <gloss>diaphragm</gloss>, it is not possible to draw it out from that place. Likewise, if it is shot into a pipe <note>likely referring to a bone marrow cavity or a duct</note> and the bullet sinks downward in the pipe, it is also a different <term>region</term>. And even if the <term>Mumia</term> were strong enough to draw the bullet out, the <term>Rewe</term> <gloss>the marrow/inner lining</gloss> that is inside the pipe would not permit it. Therefore, in such matters, it is good to take heed of what one is dealing with.

# CAPVT V.

### On the Healing of the Aforementioned, and What Belongs to It.

<margin>C</margin>Now the healing of such wounds is similar to the process for common wounds: it differs only in that the <term>Mumia</term> must be fed with <term>attractiva</term> <gloss>drawing substances</gloss>, and these <term>attractiva</term> should be those that do not draw <term>humores</term> <gloss>fluids/bodily humors</gloss> to themselves, nor <term>liquores</term> <gloss>liquids</gloss>, or the like, but only that they take up metals, wood, or bone, etc. For if common <term>attractiva</term> were used, fluxes would be drawn there.

Although it also sometimes happens that a bullet or such iron heals within the <term>lacertis</term> <gloss>muscles</gloss> because of the good <term>Mumia</term>, which has not fallen into any <term>Anfall</term> or has not been severely angered. Sometimes, after many years, it changes over time and falls out again. This is left to nature, and one should not attempt to interfere. For if nature heals it, who would want to act against it?

To speak of the <term>attractivis</term>, there are some that draw wood, splinters, and such things, such as <term>Asphaltum</term> <gloss>bitumen</gloss> and <term>Carabæ</term> <gloss>amber</gloss>. Some draw iron, such as <term>Magnes</term> <gloss>magnet/lodestone</gloss>. Some draw copper and tin, such as colored amethysts. Some draw lead and stone, such as alabaster. Some draw rags from the flesh or bone fragments, such as gums, turpentine, and <term>Asphaltum</term>. Some draw everything, such as <term>Serpentina</term> <gloss>a serpent-stone or specific mineral</gloss>. How all such powers are, a doctor should not be ignorant of. For in the operation of nature, when they are applied to the wounds, they all attract equally. Thus, that which draws heaps of straw and wood, that also draws iron, lead, stone, and bone into the wounds. Conversely, that which draws only iron, that draws whatever is lying free within the wound. Therefore, a doctor should not pursue the external powers, but the internal ones, as they unite themselves with nature.
