¶ **To free the eyes and eyelids.**
¶ Take one cup of the best wine you can have; if it were Malmsey <note>original: "malualia" referring to Malvasia wine</note>, it would be better, and let it be white wine. Then take a quarter of one ounce of Alexandrian tutty <note>original: "tucia alexandrina", a zinc oxide mineral used for eye ailments</note> and extinguish the said tutty in the said wine at least ten times and permit it to settle for an hour. Then pour off the clear part into another glass. Then take the said tutty, specifically the fourth part, and grind it very finely and put it into the said wine, and with that, let the sick person wash their eyes often. And if they are not freed by this, take a little of the bile of a pig and put it into the said wine and similarly let them wash themselves often as stated. And if the redness still does not recede from this, then take the egg white of one egg and put it into a bowl, beating it well until it becomes clear like water. And do not allow the sick person to lie down on a bed stretched out for at least three hours. First, wash the eyes with the aforementioned water or wine. Then take a linen cloth or tow and dip it in the egg white and place it upon the eyes, and thus let them lie for three hours. Then let them rise and walk about the room, often washing their eyes with the said wine. And do this for three or four days or more, and without fail, they will be freed.

¶ **For a blow to the eye if any cloudiness occurs through the blow, whether in a man or a horse.**
¶ Take of the juice of ivy and a little of the best Malmsey; mix together and with a feather, put it into the eye twice a day, and it will immediately be freed.

¶ **To make silver wax for seals.**
¶ Take one part of wax and two of mercury and heat at the fire, rubbing with the fingers until it is totally incorporated and deadened <note>a term for the chemical stabilization of mercury</note>. And afterwards, you will seal with the heated wax itself.

Soon after, however, Nur ad-Din made the Christians feel the folly of having stripped their land of men to wage war in Egypt. He attacked the castle of Harem or Hasrenk and would have taken it by surprise had not Toros, Prince of Armenia, Raymond, Count of Tripoli, Bohemond III, Prince of Antioch, along with the Templars, hurried there and compelled him to lift the siege. The Sultan withdrew toward Artesia, and the Christians dared to attack his right flank. This flank pretended to flee, but while the Christians pursued them with great heat, the remaining Muslims fell upon the Christians and inflicted a great slaughter i). The Templar soldiers and the <term>Turcopoles</term> <gloss>light cavalry of the Crusader states, often of mixed heritage</gloss> remained almost all on the field, and of sixty knights, only seven escaped with their lives. Both sides fought like desperate men; ten thousand of the Christians remained on the field, and the number of captives was even greater. Raymond, Bohemond, Joscelin, and Hugh of Lusignan were taken prisoner and brought to Aleppo, while Nur ad-Din pursued his victory, immediately returned, and captured the castle of Harem. These two events, which William of Tyre places in the years 1165 and 1167, belong to the second year of the reign of Amalric, and consequently to the year 1164. It has been claimed, without any basis, that Blanquefort was present at this defeat

This instrument consists of a long, hollow wooden body, narrow at the top and widening toward the bottom, where it is open. Only one string is stretched over it, resting at the bottom on a bridge that lies only loosely on the soundboard on one side, which makes the sound somewhat buzzing and similar to the sound of a trumpet. The string is touched with the finger at a vibrational node near the top and bowed with a violin bow between the upper end and the touched node.

<meta>continues from previous page: my portion.</meta> It seemed best to us to claim the estate by right of kinship, and we each claimed our share. But when we were about to proceed, this man Leochares entered a formal protest <term>diamartyria</term> <gloss>a legal procedure asserting that an estate is not subject to a claim</gloss>, claiming the estate was not subject to our suit. Upon our lodging a charge of false witness, the filing for the estate was set aside, and the suit for false testimony proceeded. In the courtroom, while we stated everything just as we do now, and Leochares himself offered many defenses, the jurors judged that Leochares had given false testimony. Once this became clear after the votes were counted, I do not know what I need to say regarding what the jurors did or what we were able to accomplish at that time. But hear what was agreed upon with us. As we allowed the magistrate not to count the votes separately but to mix them, Dicaeogenes withdrew from two parts of the estate in favor of Dicaeogenes’ sisters. He agreed that he would make these parts uncontested for us, and this man, Leochares, guaranteed this for him. He agreed to do this, and not only this, but also to yield the bathhouse to Micion; and I will provide you with the witnesses for these things.

->Witnesses.<-

We, then, having suffered these things at the hands of Leochares, and having him as our guarantor, did not punish him once we had convicted him of false witness, but it sufficed for us to have recovered our own and be finished with it. Yet, by being caught up with Leochares and Dicaeogenes, we were deceived by them, men. For neither did Dicaeogenes deliver to us the two parts of the estate, as he had agreed in the courtroom, nor does Leochares admit to having guaranteed him at that time. Yet if he had been guaranteeing him in front of the jurors, five hundred in number, and in front of the bystanders, I do not know what more he could have done. That they are lying openly, I provide you as witnesses those who were present when Dicaeogenes withdrew from the two parts of the estate, which he agreed to deliver as uncontested to the sisters of Dicaeogenes, and Leochares guaranteed that he would do what he had agreed. We believe that if any of you, men, happened to be present then, you remember that what we say is true and will assist us. For if Dicaeogenes speaks the truth, men, what profit do we have by winning, or how is he harmed by losing? For if he merely withdrew, as he says, from two parts of the estate, and did not agree to deliver them as uncontested, how was he harmed by withdrawing from that which he did not possess? For he did not hold what we are claiming before losing the suit, but rather those who bought from him and placed their claims were the ones to whom he should have returned the price, and to us he should have returned the shares. It is for this reason that we took the guarantors from him, not trusting him to do what he agreed. For we have received nothing of the two properties outside the wall, nor of the sixty <term>plethra</term> <gloss>a unit of land measurement</gloss>. Instead, those who placed their claims and bought from him have them. We do not evict them, fearing that we might lose in court. For when we evicted them from the bathhouse at the order of Dicaeogenes, who claimed he would not guarantee it, we lost forty <term>minae</term> because of Dicaeogenes, men. Thinking that he would not guarantee to him anything of what he had renounced to us in the courtroom, he placed it with Micion in front of the jurors, willing to suffer anything if Dicaeogenes would guarantee the bathhouse to him, never imagining he would do the opposite of what he had agreed. And this was for no other reason than because of the guarantors who had been established for us. But Dicaeogenes, having renounced those shares which even now he admits to renouncing to us, guaranteed the bathhouse to Micion. And I, the miserable one, far from having taken anything from the estate, but having lost an additional forty <term>minae</term>, depart having been insulted by Dicaeogenes, and I will provide you with witnesses of these things.

And he agreed that he would make these portions undisputed for us. And Leochares here guaranteed this for him. And he agreed to do this, and not only this, but also to yield the bathhouse to Micion, and I will provide you with the witnesses for these matters.

->Witnesses.<-

We, therefore, having suffered these things at the hands of Leochares, and having him as our guarantor, did not cast our vote to disenfranchise him once we had convicted him of false witness. Instead, it was enough for us to have recovered what was ours and to be done with it. But having become involved with Leochares and Dicaeogenes, we were deceived by them, men. For neither did Dicaeogenes hand over to us the two portions of the estate, despite having agreed to it in court, nor does Leochares admit to having guaranteed it for him at that time. Yet if I had been standing before the jurors, who were five hundred in number, and he had given his guarantee in front of the bystanders, I do not know what else he could have done. That they are clearly lying, I provide you with witnesses who were present when Dicaeogenes withdrew from the two portions of the estate, which he agreed to deliver as undisputed to the sisters of Dicaeogenes, and Leochares guaranteed that he would do what he had agreed. We also believe that if any of you, men, happened to be present then, you remember that what we say is true and will support us. For if Dicaeogenes speaks the truth, men, what profit did we gain by winning, or what penalty did he suffer by losing? For if he merely withdrew, as he says, from the two portions of the estate, but did not agree to hand them over as undisputed, what harm was done by withdrawing from things he did not possess? For he did not possess the things we were claiming before he lost the lawsuit, but rather those who had purchased and held them from him were the ones who should have returned the price to him and given the shares to us. For this reason, we also took the guarantors from him, not trusting him to do what he had agreed. ### On the same day, the memory of the holy women
### Xanthippe and Polyxene:

The holy Xanthippe lived during the time of Claudius Caesar of the Romans, being the wife of Probus, the governor of Spain. She had a virgin sister named Polyxene. When the holy Apostle Paul came to the region of Spain and preached Christ, Xanthippe approached him and was catechized by him, being initiated by him into the faith of Christ. Afterward, through her, her husband Probus also became a Christian. Likewise, her sister Polyxene was taught by the same apostle at that time. After his departure, having heard that the blessed Apostle Andrew was preaching the truth of the faith in Patras of Achaia, she went to him. Having learned the tenets of religion more perfectly, she was baptized. And having returned again to her own land, she found her sister Xanthippe shining with all virtues, and she received her with joy. And both, having taught many to believe in Christ, passed away.

### On the same day, the memory of the holy women
### Xanthippe and Polyxene:

The holy Xanthippe lived during the time of Claudius Caesar of the Romans, being the wife of Probus, the governor of Spain. She had a virgin sister named Polyxene. When the holy apostle Paul came to the region of Spain and preached Christ, Xanthippe approached him and was catechized by him, being initiated into the faith of Christ by him. Afterwards, together with her, her husband Probus also became a Christian. Likewise, her sister Polyxene was taught by the same apostle at that time. After his departure, hearing the blessed apostle Andrew preaching the truth of the faith in Patras of Achaia, she went to him. Having learned the matters of religion more perfectly, she was baptized. Returning again to her own country, she found her own sister Xanthippe, shining with every virtue, and welcomed her with joy. Both, having taught many to believe in Christ, died.

If you yourself know nothing of this kind, you must bitterly rebuke those who err, both with letters and with your tongue. Become far more formidable when your anger strikes the mark. Do not spare the injustice, but rather even exceed the faults, for this is how those in charge must ensure that their subordinates commit no errors. But when time has passed, if you yourself feel from your conscience that you have suffered something wrongly, as if you had erred, or if another of those under you has done what was required well, it would not be unreasonable to marvel at repentance. If, therefore, one must act according to the commands from time to time, one should not overstep. Regarding matters of temper, it is useful to understand that there is no place where a person wishing to rule must deliver many rebukes, nor should he treat everyone harshly or refuse to grant forgiveness. For one should not treat those who are temperate, both in speech and in simply doing nothing harmful, in the same way as those who err. For the former, because they seek to do nothing strange and because this <term>logos</term> <gloss>reason</gloss> is aware of what is irrational and senseless, are not to be treated as such. If they should seem to signify things not in harmony with the law, such laws should not be used by a private citizen who is shining and in command, as if appearing from a machine <note>an allusion to the <term>deus ex machina</term> of Greek theater</note>, to bear and restrain. Hence, one should not easily incline to anger. If the harsh things are according to nature, but come from a different nature, these things, then, seem to me to concern how one becomes temperate. For this reason, those who punish others for their faults must not do so with any anger or harshness, for one must acknowledge that such people stumble before God; for the transgression is evil for all. After this, one must know that it is not fitting to act against an irrational person based on one's own faults, but one must consider the sins of one's neighbor so as not to be ignorant even while they are living. Do not become a law to a temperate person, and do not defend yourself beyond what is fitting. In this way, one might escape being harsh to another, but if not, then that is the case. For such a person would not want to do this, yet it would be better for the one to whom it happens. But this does not lie in the magnitude of the fault, nor in wanting the servants to be foolish. Rather, it is better to apply the punishments according to all the laws and the mind, so that it is not a matter of wishing, nor acting with temperance, nor acting irrationally or through sin. For because of such a wonderful law, one serves; but to act irrationally and senselessly is [wrong].

If you yourself know nothing of this kind, you must bitterly rebuke those who err, both by writing and by speech; become much more fearsome when the impulses of anger hit their mark for you. Do not spare the injustice, but rather even exceed the errors; for this is how those who oversee must act so that those under their authority do not err at all. But when, after some time has passed, you yourself feel by your conscience that you have suffered some harm as if you had erred, or that someone else under your authority has performed their duty well, it would not be unreasonable to marvel at repentance.

If, therefore, it is necessary to follow orders part by part, one should not overreach. Regarding matters of passion <note>original: "θυμός" <gloss>anger/wrath</gloss></note>, it is not the case that there is nowhere one must rebuke heavily; for one who wishes to rule, do not act harshly toward everyone nor grant forgiveness for everything. For one should not treat those who are temperate, both in reason and in essence, as those who commit no harm, in the same way as those who do err. For, because they seek and do nothing absurd, and because this reason—that of being conscious—is devoid of the irrational and the senseless. But if they seem to signify things that do not harmonize with the law, let the laws not treat such people with horses <note>likely a reference to the pomp of state officials</note> and brilliant displays as if they were a private individual in charge. For it is custom, as if from a *deus ex machina*, to stand by and endure and restrain; whence it is not easy to yield to anger. For if harsh things are according to nature, but come from another nature, these things, then, seem to me to pertain to the cultivation of temperance <term>sophrosyne</term> <gloss>temperance/moderation</gloss>. Therefore, those who punish others for their errors must do so not with some anger and harshness, as those who offend against God must be acknowledged; for transgression is wicked in all cases.

After these things, one must know that to act toward an irrational person on the basis of their own errors would be to act base. But one must weigh the errors of one's neighbors so that, even while living, one is not ignorant. Do not become a temperate person by law and take vengeance beyond what is necessary. Through this, one might escape being harsh toward another; if not, then such is the case. For such a person would not wish to be so, and to whomsoever it happens, it would be better. But this does not depend on the magnitude, nor on the will to let the servants be foolish. Rather, one must apply the impositions in accordance with all the laws and the mind; so that it would not be a matter of will, nor of temperance, nor of something irrational and due to error. For because of such a wonderful law, one serves; but also, it is irrational and foolish to act.

### CCXXXV. — TO HIERAX THE DEACON.
<margin>Beware lest you be deceived by the appearance of utility. We do not see the bag on our own back.</margin>
> You perhaps deceive yourself, thinking that you discern what is to your advantage. You appear to discern, yet you do not discern, but for the most part you are blind in your own affairs. If, therefore, you consider that which is ambiguous and uncertain to be honorable, do not entrust the judgment to me, nor to yourself, but by sharing it with those who excel in discernment and prudence, receive the verdict from them.

### CCXXXVI. — TO JAMES THE LECTOR.
<margin>One must flee from the wicked. For habit is a second nature.</margin>
> Flee, O dearest one, from the wicked: for they secretly engender in the soul a certain harmful condition through use and habit. For many, deceiving themselves as if they were most excellent and strongest, and as if such occurrences could not harm them, slowly and gradually cast themselves into the same abysses as those others. For habit is a great thing, and it gradually transitions into nature; and some have affirmed that habit is a second nature. Others also assert that nature is overcome by habit, employing that saying of the ancient poet:
> 
> A drop hollows out the rock, while it falls continuously.
> 
> And indeed, what is harder than a rock? What is softer than water? Yet through constant impact, the hardness of nature is overcome.

### CCXXXVII. — TO HIERAX THE DEACON.
<margin>Temperance is the mother of health.</margin>
> If you care for the health of your body, be content with a sufficient supply for yourself. For this gives birth to that. But if you desire to make it swell and become wanton through luxury, you are deceived: not only are you arming it against the soul and making it unbridled, but you are also making it the root and source of incurable diseases.

(64) This is a proverbial verse by the poet Choerilus, not as inept as it seemed to Quintus Flaccus <note>Horace</note>. It is praised by many and invoked by Clement of Alexandria and Eusebius in Book IX of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, and by Simplicius in Book VIII of Aristotle's *Physics*. The passage is also expressed by Latin poets, by T. Lucretius and P. Ovid. The former in Book IV of *On the Nature of Things*, at the end:
> Do you not see even drops of liquid falling onto rocks,
> In a long span of time, pierce through the rocks?

And in Book I:
> The fall of a dripping drop hollows out stones.

But Naso <note>Ovid</note>, in Book IV of *Letters from Pontus*:
> A drop hollows out the stone, a ring is worn away by use:
> And the hooked plowshare is worn down by the pressing earth.

As for what Isidore adds here: *What is harder than rock? What is softer than water?* The poet Ovid expressed the same thing elsewhere:
> What is more hard than rock? What is softer than a wave?
> Yet hard rocks are hollowed out by soft water.

And Isidore himself in Book III, Epistle 284: *But that, he says, I would wish to be persuaded, which someone maintained: that waters smooth stones.* Tibullus in Book I, Elegy 4:
> Time itself wears away rocks with soft water.

And Plutarch in his commentary *On the Education of Children*: *Water drops hollow out a rock.* I have discussed the word *entelecheia* <gloss>actuality/fulfillment</gloss> in the definition of the soul at length in my *Tullian Questions*, Book IV, chapters 21, 22, and 23. 39. Pompey ordered some of the legions he already had in Italy to be led by the consuls from Brundusium to Epirus; they crossed immediately and safely to Dyrrachium. A barbarian king of the region, named Epidamnus, built a city on the seacoast and named it after himself. Dyrrachus, the son of his daughter and Neptune (as he is reputed to be), added a dockyard to it and named it Dyrrachium. When this Dyrrachus was at war with his brothers, Hercules—who was returning from Erythea—aided him in exchange for a portion of the territory. This is why the people of Dyrrachium claim Hercules as their founder, as he held a share of their land. They do not reject Dyrrachus, but they take more pride in Hercules, regarding him as a god. It is said that in this battle, Hercules accidentally killed Ionius, the son of Dyrrachus, and after burying the body, threw it into the sea so that it might bear his name.</meta>

The Corcyreans mingled their own colonists with them and thus it came to be considered a Greek port; but the Corcyreans changed its name, because they considered it unpropitious, and called it Epidamnus from the town just above it, and Thucydides gives it that name also. Nevertheless, the former name prevailed finally and it is now called Dyrrachium.

Then he took his departure in the early evening, leaving the bravest of his troops on the walls. These also sailed away after nightfall, with a favourable wind.

In the time of the emperor Theophilus, Scholasticius the door-keeper was chamberlain, and in the time of Michael, son of Theophilus, the patrician Damian was chamberlain and after him, in the same reign, Basil, the Christ-loving emperor, was chamberlain. In the time of Basil, the Christ-loving sovereign, there was no chamberlain during all his reign. In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Samonas was chamberlain, and after him, in the time of the same emperor, the patrician Constantine. In the time of Alexander the emperor, the patrician Barbatus was chamberlain; and in the time of Constantine, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Constantine, mentioned before in the time of the sovereign Leo, was chamberlain again; and in the time of the sovereign Romanus, the patrician Theophanes; and in the second reign of Constantine, the patrician Basil.

In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving and ever-memorable emperor, lived the late Ktenas, an aged cleric of great wealth, who was precentor of the New Church and was skilled in singing as was no other at that time. This same Ktenas besought the patrician Samonas, who was at that time chamberlain, to intercede for him with the emperor so that he might be made <term>protospatharius</term> <gloss>first sword-bearer, a high court rank</gloss> and wear the shirt and go in procession to the Lausiacus and take his seat as <term>protospatharius</term> and receive a stipend of one pound, and in respect of this remuneration might give the emperor forty pounds. But the emperor could not bring himself to do this, saying that it was out of his power, and "to the great disgrace of my imperial majesty if a cleric becomes <term>protospatharius</term>." On hearing this from the patrician Samonas, this same Ktenas added to the forty pounds a pair of ear-rings valued at ten pounds, and a silver table with animals on it in gold relief, also valued at ten pounds. And the emperor, besought by the request of the patrician Samonas, the chamberlain, took the forty pounds of gold and the pair of ear-rings and the table with its gold on silver relief work, so that the total gift of the same Ktenas amounted to sixty pounds. Then the emperor made him <term>protospatharius</term>, and he received a stipend on that occasion of one pound. After being honoured with the rank of <term>protospatharius</term> this same Ktenas lived two years and then died; and he received a stipend of one pound for each of the two years.

First, then, we do not have this statement in the four Gospels handed down to us, but in the *Gospel according to the Egyptians*. Furthermore, he seems to me to be ignorant, for he uses "anger" to hint at the male impulse, and "desire" at the female; when these have acted, repentance and shame follow. When, therefore, we no longer give in to anger or desire—which, having grown from habit and evil upbringing, overshadow and cover up the reason—but have cast off the haze from these, having been put to shame through repentance, and unite spirit and soul according to the obedience of the Word, then, as Paul says, "There is neither male nor female among you." For when this soul, which has been separated by its own configuration, distinguishes the male from the female, it is transformed into a unity, no longer being one or the other. But this noble fellow thinks, more like a <term>Platonist</term> <gloss>a follower of the philosophy of Plato</gloss>, that the soul, being divine from above, was feminized by desire and came down here into generation and corruption. He even forces Paul to say that generation consists of deception, through these words: "For I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve, your minds might be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ."

But the Lord clearly came for the sake of those who had been led astray. And they were not led astray from above into this generation here; for generation is a creation of the Almighty, who would never bring a soul down from better to worse. Rather, the Savior came to those who were led astray in name, that is, to us, who were corrupted by disobedience to the commandments, as we became lovers of pleasure. Perhaps the time of our first formation overtook us, and we reached out for the grace of marriage before the proper hour, and missed the mark. For "everyone who looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart," not having waited for the time of the will. The same person is in the Lord, and he judges then the desire that has taken hold of marriage. When, therefore, the Apostle says, "Put on the new man, who is created according to God," he speaks to us, who are molded by the will of the Almighty just as we were molded. He does not say that the "old man" refers to generation, but to the life lived in disobedience, before obedience.

<term>Cassianus</term> considers the "garments of skins" <note>a reference to Genesis 3:21</note> to be our bodies. Regarding these, and those who teach the same things as him, we shall show that they are led astray when we handle the interpretation of human generation firmly for those who need to be answered. For he says, "Those who are ruled by earthly things both marry and are given in marriage, but our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await a Savior." We have said this well, and we know it; for we ought to live as strangers and pilgrims. Let those who marry live as if they do not marry, those who acquire as if they do not acquire, those who beget children as if they are bringing mortals into the world, as those who are about to leave their possessions behind, and as those who are able to live without a wife if need be. Those who are separated by their possessions use them with thanksgiving through all things, and with greatness of mind.

And again, when he says, "It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of sexual immorality, let each man have his own wife," he explains it again, saying, "So that Satan does not tempt you." For he says this not to those who use marriage with self-control only for the sake of procreation, because of incontinence, but to those who desire to proceed even further than procreation, so that the adversary, by not yielding much, does not drive the desire into foreign pleasures. Perhaps he opposes those who live righteously out of jealousy and competes against them, wishing to draw them into his own rank, and he wishes to provide them with occasions for grievous self-control. Therefore, he reasonably says, "It is better to marry than to burn," so that the husband may render to the wife her due, and the wife to the husband, and that they may not defraud one another of the help given by God for generation.

"Whoever does not hate father, or mother, or wife, or children," they say, "cannot be my disciple." He does not command us to hate; for he says, "Honor your father and mother, so that it may be well with you." But he says, "Do not be led away by irrational impulses, nor be joined by political customs." For a household is not constituted of marriage, but cities are constituted of households, just as Paul said that those who are busy with marriage seek to please the world. Again, the Lord says, "Let not him who has married cast her away; and let not him who has not married, marry." He who has agreed to eunuchism for the sake of pleasing God, let him not marry.

This noble person <note>Cassianus</note> thinks in a more Platonic manner that the soul, being divine from above, was feminized by desire and came down here into generation and corruption. Straightway he forces Paul to say that generation is constituted out of deceit, through these words: "For I am afraid that, as the serpent deceived Eve, your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ."

The organ of pain is the mouth of the stomach. For this is what perceives the biting sensation during times of pain. As Galen says in the sixth book of his *Demonstrative* <note>original: ἀποδεικτικῆς</note> treatise: "For those who are grieving, no small amount of yellow bile flows down into the stomach, which causes them the biting sensation; and they do not stop being in pain or being bitten until they have vomited the bile." For the biting sensation occurs to them beneath the cartilage in the middle of the chest, which is called the <term>xiphoid</term> <gloss>sword-shaped</gloss> process; but the heart lies much higher up. For the stomach is lower than the diaphragm, while the heart is higher. The ancients, however, usually call both the heart and the mouth of the stomach "the heart," as Hippocrates and Thucydides do in his description of the plague, saying: "And when it settled upon the heart, it turned it about, and there were purgings of bile, all those which have been named by physicians." For it is the mouth of the stomach that turns about and is forced to vomit, not the internal organ that is the heart.

The organ of pain is the orifice of the stomach. For this is what feels the biting sensation during times of pain. As Galen says in the sixth book of his *Demonstrative Treatise* as follows: "In those who are grieving, no small amount of yellow bile flows down into the stomach, which causes them the biting sensation, and they do not cease grieving and feeling that bite until they vomit up the bile." For the biting sensation occurs for them below the cartilage located in the middle of the chest, which is called the xiphoid process <note>original: ξιφοειδής (xiphoidēs). Referring to the lower portion of the sternum.</note>, but the heart lies much higher up. For the stomach is lower than the diaphragm, while the heart is higher. The ancients commonly called both the heart and the orifice of the stomach the "heart," as Hippocrates and Thucydides do in his account of the plague, saying as follows: "And whenever it settled in the heart, it turned it and caused purgings of bile. I will only remark that in the swelling of the sound, it was necessary, during the time of the same note, to imperceptibly substitute a weak wind for a strong one, and for a stronger one, a weaker, and to simultaneously vary the movements of the lips, that is to say, to place them in their proper position for each wind.

When it was necessary to perform the soft passages, that is to say, to imitate an echo, one was obliged to make the lips advance over the edge of the Flute's hole and send a wind sufficient to form such a tone; but whose return, through an opening as small as that of its entry into the Flute, can only strike a small quantity of exterior air: which produces, as I have said above, what is called an echo.

The different tempos of slowness and movement were measured on the cylinder by means of a lever, one extremity of which, armed with a point, could, when one struck it, mark this same cylinder.

At the other arm of the lever was a spring, which caused the point to lift promptly.

The movement was released, which caused the cylinder to turn at a speed determined for all the airs.

At the same time, a person played the air one wished to measure on the Flute; another beat the measure on the end of the lever which pointed the cylinder, and the distance found between the points was the true measure of the airs one wished to note; one then subdivided the intervals into as many parts as the measure had beats.

I answered the man from Priene: "Mandraite, I conceive and share your enthusiasm; only the fanaticism of virtue and truth is not to be feared. Go! your account adds to the veneration I already held for the name of Thales. Your delirium is quite natural, and his is too. One does nothing great, one invents nothing sublime, if one does not have the measure of one's genius and the feeling of one's strengths. Thales is right to be jealous of his discovery; it is his property; it belongs to him more than the conquests of <term>Semiramis</term> <gloss>a legendary Assyrian queen known for her military campaigns and building projects</gloss> belonged to that woman. One must hold fast to the good action one has been capable of, to a strong and bold thought one has managed to produce. Modesty is the virtue of mediocrity. Well! why not do oneself justice, and claim it for oneself as for others?"

We parted at Myus, a small Ionian city, halfway from Priene to Miletus. It is there that the Meander, after so many detours, finally falls into the sea, and regrets not having made even more in such an agreeable region.

Fatigued by the weight of the heat, I went to take refuge in an old, half-open temple, because the <term>neocorus</term> <gloss>a temple warden or caretaker</gloss> was cleaning it at that moment. In the back of the sanctuary, I distinguished, not without difficulty because of the dim light, the seated statue of an old man, covered in a long, very dirty cloak. His shoulder was burdened with a dusty axe.

As soon as the blessed flame finished speaking its last word, the holy millstone began to rotate. It had not yet completed a single full turn before another circle enclosed it. Motion met motion, and song met song. It was a song that surpasses our Muses and our Sirens in those sweet pipes as much as the first light surpasses what it reflects. 

Just as two parallel and same-colored arcs turn through a delicate cloud when Juno commands her handmaid <note>the rainbow</note>, with the outer one born from the inner, like the speech of that wandering nymph <note>Echo</note> whom love consumed as the sun consumes vapors, making people here on earth presage <note>predict</note> because of the pact God made with Noah that the world would never again be flooded; so the two garlands of those eternal roses turned around us, and the outer matched the inner.

When the rejoicing and the other great festivity—both the singing and the flaming of light with light, joyful and gentle—simultaneously stopped at the same moment and by the same will, just as eyes that must close and open together at the pleasure that moves them, a voice stirred from the heart of one of the new lights. It made me turn toward it, just as a compass needle turns to the star <note>the North Star</note>.

As soon as the last word
The blessed flame ceased to speak;
The holy millstone began to rotate:
And it had not yet turned a full circle
Before another enclosed it with a circle;
And song joined to song, and motion to motion;
A song that surpasses our Muses,
Our Sirens, in those sweet pipes,
As much as the first light surpasses that which it reflects.
As two parallel and like-colored arches
Turn through a soft cloud,
When Juno commands her handmaid,
The outer one born from the inner,
In the manner of the speech of that wanderer
Whom love consumed, as the sun consumes vapors;
And they make people here foresee
Because of the covenant that God made with Noah,
That the world shall never again be flooded;
So did the two garlands of those eternal roses
Turn around us,
And the outer answered the inner.
When the dancing and the other great festivity,
Both of singing and of flaming,
Light with light, joyful and gentle,
Ceased together, at the same moment and by the same will;
Just as eyes that, moved by the pleasure that stirs them,
Must close and lift themselves together;
From the heart of one of the new lights
A voice moved; which made me appear like the needle to the star,
In turning toward its source:

<note>The commentator explains: Suspended in admiration; and looking into the sun: this is nothing other than being illuminated by divine grace, which enables one to look into the sun, that is, into the contemplation of the divinity. Nevertheless, he did not endure it for long; because if the eyes, that is, the acuity of the intellect, had endured the light for a longer time, he could have discerned the whole solar body, that is, he would have had true knowledge of the divine essence. But he did not have so powerful an eye. Nevertheless, for the little while that he did endure it, he saw the sparks and scintillations that were born from the solar body, in the form that they are born from a red-hot iron. The allegorical sense is that the purified soul can contemplate God, but not in a way that knows his essence; rather, it has knowledge of the sparks that come from the sun, that is, of the effects that proceed from God, since we know the cause through the effects, and not the effects through the cause. And that the sun had so much greater light that it seemed doubled signifies that theological contemplation illuminates the intellect much more than philosophy, because it is not without the infusion of the spirit, as you will see a little below.</note>

In all opinions and all arguments that approach the truth in human affairs, some falsehood arises. It does not arise because it proceeds naturally from the subject matter itself or from that form which gives it existence, but rather from the effort of those who favor the wicked seed out of a desire to corrupt the truth. That this is so can be seen, firstly, from those ancients who applied great care to the consideration of human affairs, and from the discord of opinions that existed between them, their predecessors, and their contemporaries.

**XL.** Virtue possesses the property of being of divine origin (1); for these three parts of it together constitute true virtue, and each of them is always found joined with the other two. And indeed, in prudence there is also fortitude, insofar as the mind labors and exerts itself in searching for the truth, and does not rest until it finds it; there is also temperance, as it is a wise thing to ignore certain things. For the Dorian harmony was named from the Dorians, who were its inventors; the Phrygian from the peoples who inhabited Phrygia; and the Lydian from those of Lydia, and so the others in order. It is very true that since each of them had in itself something proper in its song, and was accompanied by different numbers, they called some of them grave and severe; some bacchic and furious; some honest and religious, and some others they called lascivious and bellicose. Wherefore, in this respect, they took great care in matching such harmonies to the numbers, and this together with intent toward suitable subject matters, which they expressed in the oration or speech, according to their nature. Having then given consideration to all these things, they named their compositions according to the nature of the compound, as one might say, mournful modes, which are the elegies, for they contain sad and mournful subject matters. This can be seen expressly in those two volumes (besides the almost infinite others that are by other authors) which Ovid wrote after he was sent into exile by Augustus; and also from that which he writes in the Epistle of Sappho to Phaon, wishing to show that amorous things are mournful subject matters, and that they are suitable for the elegy, saying:

> Perhaps you also ask why my poems are alternating
> Songs, when I am more suited to lyric modes.
> My love must be lamented. The elegy is a mournful song.
> No lyre is suitable for my tears.

Horace made mention of these modes, saying:

> You always urge with mournful modes
> The taken-away Mystes.

And also Boethius in book 3 of the *Consolation of Philosophy*:

> Once, the Thracian poet, mourning
> The funeral of his wife,
> After he had, with mournful modes,
> Forced the woods to run,
> And the moving rivers to stand still;

Just as Cicero also commemorated them in the *Tusculan Disputations*, when (while making mention of the humble and depressed) he said: *These are sung with pressed and mournful modes, which bring sadness to entire theaters.* And in another place, making mention of the slow ones: *The same Roscius is accustomed to say that, as he aged, he would make the piper’s modes and the songs more slow and relaxed.*

Others they called lamentable modes, as can be seen in Apuleius, when he says: *And the sound of the wedding flute is changed into the querulous Lydian mode.* Some they then called sweet modes; as the same Horace shows us in another place, when he says:

> Skilled in the cithara.

## *Chirotheca marina. Sarong tangan laut.* <gloss>Sea glove.</gloss>

This is also a spongy plant, extending itself widely from a narrow beginning into many finger-like shapes, which are narrow and joined at the bottom, and broad and hollowed out with an opening at the top; it is furthermore concave, and of two forms.

The first bears many round fingers, some of which are no thicker than a thumb, bearing a narrow and round little hole at the top.

Others have the thickness of a child's arm, and are widely opened like an intestine, and are furthermore concave inside like a crater or like the cut-off fingers of woolen gloves; they are smoother inside than outside, with a substance like wool and sponge mixed together, of a yellowish-ash color like other sponges.

Without any notable root, it sits upon various rocks, and in the cavities of the fingers, small fish and shrimp reside, swimming in and out.

The second form bears longer and sharper fingers at the top, being very prickly on the outside, but the prickles are not hard; it is of a coarser and wider texture than the previous one, approaching the spongy rather than the woody nature. The fingers are also concave and smooth inside, in which similar small fish and shrimp play. They are bundles over a foot high, with many fingers grown together, which sit upon a vile root.

*Name.* In Latin *Chirotheca marina* <gloss>Sea glove</gloss>; in Malay *Sarong tangan laut* <gloss>Sea glove</gloss>.

*Location and Use.* These plants serve no use, but like the previous ones, they are kept as rare objects.

In this *Chirotheca marina* lives a small fish of a peculiar nature and form, and it is a species of *Ican batu* <gloss>stone fish</gloss>, of a flat and thin shape, red in color with blackish rings, and this fish is also found under hollow rocks; however, it inhabits these fingers, but it is not certain whether it forms them. It pecks at people like a hen if they approach too closely, but it does not cause pain.

# CHAPTER THIRTY-TWO.

## *Barba marina.* <gloss>Sea beard.</gloss>

Finally, two marine plants follow, which also agree with the <term>Zoophyta</term> <gloss>plant-animals</gloss>, but they approach the rocky nature more closely, and therefore belong in this book.

First. *Barba marina* <gloss>Sea beard</gloss> seems to be a bundle of white or gray, firm bristles, in the shape of a brush. Below, they are located upon a knotted root, which nearly bears the shape of a scrotum, and is composed of rocky grains. The bristles sit upon these, and the entire brush is over a span long, pointed at the top like a cone, smooth on the outside and slightly angular, covered with a thin substance like the linen cloth called *Tshjavoni*, under which many little eyes or small holes are seen. Once this rocky veil is removed, those white or gray bristles appear, of the thickness of horsehair, rough and sharp, especially around the lower part, where they also cause some injury. And then the hairs of that cone open themselves, and form an unkempt beard, which breaks easily upon touching, and the fragments cling to the skin with a slight itching. The rest of the cone furthermore adheres to itself like a head of hair, tangled by filth and nits. Under water, it seems to live through the mucous veil, but above water, no sign of life or sense is detected in it, except for a slight itching of the skin.

*Name.* In Latin *Barba marina* <gloss>Sea beard</gloss>; in Malay it could be called *Djangot* or *Barba laut* <gloss>Sea beard</gloss>. By others it is also called *Penicillus marinus* <gloss>Sea paintbrush</gloss>, for a species of this is also found in the Mediterranean Sea. In these lands, it rarely appears, as it is only sometimes pulled up by fishermen's hooks that have been lowered deep into the sea. It also has no known use thus far, for the fishermen consider it a harmful product, and therefore they immediately throw it back into the sea.

Finally, two marine plants follow, which also agree with the <term>Zoophyta</term> <gloss>animal-plants</gloss>, but approach more closely to the stony nature, and therefore belong to this book.

Under water, it seems to live through the mucous mist, but above water, no sign of life or sense is detected in it, except for a slight itching of the skin.

It is then enough to know that the Gospel which bears the name of Mark, just like the three others, is a product of the Holy Spirit, who has guided the hand and pen of this Evangelist. This alone is what constitutes the excellence of the Holy Books, and what gives them the authority they possess to subject our faith to themselves, and not the names of their authors, however famous they may have been in the Church. With regard to the language in which Mark wrote, the earliest antiquity has never doubted, nor said otherwise, than that it was Greek. In the following centuries there were some who wished to attribute that honor to Latin; and since the heart often has some tender interests that entangle the mind in its party, one has found, after that pleasant dream, people who have wanted to make a history of it and publish it as truth.

Since it is believable that Mark did not write his Gospel until that of Matthew, and probably that of Luke, had already seen the light, he did not, like the first two, recount the genealogy of Jesus Christ: what they had written was sufficient to show that Jesus, the son of Mary, truly had sprung from David, according to the prophecies one sees of this in the Prophets. Therefore, Mark began the history of the Gospel differently than the first two Evangelists, and he wished to let it follow immediately upon the prophecy of Malachi, which closes the <column-break/> Testament, as if to link it together with the book of that Prophet. Malachi had ended his prophecy thus:
> *Behold, I send you the Prophet Elijah, before that great and terrible day of the LORD shall come. And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers: lest I come, and smite the earth with a curse.*

These words clearly signify John the Baptist; upon this, Mark comes five hundred years after Malachi, and, linking the fulfillment to the prophecy, he makes it the beginning of his Gospel.
> *The beginning, he says, of the Gospel of Jesus Christ the Son of God; as it is written in the Prophets, Behold, I send my messenger before your face.*

He continues by speaking in a few words of John the Baptist, and then proceeds, like Matthew and Luke, to the baptism of Jesus Christ. Furthermore, he keeps almost the same order as the first up to the very end, and it appears as if he had done nothing but shorten him, whether such was indeed his intention in many places, to expand on some others a little more, or that the Holy Spirit, who illuminated him with the same understanding as Matthew, often made him agree with the same one, as Micah did formerly with Isaiah. But one need not for that reason view Mark as a mere abridger of Matthew, since that does not seem exalted enough for an inspired writer, who is an original narrator himself; besides which, this opinion is clearly contradicted by an accurate comparison of one Gospel with the other.

The tea flower’s brilliance rivals cinnabar. The osmanthus releases a fragrance like golden grain. Then there is the lofty elegance of the willow and the phoenix tree, and the rugged strength of the towering pine and ancient cypress. Applying these to painting is enough to awaken a person’s free spirit, capture the essence of creation, and stir the mind. Examining the history of the art, the painting of flowers and birds in the Tang dynasty began with the feathered creature studies of Xue Ji and Bian Luan. By the time of Liang Guang, Yu Xi, Diao Guang, Zhou Huang, Guo Qianhui, and Qianyou, all were famous for their flower and bird works. During the Five Dynasties period, Teng Changyou, Zhong Yin, and the father-son pair Huang Quan arose in succession. For instance, Changyou’s inner spirit and brushwork were not borrowed from teachers. Zhong Yin followed the methods of the Guo brothers. Huang Quan was adept at gathering the strengths of various masters: for flowers, he studied Changyou; for birds, he studied Diao Guang. Regarding dragons, cranes, trees, and rocks, each had their own sources. Later, his sons Jubao and Jucai were able to continue their family tradition. Thus, their fame carried through their own age and their methods were passed down through the ages; this is truly no empty claim. Therefore, the painting methods at the beginning of the Song dynasty took the Huang family as the definitive standard.

During the Song period, Xu Xi emerged to create a unique departure from old methods. He was truly without equal in the past and unmatched by those who followed. Although he stood between the styles of Huang Quan and Zhao Chang, his divine subtlety surpassed them alone. His descendants, Chongsi and Chongju, carried on the family study and were truly able to follow in their ancestor’s footsteps. Zhao Chang’s application of color was exceptionally refined. He did not only capture their likeness, but was also able to transmit their spirit directly. Some say that Xu Xi lived before or after Huang Quan and Zhao Chang. Yet, they say Huang Quan’s painting had spirit but lacked subtlety, while Zhao Chang’s painting had subtlety but lacked spirit. Perhaps this is what they meant. Therefore, Yi Yuanji, who initially worked in the art of painting, saw Zhao Chang’s works and said, "The world does not lack talent. One must cast off old habits and transcend the ancients to reach the peak of subtlety." Qiu Qingyu initially studied under Zhao Chang, but in his later years surpassed him and directly followed the style of Xu Xi. Cui Bai, Cui Ke, along with Ai Xuan, Ding Kuang, Ge Shouchang, and Wu Yuanyu, were all summoned to the Imperial Painting Academy, and their reputations were great.

Observe the court officials and those close to the ruler to see who is greedy and who is upright. Distinguish the noble men from the petty men among the hosts and attendants. Once we understand the situation, we can tailor our strategies accordingly to ensure our success.

Indeed, among the matters of the three armies, none is more critical than the role of the <term>xingren</term> <gloss>emissary/agent</gloss>. Among the secrets of the three armies, none is more confidential than the plans of these emissaries. If the strategies of the emissaries are leaked before they are launched, all those who informed on them must be executed. On the day a strategy is launched, the rough drafts must be scraped clean and the notes burned.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>Why is this? The merit of the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss> is inconceivable. The venerable <term>Subhuti</term> <gloss>Good Existence</gloss> said to the Buddha: "By what cause and condition is the nature of the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> considered inexhaustible and remote?"

The profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> knows that the Buddhas of the three times <gloss>past, present, and future</gloss> all study the <term>Prajnaparamita</term> to reach ultimate perfection, realize the <term>Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi</term> <gloss>unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment</gloss>, and proclaim and reveal it to all sentient beings. This <term>Prajnaparamita</term> is like the great void <gloss>empty space</gloss>; because it cannot be exhausted, those who wish to exhaust the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> are like those who wish to exhaust the limits of empty space. For this reason, Subhuti, the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> is spoken of as inexhaustible. Because it is inexhaustible, it is called immeasurable.

At that time, Subhuti said to the Buddha: "Why is the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> spoken of as inexhaustible?"

The Buddha told Subhuti: "The profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> is like empty space, because it cannot be exhausted."

The venerable Subhuti said again to the Buddha: "How does a <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term> <gloss>great enlightened being</gloss> study the <term>Prajnaparamita</term>?"

The Buddha told Subhuti: "The <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term> contemplates that all forms, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousnesses are inexhaustible. Thus, they cultivate the <term>Prajnaparamita</term>. They should contemplate that ignorance, and even up to old age and death, are all inexhaustible. Thus, they cultivate the <term>Prajnaparamita</term>. In this way, Subhuti, the <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term>..."

<summary>The Buddha explains to Subhuti that the Prajnaparamita is inexhaustible like empty space, and that Bodhisattvas must contemplate all phenomena and conditions—from the five aggregates to the cycle of dependent origination—as inexhaustible to truly practice this wisdom.</summary>

The robe does not lose its status if it is within water, fruit trees, or if there are few people, if it is placed in water, or at night. Regarding the <term>pravāraṇā</term> <gloss>conclusion of the rains retreat</gloss> enclosure, there are fifteen types: 
1. The Sangha’s absence. 
2. Trees and fruit trees that are connected; if someone guards them and prohibits entry, it is an internal barrier. 
3. The barrier of sparse trees at a distance of ten finger-widths. 
4. Fruit-bearing areas. 
5. Areas where practice is not yet established. 
6. Areas where practitioners walk, return, or overlap. 
7. Wood boundaries. 
8. Obstruction boundaries. 
9. Room boundaries. 
10. Housing boundaries. 
11. (Missing/Unclear)
12. Island boundaries (where there are lakes, rivers, or streams). 
13. Well boundaries. 
14. Secret paths. 
15. Areas where there are many people, small seas, or southern sands and stones. 

<term>Pura</term> <gloss>City/Town</gloss> and <term>Kaṭhina</term> <gloss>robe-offering</gloss>—these two boundaries are established by name.

If the sun displays a yellow vertical pillar, the sovereign remains firm, and the minister is upright. If a blue-red vertical pillar appears, the minister is setting themselves up as an independent authority.
If the sun has a red vertical pillar in the center with blue on the outside, and the one setting themselves up independently does not succeed, it means the one with a yellow-white, lustrous appearance will succeed.
Blue and red vapors shaped like two lines intersecting, appearing above, below, or to the sides of the sun, are called "Intersecting Lecherousness" <term>original: jiao jiao yin (交交淫)</term>. This vapor signifies the presence of licentious conduct. If there are intersecting red clouds beside the sun, soldiers will arrive beneath it.
If there are two vapors on either side of the sun that intersect, penetrate, or face back-to-back, all these signify the rise of a great war throughout the realm, and also internal rebellion with a military that is not harmonious. It is also said that if there are intersecting vapors beside the sun, the side towards which the intersection points will be victorious.

Various vapors that appear like the character for "mouth" <term>original: kou (口)</term> at the edge of the sun are called "Sun Mouths" <term>original: ri kou (日口)</term>. One or two "mouths" signify treachery and harm. Three, four, or five "mouths" signify that princes and dukes are plotting to establish their own rule.

If there is a yellow straight pillar by the sun, a minister will declare himself a ruler. If there are blue and red straight pillars, the ministers will declare themselves independent.

If the straight pillar is red in the middle and blue on the outside, the one who declares independence will not succeed. If the pillar is yellow and white with a lustrous appearance, the attempt will succeed.

If blue and red vapors appear in a shape like two straight lines intersecting above, below, or to the sides of the sun, this is called a **Cross-Intersection** <term>original: *Jiaojiao* (交交)</term>, which signifies licentious behavior. If there is cross-shaped red cloud beside the sun, it signifies that troops are positioned beneath it.

If two vapors cross, penetrate, or face back-to-back on either side of the sun, all of these signify that a great war will arise across the land. It also signifies internal chaos and disharmony within the army. Another interpretation is that if there is a cross by the sun, the side that attacks from the direction of the crossing will be victorious.

If various vapors form a shape like the character for "mouth" <term>original: *kou* (口)</term> at the edge of the sun, it is called a **Sun-Mouth** <term>original: *Rikou* (日口)</term>. If there is one or two "mouths," it signifies treacherous, evil, and harmful people. If there are three, four, or five "mouths," it signifies that princes and nobles are plotting to claim the throne.

### Gate Pressing <gloss>Men-Po</gloss>

Gate <gloss>... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ...</gloss>
If the Gate is forced, auspicious matters will not be realized. If an ominous Gate is forced, the disaster is even more severe.

Suppose the Open Gate <gloss>Metal</gloss> arrives at the Third Palace <gloss>Wood</gloss> or the Fourth Palace <gloss>Wood</gloss>; the Rest Gate <gloss>Water</gloss> arrives at the Ninth Palace <gloss>Fire</gloss>; the Life Gate <gloss>Earth</gloss> arrives at the First Palace <gloss>Water</gloss>; the View Gate <gloss>Fire</gloss> arrives at the Sixth Palace <gloss>Metal</gloss> or the Seventh Palace <gloss>Metal</gloss>. This is considered an auspicious Gate; if it is forced, then auspicious matters will not be realized.

Suppose the Hurt Gate <gloss>Wood</gloss> arrives at the Eighth Palace <gloss>Earth</gloss> or the Second Palace <gloss>Earth</gloss>; the Death Gate <gloss>Earth</gloss> arrives at the First Palace <gloss>Water</gloss>; the Fear Gate <gloss>Metal</gloss> arrives at the Third Palace <gloss>Wood</gloss>. This is considered an ominous Gate; if it is forced, the ominous disaster is even more severe.

If there is a <term>Jamat</term> <gloss>assembly/group</gloss> in the fifteenth house, one should derive the result from its roots. ॥ १९ ॥ If the figures in the <term>Kharij</term> <gloss>Outgoing</gloss> and <term>Vishva-shakra</term> <gloss>World-conqueror</gloss> positions are auspicious, they grant success in an <term>Nirgam</term> <gloss>Outgoing</gloss> question. If the <term>Dakhil</term> <gloss>Incoming</gloss> figures are auspicious, they grant success just as in an <term>Agam</term> <gloss>Incoming</gloss> question. ॥ २० ॥ If the <term>Savite</term> <gloss>Fixed/Stable</gloss> figures are auspicious, they likewise grant success for stable tasks. If they are of medium strength, there is moderate success, and if weak, there is only minor success. ॥ २१ ॥ The result of the reversal is auspicious where it was previously auspicious, as before. One should deliberate and declare the entirety of the question and its segments as previously described. ॥ २२ ॥ <term>Mushti</term> <gloss>fist/closed hand</gloss>, <term>Muka</term> <gloss>silent</gloss>, <term>Sharu</term> <gloss>beginning</gloss>, and <term>Avadhi-prashna-hara</term> <gloss>time-limit question-destroyer</gloss>—these are successful without <term>Inkilab</term> <gloss>Transition</gloss>; therefore, it does not apply to them. ॥ २३ ॥ Thus, the determination for all houses has been stated in general terms. Now, I shall describe the specific outcomes for each respective house. ॥ २४ ॥

**Commentary—** Now, the purpose of <term>Inkilab</term> <gloss>Transition</gloss> is explained. It is said that for a question arising from <term>Inkilab</term> at this time, if there is a <term>Jamat</term> <gloss>assembly</gloss> in the fifteenth house, one should predict the outcome based on its roots, the thirteenth and fourteenth houses. ॥ १९ ॥ The rule is as follows: if the figures in the thirteenth and fourteenth houses are <term>Kharij</term> <gloss>Outgoing</gloss> and auspicious, they grant success to an <term>Nirgam</term> <gloss>Outgoing</gloss> question. If they are <term>Dakhil</term> <gloss>Incoming</gloss> and auspicious, they grant success to an <term>Agam</term> <gloss>Incoming</gloss> question.

Now I shall explain the results derived from the **Inversion** <term>Inkilab</term> and the question arising from it. If the figures are of medium strength, there is moderate success; if they are weak, the success is minimal. ॥ २१ ॥ Success by inversion happens where auspicious and other figures are present, as described before. One should carefully explain the entire segment of the question just as before. ॥ २२ ॥ Questions regarding hidden objects held in the fist, mute inquiries, and specific time-bound questions are successful without using the **Inversion** <term>Inkilab</term>; therefore, it is not applied to these. ॥ २३ ॥ Thus, the general rules for all houses have been stated. Now, I shall explain the specificities of each individual house. ॥ २४ ॥

**Commentary—** Now, we describe the purpose of the **Inversion** <term>Inkilab</term>. If the **Incoming** <term>Dakhil</term> figures are auspicious, they provide success for an **Incoming** question.

Just as light is the cause of the perception of form, so also is the external object <note>meaning the sensory stimulus</note> the cause of the modification of the mind. Just as fire is to that which is to be cooked. The knowledge of smoke is the cause of the knowledge of fire. The practice of the limbs of yoga is the cause of the attainment of discriminative realization. 

That same practice is the cause of separation from impurity. The cause of differentiation is like the goldsmith for gold. Thus, ignorance (<term>avidyā</term>) is the cause of delusion regarding the idea of a woman, and aversion (<term>dveṣa</term>) is the cause of suffering.

<column-break/>

Whether through the sense organs or on its own, the processing and manifestation of an object is like light for the perception of form. It is the cause of the modification of the mind. Just as, for a focused mind, upon hearing the fifth note played on a lute, someone with opened eyes <note>original: "unmīlitākṣasya"</note> might see the nymph Pramlocā, who is endowed with beauty, radiance, and youth, and thus abandon their concentration and have their mind attached to her. Regarding this very thing, it provides an example: just as fire is the cause of the transformation <note>original: "vikāra"</note> of that which is to be cooked—such as rice—characterized by the loosening of the combination of the parts of what was a difficult-to-penetrate structure. 

The knowledge of smoke is the cause of the perception of fire, which already exists as an object. That which is known is "knowledge," and that which is fire is also "knowledge"—therefore, the "knowledge of fire" is the knowledge of that <note>the fire itself</note>. This is what is meant: the fire, which is already present and is the object to be known, serves as the cause of the perception because it acts as the cause of that knowledge. 

There is a natural attainment of the effect by causes that are not obstructed; a deviation from this—non-attainment—is caused by some obstacle. Just as there is an obstruction by a dam for water that has a natural tendency to flow downward, so too here, the natural capacity of the <term>buddhi-sattva</term> <gloss>the intellect, which is characterized by clarity and illumination</gloss>, is to produce discriminative realization. That does not occur due to some obstruction caused by merit/demerit or darkness (<term>tamas</term>). Upon the removal of that obstruction through merit or the practice of the limbs of yoga, it attains that capacity to produce it, as it is by nature of unobstructed function. As it will say: "The cause is not the motivator of the primary causes, but rather it removes the barrier, just as a farmer."

Thus, the "cause of attainment" has been described in relation to the effect characterized by discriminative realization. In relation to the secondary effect, it is the "cause of separation," as it says: "cause of separation." 

It describes the "cause of differentiation": the goldsmith is the cause of differentiation for gold. For gold, which is identical to and different from bracelets, earrings, and armlets—being different from the bracelet in terms of the intention to differentiate, and non-different from the bracelet in terms of the intention of its essence—the difference from the earring is [caused by the goldsmith]. Thus, the goldsmith who makes the bracelet is the cause of the differentiation, making it something other than the gold which is identical to the earring. Although fire is also the cause of the differentiation of that which is to be cooked, because the essence (<term>dharmin</term>) and its properties (<term>dharma</term>)—such as the state of being unhusked rice or cooked rice—are not distinguished by the intention of difference, and because the essence persists even when the properties arise and pass away, it is not possible to speak of its difference. Therefore, it is said to be only the cause of modification, so there is no confusion. Nor should the difference in structure be explained as the cause of the difference of the essence. This would make the example of the goldsmith inconsistent. Having posited the external cause of differentiation, it illustrates the internal one: "Thus, for one..." Ignorance is the knowledge that "this maiden is desirable," etc. Due to the association with that delusion, the idea of a woman...

[The manifestation of an object], either through the sense organs or on its own, is the transformation of the mind. Its cause is like light to form. It is the cause of the modification of the mind toward an external object. For example, when a person with a composed mind hears the fifth note played on a <term>vallakī</term> <gloss>lute</gloss>, they open their eyes and see an <term>apsaras</term> <gloss>celestial nymph</gloss>, like Pramlocā, who is adorned with natural beauty and youth; their mind, abandoning <term>samādhi</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss>, becomes attached to her. Here, it provides an illustration: **"Just as fire is to that which is to be cooked,"** such as rice, which is the cause of the transformation—specifically, the loosening of the cohesion of the hard components. The knowledge of smoke is the cause of the perception of fire for an object that is already present. That which is known is "knowledge," and that which is fire is "knowledge"; thus, it is the "knowledge of fire." This is what is meant: that the fire, which is the object of knowledge and is already present, is the cause because it is the ground of the perception. The attainment of the action of an effect from causes that are independent is natural; an exception to this—a non-attainment—arises from somewhere. Just as water, which has the nature of flowing downward, is obstructed by a dam, so too here, the <term>buddhisattva</term> <gloss>the essence of the intellect</gloss>, which is characterized by happiness and illumination, has the natural capacity to generate discriminative realization. That capacity does not occur due to some obstruction—either from <term>dharma</term> <gloss>merit</gloss> or from darkness (<term>tamas</term>). Through the removal of that, by the practice of the limbs of yoga, it attains the capacity to generate it because its nature is to function without obstruction. As it will say: "The cause is not the motivator of the primary causes; rather, it is the removal of the barrier, like a farmer."

Thus, the cause of attainment has been stated with regard to the effect characterized by discriminative realization. Regarding the secondary effect, it says it is the "cause of separation." It states the "cause of differentiation": just as a goldsmith is to gold. Gold is different from bracelets, earrings, etc., if one wishes to emphasize the distinction; or it is non-different from the bracelets, etc., if one wishes to emphasize the non-distinction. Thus, the goldsmith, by making something different from the gold that was previously indistinguishable from the earring, is the cause of differentiation. Even though fire is the cause of the differentiation of that which is to be cooked, because the substratum persists—the <term>dharmin</term> <gloss>the subject or substance</gloss> remains while its attributes, like "being a grain of rice" or "being a boiled grain," arise and pass away—one cannot speak of it as being different. Therefore, it is said to be the cause of mere modification, so there is no confusion. It should not be explained that a change in form is the cause of the substratum's differentiation; that would be inconsistent with the example of the goldsmith. Having presented the external cause of differentiation, it illustrates the internal one: "Similarly, in the case of one..." <term>Avidyā</term> is the knowledge that "this is a desirable maiden," etc. Due to that delusion, the perception of the woman...

His students asked Rabbi Akiva: "Our teacher, why is it written, 'Sanctify to Me every firstborn' <note>Exodus 13:2</note>? Is the Holy One, blessed be He, a firstborn?" He said: "Sanctify to Me every firstborn" means nothing other than in holiness, and it is named after Israel, as it is written, "My son, My firstborn, Israel" <note>Exodus 4:22</note>. As if it were possible to say, He was with them at the time of their servitude. And this is what is written, "You shall surely send away the mother, etc." <note>Deuteronomy 22:7</note>. And it does not say, "You shall surely send away the father," but "You shall surely send away the mother"—in honor of those who are called the world, as it is written, "The mother is the firstborn" <note>a reference to the mystical status of the Mother/Binah</note>. And others say: "Firstborn of the firstborn," and it is this that is called <term>Atzeret</term> <gloss>the concluding festival of Shavuot</gloss>, which is called "mother," as it is written, "For you shall call Binah a mother" <note>Proverbs 2:3</note>. And what is "And you shall take the sons for yourself"? Rabbi Rechumai said: Those sons that she raised. And what are they? The seven days of Tabernacles, and these are the days of the week, which are seven. Is there a difference between them? For they are more in holiness, as it is written concerning them, "A holy convocation" <note>Leviticus 23:7</note>. And this is therefore <term>Atzeret</term>, for it is a holy convocation. Is it not? No, but this is <term>A-H-W-H</term> <note>a mystical permutation of the Divine Name</note>, as it is written, "On the first day a holy convocation, and on the seventh day a holy convocation." He said: Why is there another <term>Atzeret</term>? Because on it the Torah was given to Israel. And when the Torah was created in the beginning, the Holy One, blessed be He, was ruler in His world with it alone, as it is written, "The beginning of wisdom" <note>Proverbs 4:7</note>. He said: Since it is so, let your holiness be for you alone. And what is it? Tabernacles. He said: A house, as it is written, "Through wisdom a house is built" <note>Proverbs 24:3</note>. And from where do we know that Tabernacles is a house? As it is written, "And Jacob journeyed to Sukkot and built himself a house" <note>Genesis 33:17</note>.

His students asked Rabbi Akiva: "Our master, what is meant by 'Sanctify to Me every firstborn' <note>Exodus 13:2</note>? Is the Holy One, blessed be He, a firstborn?" No, but this is <term>YHWH</term> <gloss>the Tetragrammaton</gloss>, as it is written: "On the first day shall be a holy convocation, and on the seventh day a holy convocation" <note>Leviticus 23:35-36</note>. He said: Since that is so, may your holiness be for you alone. And what is this? Sukkot. He said: A house, as it is written: "Through wisdom a house is built" <note>Proverbs 24:3</note>. It is the established custom for the Rabbi to arrange the divorce document <term>Get</term> <gloss>religious divorce decree</gloss>. He turns the pages and sends the husband and the witnesses outside. He also gives the husband the white paper prepared for the writing of the document, as well as the reed pen, the ink, and the knife with which the scribe will sharpen the writing implement. The Rabbi instructs the husband to say to the scribe in these words: "Write, sign, and acquire [ownership] on my behalf and on behalf of my wife, so-and-so, daughter of so-and-so. I hereby give as a complete gift this document as a fundamental, lasting mystery for the needs of the divorce." He commands him to write and sign it as a complete mystery. The scribe acquires everything through the act of pulling <term>meshikah</term> <gloss>a formal mode of acquisition by taking possession</gloss> and holds them as a complete mystery. The intention is that he shall write and sign it truly as an agent of the husband. It is good for the husband to return and say to the scribe and the witnesses at the time of the divorce that it is a complete mystery before them.

I have found it written in the books that the angel appointed over dreams is <term>Gabriel</term>, and he is in charge of all matters concerning dreams and everything a person sees in their dream. Therefore, a person must be very careful not to see vain dreams and not to occupy themselves with idle things before sleeping, so that evil thoughts do not come to them in their dream. Furthermore, a person must recite the <term>Kriat Shema</term> <gloss>the Shema prayer</gloss> upon their bed with great concentration, so that the angels may protect them from all harm, from all bad dreams, and from all evil thoughts. 

I have also found it written that whoever wishes to know something in their dream should fast for one day, immerse in pure water, wear clean clothes, and pray a pure and clear prayer, requesting that the blessed Name <note>referring to God</note> reveal to them the matter they wish to know. Then, they should go to sleep in purity and holiness, and with the help of the blessed Name, they will see what they seek in their dream. 

A person must also be careful not to tell their dream to just anyone, but only to a trusted friend or a sage who knows how to interpret dreams properly, so that the dream does not manifest for evil, God forbid, for the dream follows the mouth <note>a Talmudic principle that the interpretation of a dream dictates its outcome</note>. Therefore, one must be very careful with their words and thoughts.

I have also found it written that there are dreams that come from the blessed Name, there are dreams that come from <term>Satan</term> <gloss>the Accuser/Adversary</gloss>, and there are dreams that come from a person's own thoughts. Therefore, a person must be wise and distinguish between one dream and another. Whoever wishes to know if the dream is from the blessed Name should check if the dream is a good thing and if it is something that brings the person to the fear of Heaven and the service of the blessed Name. If it is so, then it is a good dream from the blessed Name. If it is an evil thing or something that leads the person to sin or to sadness, then it is a dream from <term>Satan</term>, and the person must distance themselves from it and not pay any attention to it at all.

Furthermore, a person must always pray to the blessed Name that He may protect them from every bad dream and every evil thought, and that He may merit them to see good dreams that bring tidings of good for them and for all of Israel. Amen and amen.
