# The Portion of Toldot, The Written Torah
## This Is His Name By Which They Call Him, The Source of Blessings

### The Candle of the Commandment

<margin></margin>
"And Isaac sowed in that land, and found in the same year a hundredfold; and the Lord blessed him." <note>Genesis 26:12</note> The sages of blessed memory said: it was an estimation. Rashi brings in his commentary: "A hundredfold" means that people assessed how much it was fit to produce, and it produced a hundredfold. And our rabbis of blessed memory said: this assessment was for the sake of the tithes.
</margin>

Behold, the Patriarchs fulfilled the entire Torah, and the Torah detailed this measure in its specific commandments that are practiced, as we found with Abraham our father, who "gave him a tithe of all" <note>Genesis 14:20</note>. And here with Isaac, and likewise with Jacob, who said "and of all that Thou shalt give me I will surely tithe it unto Thee" <note>Genesis 28:22</note>. And Jacob our father tithed even from human souls, as our sages of blessed memory said: there were fourteen tribes, including Ephraim and Manasseh. They were separated for the mothers, who were themselves holy. Ten remained and were separated for the Levites to be holy to the Lord. Thus, the Patriarchs fulfilled the commandment of the tithe with all their hearts, and with all their souls, and with all their might. "With all their might" is taken literally: a tithe of everything, including a tithe of money. And "with all their souls": this refers to Jacob, who tithed from the souls of his sons. And "with all their hearts": this belongs to the <term>Terumah Gedolah</term> <gloss>Great Offering</gloss>, which has no fixed measure except according to the generosity of one's heart. And the <term>Terumat HaShem</term> <gloss>Offering of God</gloss> came. Our sages of blessed memory said: a generous eye is one-fortieth; a mediocre one is one-fiftieth; an evil eye is one-sixtieth. And everything is alluded to in the verse: "and he gave him a tithe of all." It would have been sufficient to say "and he gave a tithe," but "of all" alludes to the <term>Terumah Gedolah</term>, because the <term>Terumat Ma'aser</term> <gloss>Tithe Offering</gloss> is included in the tithe, as I shall explain later, for he gave the tithe to Melchizedek, and also the <term>Terumat Ma'aser</term>. And behold, our sages of blessed memory say one-fiftieth, which is a mediocre eye, the one who gives one out of fifty. But Abraham, the pious one, gave ten out of fifty in order to give from them a <term>Terumah Gedolah</term>, for by removing ten out of fifty, forty remained—that is to say, he gave one part out of four for the <term>Terumah Gedolah</term>. And even though the way of the mediocre is one in fifty, if he took <term>Terumah Gedolah</term>, he removed ten out of fifty, and afterwards separated one for the <term>Terumah Gedolah</term>, for he was generous of heart. And regarding the matter of <term>Terumah Gedolah</term>, it seems one can answer what was said, "this assessment was for the tithes." But this is difficult, for we learned in the Mishnah: "Do not tithe by assessment." Yet Isaac our father was cautious and tithed, and the assessment was for the <term>Terumah Gedolah</term>, as we learned in Tractate Terumot, chapter 1: "One does not separate offerings by sight, nor by weight, nor by counting," even though the sages gave a measure as stated above—a good eye, etc. Nevertheless, it is called "by assessment," and we derive this from what is written: "And your contribution shall be reckoned unto you," <note>Numbers 18:27</note>—"reckoned" means as an assessment. And even though it is written regarding the <term>Terumat Ma'aser</term>, if it is not relevant to <term>Terumat Ma'aser</term>, since the Torah gave a measure and it is necessary to measure, apply it to the <term>Terumah Gedolah</term>.

However, if you examine it well, it implies that the assessment was for all the tithes, for this assessment was before the <term>Ma'amar</term> <gloss>statement</gloss> that they said, "The field, how much is it fit to produce, etc." It seems certain that at the time of the separation of the tithe, he would measure to separate the tithe. And the assessment that was before the sprouting of the produce—the piety of the law comes upon them, for the law is that one is not obligated until the completion of the work and after one sees the face of the house <note>i.e., the house where the produce is brought</note>. And what he eats—he acts with complete piety regarding the tithe. Isaac wanted to be stringent, and therefore he would assess, etc., to separate even from what is eaten <unclear>by mistake</unclear>. This rule: "Do not tithe by assessment" was only said regarding the obligation of the tithe, but this was a stringency from Isaac our father. And since this verse speaks of the commandment of the tithe, therefore it says "and the Lord blessed him." And as it is written in Malachi: "Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, etc., and test Me now herewith, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall be more than enough" <note>Malachi 3:10</note>. And what I wrote, that they gave the offerings and tithes to Melchizedek—are the tithes not only relevant to the Levites? Know that Melchizedek was Shem the son of Noah, and with all his power he was a Levite, according to what we have received from our sages of blessed memory. And the mystery: that Aaron the Priest is from the kingdom of Melchizedek. Therefore, Melchizedek was the supreme righteousness, and Samuel the Prophet, who was a Levite, is from the soul of Aaron. And this is the allusion: "And his outgoings, and your brother the Levite." And Melchizedek is Shem the son of Noah, and you shall see that there the seat of Shem and Eber was, etc. And then the name <note>Hebrew: "Shem"</note> rested upon Salem <note>Jerusalem</note>. Therefore, Melchizedek's power is in the power of his soul.

### The Light of Torah

<margin></margin>
Know that the secret of the tithes and the secret of the blessings all go to one place. In the <term>Ayin Bet</term> <gloss>72 [Name of God]</gloss> it is said: "A blessing is like a tithe." And the secret of the matter "and he found a hundredfold" also pertains to the matter of blessings. Our sages of blessed memory said: "A man is obligated to recite one hundred blessings every day." The matter of the "hundredfold" was written by Recanati.
</margin>

And his words are: Know that the sages of Kabbalah said that the Upper Earth has one hundred gates, for every gate is a receptacle flowing from the fountains of blessing to the world. And from there, Isaac our father, peace be upon him, drew one hundred kinds of blessings. For those one hundred gates mentioned there—there the abundance and the emanation for all created beings dwell. And therefore one finds in the Tabernacle one hundred sockets for the one hundred talents, as with the earth: there is no earth that does not have a receptacle, etc. What I said—I will reveal the secret further. Behold, the secret of the tithe is <term>Yod</term> <gloss>the letter Y, numerical value 10</gloss>. And it has fifty aspects: 1. The <term>Yod</term> itself. 2. The tip of the <term>Yod</term>, which is a point, and every point is a small <term>Yod</term>. 3. The fullness of the <term>Yod</term> is also ten, like this: <term>Yod-Vav-Dalet</term> <gloss>spelling of the letter Yod</gloss>, which totals ten. And behold, the emanation is nine <term>sefirot</term> <gloss>divine emanations</gloss>, and that which is ten is from the aspect of <term>Chokmah</term> <gloss>Wisdom</gloss>, which the Holy One, blessed be He, alluded to, etc., as is explained at length in the <term>Pardes</term> <gloss>Orchard (of Pomegranate)</gloss>. The number of <term>sefirot</term> is from the aspect of <term>Chokmah</term>. And this is: "And she <note>wisdom</note> is in the <term>Keter</term> <gloss>Crown</gloss>," completing the number. And the tip of the <term>Yod</term> alludes to the <term>Keter</term>, as the Kabbalists said: there are ten <term>sefirot</term> in <term>Chokmah</term>, and the subtleties are alluded to in the tip of the <term>Yod</term>, which was hidden. And the fullness of the <term>Yod</term> is the expansion of the ten <term>sefirot</term> such that each is included in ten. And the measure <term>Adonai</term> <gloss>My Lord (Name of God)</gloss>, which is the secret of the Upper Earth, receives them, and they are the secret of the one hundred sockets. Here you have the secret of the tithe of the tithe, for in <term>Adonai</term> there are one hundred gates, and they are hidden in the <term>Chokmah</term> which includes ten in the world. And afterwards they are hidden even more, to the ultimate concealment, in the tip of the <term>Yod</term>, until it is glorified and hidden in complete concealment. And the <term>Yod</term> itself, which is <term>Chokmah</term>, is connected in its tip, which is <term>Keter</term>. And it is the secret of one hundred in the secret of the expansion of the emanation and their inclusion. And it is the fullness of the <term>Yod</term>. And afterwards they are hidden in their root in <term>Chokmah</term>, which is the essence of <term>Yod</term>. And afterwards they are united in absolute unity in the tip of the <term>Yod</term>. And here is the secret of the tithe and the secret of the tithe of the tithe. And behold, the essence, which is <term>Chokmah</term>, is unified with the tip, which is <term>Keter</term>, and the <term>Binah</term> <gloss>Understanding</term>, for both of them are called "Thought," as we found in the <term>Zohar</term> in many places. Look in the <term>Pardes</term> under the entry of titles under "Thought." And he wrote there in the name of the great Kabbalist, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, in the *Book of the Name*: Thought is in the Upper <term>Keter</term> and in <term>Chokmah</term>. And in the Upper <term>Keter</term> it is thought, but it is not grasped at all, and thought is before all <term>Chokmah</term> and <term>Binah</term>, and it cannot be grasped at all. And also <term>Chokmah</term> is called thought, because it is not grasped except for the thought in it, which is the beginning of thought and contemplation, but in small measure. And regarding the hidden, it is said: "How deep are Thy thoughts" <note>Psalm 92:6</note>, for through the calculation that is in <term>Chokmah</term>, one comes to think in the Upper <term>Keter</term> through the speaker, etc. And now contemplate the secret of the tithe and the tithe of the tithe, which is the <term>Terumat Ma'aser</term>, and the secret of the <term>Terumah Gedolah</term>. And this is the <unclear>portion</unclear> that exempts, etc., and it takes by assessment, every measure, as it is said, "a hundredfold," in the secret of the expansion and the secret of the tithe, and it is its root, and it is its essence. And the <term>Terumat Ma'aser</term> is its attachment to the tip of the <term>Yod</term>. And all of this is taken by measure, for thus the emanation is called "measures" that instruct all beings. And in <term>Chokmah</term> is the root of the measures, and there is the <term>Terumat Ma'aser</term>. But the <term>Terumah Gedolah</term> alludes to the essence of the tip of the <term>Yod</term>, which is a level higher than the level of the attachment of the essence to its tip. For the attachment of the essence of the <term>Yod</term> to its tip is the attachment of <term>Chokmah</term> to <term>Keter</term>. However, the essence of the tip is the level of the <term>Keter</term> itself, and there is the secret of the thought, hidden from thought in the assessment of knowledge. This is the secret of the <term>Terumah Gedolah</term>—it takes by assessment. And according to our sages of blessed memory, the verse states: "And it shall be reckoned unto you," that is, in thought and assessment. And even though this verse was written regarding <term>Terumat Ma'aser</term>, they learned that if it is not relevant, it refers to the <term>Terumah Gedolah</term>, for there it is like an assessment. And behold, certainly, for everyone it is not here—our praise is not here. What is required in the Torah surely has a secret: why was it written here and not in its context? And here I say that they alluded to the aforementioned secret; it was written with <term>Terumat Ma'aser</term> because it is the upper level of <term>Chokmah</term>, which is also called thought. And this thought attaches to the power in it, which is by assessment, even though this thought is the power of the <term>Terumah Gedolah</term> and can be in the <term>Keter</term>—<term>Keter</term> is the virtue of one in a hundred—nevertheless, it is the level of the thoughts for the thought which is assessment, and not a measure, for it is the root of the measures. And even though it is the count of one—that is, one out of a hundred—it is a light, it is not from the count, even though it is the head of the count. Therefore, it was written "And it shall be reckoned unto you" next to the <term>Terumat Ma'aser</term>, even though its matter is the <term>Terumah Gedolah</term>. And all these things are wondrous.

### And Already, I Have Shown

<margin></margin>
Know that <term>Yakin</term> <gloss>reference to a commentary</gloss> in the <term>Tikkunim</term> <gloss>corrections/emendations of the Zohar</gloss> explains the secret of "Blessed," which is the Holy One, blessed be He, as the <term>Dalet-Aleph</term> <gloss>the numerical value of the Name of God</gloss> and the <term>Kaf-Lamed</term> <gloss>measure</gloss>, which teaches to the place of the Holy of Holies.
</margin>

I have said that in the tithes and the blessings, there is one secret and one place, etc., as written by Recanati, of blessed memory. And in the explanation of the inner essence of the tenth in the binary of the blessing, the sages of blessed memory explained the secret of one hundred gates and the secret of "and the Lord blessed him." And to explain what I have already established in the book <term>Shiurei Orah</term> <gloss>Measures of Light</gloss>, in the first chapter, in the binary of the blessing, the sages of blessed memory said: "And there were one hundred sockets" in the Tabernacle—they are in the image of the one hundred blessings that are filled from the Great Pool, called <term>Adonai</term>. And therefore, a man is obligated to recite one hundred blessings every day, in order to draw from each one of the one hundred blessings. And if one is missing, it is a blemish and casts a defect, and it will be lacking in the glory of God, as it is written: the secret of Priest, Levite, and Israelite, which is the secret of soul, spirit, and breath. And according to this foundation, Rabbi Chiyya said in "Bless the Lord, O my soul": the blessings depend on the soul in the secret of the three tithes.

# The Portion of Toldot, Written Torah
## This Is His Name That They Shall Call Him: The Source of Blessings

### The Lamp of the Commandment

<margin></margin>
"And Isaac sowed in that land, and found in that same year a hundredfold; and the Lord blessed him." <note>Genesis 26:12</note> The Sages of Blessed Memory said that this was by estimation, and Rashi brings in his commentary that a "hundredfold" means they estimated how much it was fit to produce, and it produced one hundred times that amount. Our Rabbis of Blessed Memory said this estimation was for the <term>ma'aserot</term> <gloss>tithes</gloss>.
</margin>

Behold, the Patriarchs fulfilled the entire Torah, and the Torah detailed this measure in its specific commandments, just as we find with our father Abraham, who "gave him a tenth of all." <note>Genesis 14:20</note> And here, with Isaac, and similarly with Jacob, who said, "And of all that You shall give me, I will surely tithe it to You." <note>Genesis 28:22</note> Our father Jacob tithed even from his children, as the Sages of Blessed Memory taught, for there were fourteen tribes including Ephraim and Manasseh. Subtracting the four born to the handmaids, who were sanctified in their own right, ten remained and were separated for the Levites to be holy unto God. Thus, the Patriarchs fulfilled the commandment of the tithe with all their heart, with all their soul, and with all their might. "With all their might" means literally a tenth of everything, even a tenth of one's money. "With all their soul" refers to Jacob, who tithed from the souls of his sons. "With all their heart" pertains to the <term>terumah gedolah</term> <gloss>great heave-offering</gloss>, which has no set measure but depends solely on the generosity of one’s heart. Then comes the "heave-offering of the Lord." The Sages say a generous eye gives one-fortieth, an average person gives one-fiftieth, and an evil eye gives one-sixtieth. Everything is alluded to in the verse "and he gave him a tithe of all." It would have sufficed to say "and he gave a tithe," but "of all" alludes to the great heave-offering, for the "tithe of the tithe" is included within the tithe, as I will explain later, because he gave Melchizedek the tithe and also the tithe of the heave-offering. Now, the Sages say "one-fiftieth" is the average eye, giving one in fifty. But Abraham, the pious one, took ten out of fifty in order to separate from them the great heave-offering. By removing ten from fifty, forty remained; that is, he gave one part out of four for the great heave-offering. And even though the way of the average person is one in fifty, when he took the great heave-offering, he removed ten out of fifty and then separated one for the great heave-offering because he was generous of heart. Regarding the matter of the great heave-offering, it appears one can reconcile what was said about this "estimation for tithes." A difficulty arises: did we not learn, "Do not tithe by estimation"? <note>Mishnah Terumot 3:5</note> However, Isaac our father was a man of piety and he tithed, and the estimation was for the great heave-offering, as we learned in Tractate Terumot, Chapter 1: "One does not separate heave-offering by measure, nor by weight, nor by counting." Even though the Sages gave a guideline—a good eye, etc.—nevertheless, it is called "by estimation," as we derive from the verse, "Your heave-offering shall be reckoned to you," <note>Numbers 18:27</note> which means "reckoned" as an estimation. Even though this is written regarding the tithe of the tithe, if it is not relevant to the tithe of the tithe—for the Torah gave a measure and one must measure—apply it to the great heave-offering.

However, if you examine it well, it implies that the estimation was for all the tithes, for this estimation occurred before the "great man" said, "the field, how much is it fit to produce," etc. It appears certain that at the time of separating the tithe, he would measure to separate the tithe. The estimation that occurred before growth implies piety, for the law is that one is not obligated until the completion of the work and after one sees the face of the house. Whatever he eats, he practices total piety with the tithe. Isaac wished to be strict, and therefore he would "estimate" in order to separate even from what was eaten. This is the general rule: "Do not tithe by estimation," for that was only said regarding the obligation of the tithe, but this was a common stringency from Isaac our father. And since this verse speaks of the commandment of the tithe, therefore it says, "And the Lord blessed him." And as it is written in Malachi, "Bring all the tithes into the storehouse... and test me now herewith, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall be more than enough." <note>Malachi 3:10</note> And what I wrote, that they gave Melchizedek the heave-offerings and the tithes—for tithes belong only to the Levites—know that Melchizedek was Shem, son of Noah, and with all his power he was a Levite, according to what we have received from our Sages. It is said that Aaron the Priest is from the kingdom of Melchizedek. Therefore, Melchizedek was "righteousness on high," and Samuel the Prophet, who was a Levite, is from the soul of Aaron. This is the hint of "and his offspring, and your brother the Levite." Melchizedek is Shem, son of Noah, and you see that "there dwelt Shem and Eber," and then the name of God rested upon Salem. Therefore, Melchizedek is the power of his voice through the power of his soul.

### The Light of Torah

<margin></margin>
Know that the secret of the tithes and the secret of the blessings all go to one place. In the <term>Ayin Bet</term> <gloss>numerical value of 72</gloss>, it is said that a blessing is like a tithe. And the secret of the matter "and he found a hundredfold" also pertains to the matter of blessings. Our Sages said: A person is obligated to recite one hundred blessings every day. The matter of "a hundredfold" was written by Recanati.
</margin>

He wrote as follows: "Know that the Kabbalistic Sages said that the upper earth has one hundred gates, and for every gate there is a receiving vessel, flowing from the fountains of blessing to the world. From there, Isaac our father, peace be upon him, drew one hundred types of blessings, for the one hundred gates mentioned there are where the abundance and emanation for all created beings reside. And therefore, one finds in the Tent of Meeting one hundred sockets for the one hundred talents, just as in the earth, for there is no earth that does not have a receiving vessel, etc." What he revealed, I will reveal as a greater secret: The secret of the tithe is the letter <term>Yod</term> <gloss>the tenth letter, numerical value 10</gloss>. It has fifty aspects: 1) The <term>Yod</term> itself. 2) The "thorn" of the <term>Yod</term>, which is a point, and every point is a small <term>Yod</term>. 3) The filling of the <term>Yod</term> is also ten, as in <term>Yod-Vav-Dalet</term>, which equals ten. Now, the emanation consists of nine <term>sefirot</term> <gloss>divine attributes</gloss>, and that which makes it ten is from the side of <term>Chokhmah</term> <gloss>Wisdom</gloss>, which the Blessed Name alluded to, as elaborated in the *Pardes*. The number of <term>sefirot</term> is from the side of Wisdom. This is "and He established it in the Crown," completing the count. And the thorn of the <term>Yod</term> alludes to the <term>Keter</term> <gloss>Crown</gloss>, as the Kabbalists say that there are ten <term>sefirot</term> in Wisdom, and the subtleties are hinted at in the thorn of the <term>Yod</term>, which is hidden. The filling of the <term>Yod</term> is the expansion of the ten <term>sefirot</term> in such a way that each one is included in ten. And the measure <term>Adonai</term>, which is the secret of the upper earth, receives them, and they are the secret of the one hundred sockets. Here you have the secret of the "tithe of the tithe," for in <term>Adonai</term> are the one hundred gates, and they are hidden in Wisdom which includes ten in the world. And afterwards, they are hidden even more in the ultimate concealment in the thorn of the <term>Yod</term>, until they are glorified and hidden in absolute concealment. And the <term>Yod</term> itself, which is Wisdom, is embedded in its thorn, which is the Crown. And this is the secret of one hundred, in the secret of the expansion of the emanation and their inclusion. This is the filling of the <term>Yod</term>, and then they are hidden in their root in Wisdom, which is the essence of the <term>Yod</term>. And then they are united in absolute unity in the thorn of the <term>Yod</term>. Here is the secret of the tithe and the secret of the tithe of the tithe. Now, the essence, which is Wisdom, is unified in the thorn, which is the Crown, and the "average" state, for both are called "Thought," as we find in many places. See the *Pardes* under the entries for "Thought." He wrote there in the name of the great Kabbalist, the Rashbi, in the *Sefer HaShem*: "Thought is in the Crown on high, and in Wisdom. In the Crown on high, it is thought, but not grasped at all from his trouble. Thought precedes all Wisdom and Understanding, and it cannot be grasped at all. Also, Wisdom is called Thought, for it is not grasped except by the Thought that is within it, the beginning of thought and contemplation, but in a limited way. And regarding these, it is said, 'How deep are Your thoughts,' for through the calculation that is in Wisdom, it comes to calculate in the Crown on high through speech." End quote. Now, contemplate the secret of the tithe and the tithe of the tithe, which is the tithe-heave, and the secret of the great heave-offering. This "portion releases," etc., and takes by estimation every measure, such as the "hundredfold" in the secret of expansion and the secret of the tithe, which is its root, and it is its essence. The tithe-heave is its attachment to the thorn of the <term>Yod</term>, and all this is measured, for so the emanation is called "measures" that instruct all existence. In Wisdom is the root of the measures, and there is the tithe-heave. But the great heave-offering alludes to the essence of the thorn of the <term>Yod</term>, which is a level higher than the level of the attachment of the essence to its thorn. For the attachment of the essence of the <term>Vav</term> to its thorn is the attachment of Wisdom to the Crown; however, the essence of the thorn is the level of the Crown itself, and there is the secret of Thought, hidden from thought in the estimation of the mind. This is the secret of the great heave-offering, which takes by estimation. And according to the Sages of Blessed Memory, the passage "shall be reckoned to you" <note>Numbers 18:27</note> means by thought and estimation. And even though this verse is written concerning the tithe-heave, they learned that if it is not relevant there, it refers to the great heave-offering, for there it is like an estimation. And here, surely, for everything that is not here, our praise is here; that which is inquired into in the Torah surely has a secret for why it is written here and not in its proper context. And here I say that they hinted at the aforementioned secret; it is written by the tithe-heave because it is the upper level of Wisdom, which is also called "Thought." And this Thought attaches to the power within it, which is the estimation, even though this Thought is the power of the great heave-offering and can be in the Crown, the crown being the treasure of one in a hundred. Nevertheless, it is the level of "thoughts to thought," which is estimation, and not a measure, for it is the root of the measures. And even though it is a count of one—that is, one out of a hundred—it is a light that is not from the count, even though it is the head of the count. Therefore, "shall be reckoned to you" was written by the tithe-heave, even though its meaning is the great heave-offering. All these things are wondrous.

I said that in the tithes and the blessings, there is one secret and one place, etc., as the Recanati of blessed memory wrote. And to explain the inner depth of the tenth, in the "average" state, in the blessing, it is explained. The secret of the hundred gates and the secret of "and the Lord blessed him" are explained. And to explain our grace, we rely on the *Sha'arei Orah* <gloss>Gates of Light</gloss> in the first gate, in the "average" state, in the blessing. "And there were a hundred sockets" in the Tabernacle are in the likeness of the one hundred blessings that are filled from the great pool called <term>Adonai</term>. Therefore, a person is obligated to recite one hundred blessings every day in order to draw from each one of the one hundred blessings. And if one is missing, it is a flaw and brings a blemish, and it will be lacking in the glory of God, as it is written. This is the secret of Priest, Levite, and Israelite, which is the secret of *Nefesh*, *Ruach*, and *Neshamah* <gloss>the three levels of the soul</gloss>. And according to this foundation, Rabbi H.H. said in "Bless the Lord, O my soul," the blessings are dependent on the soul in the secret of the three tithes.

<meta>continues from previous page: shedding them little by little</meta> in their later generations, until all their stipends fail to meet the requirements of luxury and its habits. Need touches them, and their kings demand that they restrict their expenditures to raids and wars. They find no refuge from this, so the rulers inflict punishments upon them and seize what is in the hands of many of them, either to keep it for themselves or to favor their own children and the clients of the state. Consequently, they become too weak to maintain their own affairs, and the ruler of the state becomes weak by their weakness. 

Furthermore, when luxury increases in the state and the stipends provided are insufficient for their needs and expenditures, the ruler of the state—that is, the sultan—finds it necessary to increase their stipends to remedy their deficiencies and resolve their grievances. The tax revenue has a known limit: it does not increase or decrease. Even if it increases through the imposition of new taxes, its amount remains finite after the increase. When the revenue is distributed among the stipends after an increase has been added for each individual due to their luxury and high expenditures, the number of the garrison must necessarily decrease compared to what it was before the increase in stipends. Then, luxury grows, and the amounts of the stipends increase further for that reason, so the number of the garrison decreases a third and a fourth time, until the military returns to the smallest possible numbers. The garrison weakens because of this, the strength of the state collapses, and neighboring states or the <term>asabiyat</term> <gloss>tribal solidarities</gloss> (1) under its control become emboldened against it, and God permits the destruction that He has written for His creation.

This is his statement, and he says: sometimes a wound occurs where it requires complete amputation. Regarding the limb, if the wound entails amputation from it, it does not increase, so it requires agents that promote the growth of flesh. It is not enough to simply dry and prevent [matter from accumulating]; rather, sometimes the drying and preventing agent might, in a certain way, repel the substance from which it grows. There may also be a cavity and deficiency in the bone such that it cannot grow completely, leaving a cavity, as may happen. It may occur that more grows than is required, resulting in proud flesh <note>original: "لحم زائد" (excessive flesh)</note>. It is necessary that the patient whose flesh is intended to grow in a wound should be prepared without that [excessive] growth, as it can sometimes be such that the flesh can grow. As for the skin, because if it has been severed entirely, it does not grow back in its place; rather, firm flesh grows there upon which hair and veins do not grow. Instead, it generates branches and grows like flesh.

Among the wounds are those of high risk: wounds occurring in the nerves and the muscles of the arm, and we will mention this in the chapter on nerves. You will see the serious and harmful symptoms that follow them. The worst thing that follows a wound to the area of the arm is discoloration, a drop in the pulse afterward, and smallness, leading to evening <note>an observation of physical decline towards the end of the day</note> and a collapse of strength. Convulsions may also follow it. Likewise, those that occur in front of the knee at the kneecap, for they are followed by harmful symptoms, and they are fatal, rarely escaping from them. If convulsions occur from such arm wounds and treatment does not heal them, the treatment is amputation of the arm. And God knows best.

This is what he says. He also says: Sometimes a wound occurs in a place where it requires you to perform a complete amputation. Regarding the limb, if the wound requires amputation of a part of it, and it is extensive, then it requires flesh-regenerating agents. It is not enough to use substances that dry and prevent [the influx of matter]; rather, sometimes the drying and preventing agent, in a certain respect, blocks the matter from which the flesh should grow. There may be a depth and a deficiency in the bone such that it cannot grow back completely, leaving a depression, as a condition that may occur. It may also happen that more than is necessary grows, resulting in excess flesh <note>likely referring to proud flesh or granulation tissue</note>. It is necessary that the patient, whose flesh is intended to be regenerated in a wound, should observe proper caution, for excessive growth can sometimes be such that it is possible for the flesh to grow. As for the skin, if it has been completely severed, it does not regenerate in its place; instead, hard flesh grows, upon which neither hair nor veins grow. However, branches are generated, and it grows like flesh. Among the wounds are those that are dangerous, such as the wounds occurring in the nerves and the muscles of the upper arm, and we will mention them in the chapter on nerves. Often, unpleasant and severe symptoms follow them. The worst thing that follows a wound to the upper arm is discoloration, a drop in the pulse afterwards, a trace [of injury], shrinkage, a tendency toward necrosis, and a loss of strength. Convulsions may also follow it. Likewise, those [wounds] that occur in front of the knee at the patella are followed by severe symptoms, and they are usually difficult to recover from. If a convulsion occurs from such wounds of the upper arm and treatment does not result in healing, then the treatment is the amputation of the upper arm.

Just as the teacher is seen in the water,
So the host of the Sons of the Victorious One perceive the All-Pervading.
The fully enlightened Buddha is seen within the assembly.

So it is said. And:
Just as the reflection of a fully enlightened Buddha appears,
Just as the reflection of a god’s form appears,
Likewise, for those whose minds turn toward the living,
The image of the body of the Lord of Sages arises.

So it is said. And:
This is a manifestation of one's own mind,
Though ordinary beings do not know it.

So it is said. And:
Because they arise and perish,
The forms of the Buddha are subject to birth and decay.
Like Indra, the Sage’s

# The Song Ministers Congratulate the Appointment of Zhang Jun and Zhao Ding as Prime Ministers, Attracting Talented Scholars to the "Lesser Yuanyou" Era

BY PROFITABLE plants, I understand those that, besides providing food for the house, bring money to their owner. The opinion of those who can attribute nothing to mineral waters, such as acidulous ones, etc., except for spiritual mixtures and immature seeds, or first beings, which are supposedly taken up by the waters before they can coagulate and acquire a form, is refuted by this kind of generation. It must be admitted that this can indeed happen; but it should not be held as a universal rule, since art itself not infrequently extracts those juices, perfected in their substance, from mineral waters by coagulation. Truly, to refuse to have such waters in minerals is the mark of a very narrow and self-loving mind. Who can truly name and show a metallic water which carries with it the <term>prima materia</term> <gloss>first matter</gloss> of metals before it stands firm and has neither the form nor the virtues of a perfected metal? How will they call this water "iron-bearing" and that one "copper-bearing" if they have never known the qualities of the first matter of individual metals? All things can be reduced into <term>hydrargyrum</term> <gloss>mercury/quicksilver</gloss>, and from all things salt and <term>calcanthum</term> <gloss>vitriol</gloss> are elicited; who will distinguish these in their first origins and rawness? More probable is the opinion of our Philosopher <note>likely Aristotle</note>, namely that such things occur through resolution either into spirits, of which we spoke above, or into soluble juices or <term>calces</term> <gloss>powders produced by heating</gloss>, since art testifies that calcined metals are dissolved into liquors, and other juices are also extracted from them and washed away by percolated elemental waters. Indeed, they are even corroded by sharp things (<term>aquis acutis</term> <gloss>corrosive acids</gloss>, cements, coloring agents, etc.), and the corrosion is so mixed with the waters that they are clearly not apparent except after coagulations; in which manner the strength of so many things is in the clearest wine, the juice of decocted things in purified decoctions, metallic filings in <term>aqua forti</term> <gloss>nitric acid</gloss>, and soluble juices in solutions.

# CHAPTER XII.
## Analogs of Minerals.

To this class of corporeal mixtures can also be recalled those waters which acquire nothing at all in the mine, or rather in the caverns of the earth, but bring with them a virtue already made by a mixture on the surface of the earth. Thus, if the sea entered a gap in the earth and broke forth again at another head, it could be held as a mineral spring. Likewise, if water from the sky, river water, stagnant water, or marshes, having accepted power from the juices of plants, the excrement of animals, or other things, descended to some depth and came out again affected in the same way, or at least changed to some extent from that principle. It is well known that where herds of animals are stabled, places soaked with excrement receive the beginnings of <term>kalinitrum</term> <gloss>saltpeter/nitre</gloss>. If these are then drunk up by a stream creeping here and there and finally emerging as one spring, the water will turn out to be nearly called mineral. It is also known that various things, especially animal and vegetable, can rot in stagnant waters. From that also, an origin representing a mineral will exist.

# CHAPTER XIII.
## The Opinion of Paracelsus.

<margin>The first matter of metals.</margin>
Paracelsus was also taught this by his teachers and the evidence of experience. For although he sometimes attributes to mineral waters a proper and primeval nature from the birth of the world, and says that mineral waters were one and the same with simple ones, but were separated for the health of animals and plants to flow separately thereafter; yet he seems either to have corrected his opinion, or to have varied it later according to the habit of his inconstancy or Socratic and Skeptical uncertainty, when he left written that cold mineral waters arise either from alum, salt, and ink <note>vitriol</note> which are immature and unmixed in their own vein: is it so that no elemental water approaches, but those very immature, uncoagulated things existing in the form of a liquor come forth purely and constitute a mineral spring by perennial flow? (If this is so, it is necessary that an immense power be collected in reservoirs or a vast space so that the flows suffice for a long time, or that nature is frustrated in its attempt in that place and emits nothing but imperfect abortions into the light.) Or they arise from the three principles of the seven metals before they stand firm, if the waters of a cataract run through and corrupt them so they cannot be perfected, or at least from the first matter of those three in each metal, both simply and mixed: (as if by the influx of elemental water the operation of nature were anticipated, and it dissipated the salt, sulphur, and mercury of gold, silver, tin, lead, iron, copper, and hydrargyrum which were about to be coagulated; although that thing cannot be called the first matter, since it is nothing other than dissolved salt, uncongealed sulphur, and unsolidified mercury. For the first matter of these is either a vapor and a seminal breath having power toward those things, or a viscous principle fertile with such a spirit; which, if it is snatched away before its maturity and diluted by waters, can in no way imprint a metallic nature on the waters, since it has it not in act, but in potential. Just as a liquid of a chick, if shaken and weakened with water, does not take on the nature and powers of a hen, nor can it even be recognized.) It is ridiculous, however, that such a principle could flow forth even simply, since it is established that it is enclosed in the mine and matures in the manner of the fruits of plants and animals; because if it flows together, it either is not that much, or it has already accepted its form in the mine, lacking only the proper coagulation which it finally acquires in its pool. It is certainly easier to imagine such a thing than to show it. Yet it is not to be denied that from the immature beginnings of metals, whether they be spirits or liquors, through the mixture of wild waters, metallic waters emerge in some way. But if you add further that those three principles are to be understood separately, so that <margin>Doubt concerning metallic origins.</margin> twenty-one mineral flows could exist therefrom, you will rave even more. For they do not exist separately, nor are metals made by a composition from those separated things, but they are brought forth as if from a seed, in which those principles were together in potential—if indeed they are to be held as true principles, and not rather as chemical masteries elicited by art from differently affected metals, in which way we can make vitriol, flowers, calces, liquors, etc., from the same things, which nevertheless are not held as true beginnings, etc. Or they arise from the spirits of the three metallic principles: (The same is said: for it matters nothing whether they appear outwardly in the form of a spirit or a liquor, if they are imperfect in their interior. We can nevertheless also understand the breaths of resolved things, and take those principles figuratively for salt, sulphur, and mercury, not those which are the beginnings of the composition or generation of things, but those things perfected in themselves, just as we consider the elements in themselves, insofar as they are simple bodies by themselves.)

D. In no way at all.
M. What if a figure is formed by three straight lines that are unequal? Can there also be equal angles in that? Or do you understand it otherwise?
D. They absolutely cannot.
M. You speak correctly. Tell me, I ask, which figure seems better and more beautiful to you: the one that stands with equal lines or with unequal lines?
D. Who doubts that the one in which equality prevails is better?
M. Therefore, you prefer equality to inequality?
D. I do not know if anyone would not prefer it.
M. Look now at the figure which is perfected by three equal angles <note>an equilateral triangle</note>. What is it that is placed opposite in it, that is, on the other side? Is it a line or an angle?
D. I see a line.
M. What then? If an angle corresponds to an angle and a line to a line, would you not admit that equality is more powerful in that figure in which this occurs?
D. I admit it. But how this could be done with three lines, I do not see at all.
M. Can this happen with four lines?
D. Much more so.
M. Is that figure better which stands with four equal lines than the one which stands with three?
D. Certainly it is better, for equality has more power in it.
M. What then of this figure made of four equal straight lines <note>a square</note>? Do you think it can be made so that the angles in it are not equal, or do you think not?
D. I see it can be done.
M. In what way?
D. If two are narrower and two are wider, like this <note>D likely gestures or draws a rhombus/diamond shape</note>. And it is seen how both the narrower ones and both the wider ones are opposite to each other.
M. Most truly and aptly said. You see how much equality has been maintained here as far as it could be. For you see indeed that it cannot happen that when a figure is completed with four equal lines, either all or at least the pairs of angles are equal; and yet those which are equal to each other correspond from the opposite side.
D. I see it and hold it most firmly.
M. Does not a certain great and almost inexpressible justice move you even in these things?
D. In what way?
M. Because I think justice is nothing other than equity <term>aequitas</term> <gloss>fairness or justice</gloss>. Now equity is evidently named after equality <term>aequalitas</term>. But what is equity in this virtue <note>justice</note> except that which grants to each their own? Furthermore, things cannot be granted to each as their own unless they are granted with a certain distinction. Or do you think otherwise?
D. It is manifest, and I entirely agree.
M. Which distinction, I judge, would be necessary for nothing if all things were equal, such that they did not differ at all among themselves.

Paulus <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note> commended its use in vinegar and oil, because it both invites the appetite, relaxes the spleen, and drives out phlegm through the bowels. It has retained its name in the apothecaries. The common people, happy to shorten names, pronounce it as <term>capres</term> as if for <term>cappares</term>, having worn away two letters. Some of the Latins call it <term>inturim</term>, for it is seen as a shrub of a thorny kind, spreading itself in a circle on the ground. It has thorns like a bramble, curved into a hook, leaves like a quince, and fruit like an olive, which when gaping open, a white flower breaks forth; when this falls, an oblong acorn-like pod forms, which finally opening itself represents reddish grains, such as are seen in a pomegranate, with large, woody roots. The small stalks, leaves, flowers, seeds, and pods are brought to us preserved in salt in this appearance and shape which we have described. Gaul now nourishes the shrub. In Cyprus, the caper occurs in great abundance. It provides little nourishment to those eating it, because it is powerful in the thinness of its parts, being born for medicine rather than for food. The fruit is kept sprinkled with salt, otherwise it quickly feels corruption. Fresh fruit that has not experienced salt nourishes more than that which is aged in the same way, yet it moves the bowels more. When washed and soaked for a time until it lays aside all the nature of the salt, it nourishes very little indeed, but invites a fainting appetite. It dispels a loathing of food, casts down phlegm which had gathered in the belly, and clears obstructing blockages of the spleen and liver. But to provide these uses, it ought to be placed before other dishes with honeyed vinegar, or oil and vinegar. They eat the tender buds while they are green with vinegar and salt, and store them away for use. They say those who eat them daily do not run the risk of a loosening of the nerves <note>paralysis</note>, nor of pains of the spleen. The root removes white leprosy <note>vitiligo or skin spots</note> if rubbed on when crushed in the sun. It is beneficial for those with spleen disease when drunk in wine, using two drachms of the root bark, provided the use of baths is removed. And they say that in thirty-five days, the whole spleen is emitted through the urine and the bowels. It is drunk for pains in the loins and for paralysis. The seed boiled and crushed in vinegar, or the root chewed, settles toothaches. A decoction in oil is poured in for ear pain. The fresh leaves and root with honey heal the ulcers which they call <term>phagedenas</term> <gloss>consuming or spreading ulcers</gloss>. Thus the root also dispels scrofula <note>swollen lymph nodes</note> and tumors behind the ears. It removes ulcerations of the mouth when boiled in vinegar: it also heals the maladies of the liver, and kills worms in the ears. They give it in vinegar and honey for skin-worms <note>tineas</note>. It is agreed among authors that they are useless for the stomach. The stem and fruit are preserved for the sake of food. It disturbs the bowels, hurts the stomach, and creates thirst. However, when cooked it is more useful to the stomach than when raw. Two drachms of the seed itself swallowed in wine for forty days consumes the spleen. It draws out urine and drives out bloody scrapings. It is beneficial in pains of the hips <note>sciatica</note> and loosening of the nerves: likewise for ruptures and convulsions. It moves the menses and draws out phlegm from the head. The seed boiled in vinegar settles toothaches if the mouth is rinsed. The dried bark of the root has the same effects. It cleanses all old and foul ulcers and those which have become hardened. It is smeared on for those with spleen disease with barley flour. The root gripped by the tooth in a bite relieves that pain. It removes white leprosy when crushed with vinegar. The root and leaves rubbed together dispel scrofula and hardnesses. The juice is poured in against worms in the ears. The foreign caper which is brought from Marmarica in Libya excites great flatulence. The Apulian kind induces vomiting. The African is very harsh, as is that which is conveyed from the Red Sea; indeed it raises blisters in the mouth and is an enemy to the gums, for it eats them away even to the bone, wherefore it is condemned for foods.

## VII.

<note>A decorative blue initial O</note>
Ummidia Quadratilla has died just before her eightieth year of age. Until her final illness, she was vigorous and, even beyond the usual standard for a matrona <gloss>a respected married woman</gloss>, she possessed a compact and robust body. She died leaving a most honorable will: she left as heirs her grandson for two-thirds of the estate and her granddaughter for the remaining third. 

I am very closely fond of this grandson; he is a remarkable young man. It is not only those related to him by blood who should love him among his kin. First, being conspicuous for his beauty, he escaped all the talk of malicious people both as a boy and as a youth. He was a husband before his twenty-fourth year, and, if God had willed it, he would have been a father. He lived in the household of his luxury-loving grandmother with great austerity, and yet with great obedience. 

She kept <term>pantomimi</term> <gloss>pantomime actors</gloss> and cherished them more effusively than was appropriate for a lady of her high standing. Quadratillus did not watch these men in the theater nor at home, nor did she demand that he do so. I heard her say herself, when she was commending her grandson's studies to me, that she was accustomed, as a woman in the leisure of her sex, to relax her mind with the game of stones <note>an ancient board game similar to checkers or chess</note> and was accustomed to watch her actors. But whenever she was about to do either, she said she always instructed her grandson to go away and study. She seemed to me to do this not more out of love for him than out of reverence for his character. 

You will wonder, as I myself wondered: at the recent sacerdotal games, when the pantomime actors were brought out in the opening performance, as Quadratillus and I were leaving the theater together, he said to me: "Do you know that today was the first time I have ever seen my grandmother's freedman dancing?" I am poor, sick, old, and now deprived by injustice of my excellent son, a youth of greatest hope and most loving toward me. My other son remains with modest and very slight hope of good fortune or of propagating my lineage; and my daughter, now in her ninth year of marriage, is sterile. Formerly, I was flourishing in every way: in friendships, sons, profits, and good health. As a youth, I was raised with great expectations, accustomed not only to comforts but even to luxuries. But now, though entirely burdened by hardships and despised, with many enemies, I do not only consider myself not unhappy, but far more fortunate than ever before. Neither am I insane, nor do I boast; my actions show it. I profess this with a most steadfast mind, and for that reason my lecture hall is most crowded. I manage everything better than before. If anyone compares the writings I have recently completed with my earlier ones, they will understand that a fuller, more vivid, and purer mind dwells within me. 

But you, whoever you are, wail like a woman over a single misfortune, even the lightest one; we bear so many and such great ones. We have gained this one thing: that we neither regret life, because of virtue and knowledge, nor do we fear death, the end of so many dangers and inconveniences, and a thing so very necessary. Another man is far more tortured by a calamity that is not even a calamity; because a horse goes lame through a servant’s carelessness, he cries out and spends sleepless nights. So many handles of happiness bring him no consolation, as if his entire being resided in his horse’s hoof. Another is wretched because he is despised; another because he has a son but no grandson; another because he fears for his wife's chastity; another, because he fell from a Magistracy, tries to end his life with a noose. Therefore, the delicate senses and tastes of men, as well as ignorance of our affairs and condition, and despair regarding the future life, make men miserable even for the smallest reasons. Thus, men of this sort can in no way be happy, nor can they be consoled in adversity. 

Consider the nature of our life. There are two men, each of whom sleeps for six continuous months (as they report of Alpine mice <note>marmots</note>). One of them dreams of prisons, chains, crosses, nooses, torments, the slaughter of his sons, fears, destructions, flights, storms, diseases, want, and hunger. Now he is tossed alone on a wandering sea, with his hope of safety placed in God; now through deserts, destitute of all things, he flees the tyrant’s horsemen; now he is bound and cast into a foul pit; at another time he is led to execution; now he is hissed at by a crowd as if insane. In contrast, the other dreams of kingdoms, honors, banquets, games, companionships, gardens, fortresses, pleasant journeys, mistresses, a beautiful wife, and sons, and he passes from one pleasure to another. Furthermore, not content with these human delights, he is carried to heaven; he sees most beautiful things, greenery, hunts, fowling, and fishing. Then both wake up at the same time. Who is so foolish as to call the latter happy and the former unhappy? 

But you reply: "This dream is brief, it affects one less, and nothing is left from it for others; but life is longer, with a true sense of things and greater pleasure and pain, from which, when we depart, things remain for others: sons, descendants, and wealth, which do not vanish entirely as in a dream." You are talking nonsense. If anyone considers rightly, no one in however long a life equals this six-month period 

<column-break/>

of perpetual happiness. Regarding sensation, cares, and pleasure, all things in dreams both are and seem greater than in wakefulness; and reason suggests this, since we are not distracted from our senses. But as for what pertains to true life, this is what we contend: the interval between the future life and this one is far greater than between wakefulness and sleep. Those things that are left behind are something if referred to a foolish hope; and for that reason, it is more painful that we are forced to leave them. If we look to true opinion and the outcome of things, we are deceived by a false image. Thus anyone may imagine for themselves an immortal life, an immense and peaceful kingdom; but such trifles cannot be moved. It is necessary to decide regarding our life that it is truly a dream. 

But, as I said, if there had been something greater, I had advanced my affairs so far that from the most unhappy I could long be the most happy; and from the poorest, through my own and my son's work, we might gain up to two thousand gold <term>crowns</term> <gloss>coronatorum</gloss> each year. There would be no rank of men, no Princes, who were not in our hands. I had conquered envy, overcome rivalry, crushed conspiracies, and penetrated into the innermost circles. I had opened ways and built an approach to all things for both myself and my son. Furthermore, the opportunity of foreign Princes was no more lacking to me than to anyone else. First indeed I was called by the King of the <term>Danes</term> <gloss>Dacorum</gloss>, then by the French, and soon also by the <term>associates</term> <gloss>socios</gloss>. I will, however, tell the story that happened in the year 1551.

John Hamilton <note>original: "Ioannes Amulthon"</note>, of the Scottish Royal lineage, the Primate <term>Pontiff</term> among them, a man of distinguished faith, erudition, and piety, and most liberal, was suffering from such a heavy difficulty in breathing that those who saw him in the midst of the disease did not think he had a day of life remaining. He had, however, endured such a great illness for a whole decade, although daily matters slipped for the worse. He had tried the labor of every distinguished physician; but when he had experienced the physicians of both Kings and Emperors, and even the more illustrious professors of the art, it happened by chance that a certain friend of his, then William Cassanate <note>original: "Gulielmus Casanatus"</note>, his physician, had come across our books *On Subtlety* and *On Wisdom*. As they turned the pages, they found me boasting that I had cured some <term>consumptives</term> <gloss>phthificos</gloss>. And certainly I had cured very few of that kind of disease, yet I had healed many laboring under a similar affliction. Thus, that boast and the proclamation of my false praise benefited a man who was by no means a liar. Inflamed by these and other arguments, they persuaded him that since no hope of safety appeared anywhere, he should flee to the last anchor. The condition pleased him, and he first sent letters to us, summoning me to Lyon or Paris. And although in the previous edition of this book I included a copy of the letter itself, he thought it better, omitting superfluous things so as not to delay the reader, to insert here what was relevant to the matter; yet in such a way that neither the sense nor the words themselves were changed. His physician's letter was therefore as follows:

"The most illustrious Pontiff of the city of St. Andrews, prelate of the whole kingdom and brother of the <term>Viceroy</term> <gloss>Proregis</gloss>, and my patron, whom I have served in medicine for four years now, has been afflicted for ten years hence with a most difficult catarrh occurring in cycles, though without fever..."

Yet after that age had increased and reached its peak, the span of life was shorter; the anxious heat of pressing cares was present, which the wicked joys of the mind created. Reciprocal injury never ceased, and the Silver Age saw no reverence for the gods above and no rites of sacrifice. God, inflamed with earned anger, extinguished this race. After that age, a third succeeded, the Bronze race, in no way similar to the silver. Created from the blood of ash-nymphs <term>dryadum</term> <gloss>wood nymphs, specifically those of ash trees</gloss>, they were indeed harsh, possessing robust chests, and the whole race seethed with a wretched love for fierce Mars <note>the god of war</note>. They knew no rest and no law. It was an age harder than adamant itself, with a proud countenance that was to be feared. Invincible strength and powerful arms were never lacking from their shoulders. At that time, weapons were of bronze, and so were their houses; all labor was in bronze, for the use of iron had not yet emerged. 

However, this race was consumed by its own madness and departed without honor to the black regions of cold Dis <note>the god of the underworld, also known as Pluto</note>. And although they stood with invincible strength, they were nonetheless conquered by black death and left the light of the sun. After the Bronze Age was hidden and fell away, there was a fourth offspring, which was better; many precepts of venerable Justice clung to their whole souls. This was the divine race of Heroes, and they were the first to be called by that name.

## XII.

It is therefore established that the fanatical opinions of the Paracelsians, Weigelians, Mystics, Quakers, and others, who are commonly called by the name of the "Illuminated," agree in this: that besides the body and the rational soul, there is a certain substantial part in man granted to him divinely, and—as most do not conceal—granted from the very divine essence itself. Paul Felgenhauer explains this same doctrine of the three parts of man quite extensively in *The Forecourt, the Holy, and the Most Holy in the Temple of God* <note>original: "Vorhoff, im heiligen und Allerheiligsten am Tempel GOttes"</note>. The individual readings of this fanatical little book sufficiently declare the nature of each part and the dreams of the Fanatics concerning them. Also worthy of comparison is Bartholomaeus Sclei’s *Decent Universal Doctrine of God* <note>original: "anständige allgemeine GOttes Lehre"</note>, as well as *The Book of the Witness of the Hidden Treasure of the Field* <note>original: "Buch des Zeugnisses des verborgenen Ackerschatzes"</note>, whose author calls himself HIEL <gloss>the single life of God</gloss>, as well as the *Thorough Instruction* <note>original: "gründlicher Unterricht"</note> by the highly God-enlightened Matthes Weyer, and similar monstrous books written by those madmen, truly unworthy of anyone wasting good and irrevocable hours in reading them.

## XIII.

Furthermore, this doctrine concerning the triple part of man holds the chief place in their <term>mataeology</term> <gloss>vain or foolish discourse</gloss>. For the author of *The Forecourt* most foolishly boasts in Chapter XII that this doctrine contains the foundation not only of all Christianity, but of all wisdom in the universe which is in heaven and on earth. But truly, if someone should happen to be unaware that they have five senses, or what the nature of sight or hearing or the rest might be, must it therefore be established that those senses are unable to perform their function? I certainly do not think so. Meanwhile, Andreas Christophorus Rafelius extols this dogma with such praises that he does not fear to speak of it in *The New Year's Trumpet* <note>original: "Der Neujahrs Posaune"</note> in this manner: "This is actually the right bedrock and the certain foundation upon which the house of our Christianity must be set, laid, and founded, if it is to stand: and from this all preaching, reading, writing, hearing of God's Word, singing, praying, and good..."

Since the Professorship of Eloquence was entrusted to me not long ago by letters of vocation, as they are called, followed shortly by the confirmation of the most Serene and Most Powerful Elector of Saxony,

## JOHANN GEORG III,
## my most indulgent Lord,

I judged that I would be doing nothing foreign to the function most graciously enjoined upon me if, under his auspices and according to the custom received in this University, I were to deliver an address **ON THE MOST FRIENDLY PARTNERSHIP WHICH INTERCEDES BETWEEN ELOQUENCE AND PHILOSOPHY,** on this coming Friday, after the completion of morning services, in the Auditorium of the Philosophers. I ask and entreat with all due respect, reverence, and civility, that the Magnificent **RECTOR** of the University, the most distinguished leaders of both the academic and civil estates, the Doctors of all Faculties, Licentiates, Masters, as well as the generous and most noble students, deign to render this act more illustrious by their splendid and benevolent presence. I solemnly promise that I shall compensate for this remarkable token of favor by promptly exhibiting my service and devotion at any time. Published on the Second Sunday after Epiphany, in the Year of Our Restored Salvation 1685.

This was the first concern of the people of Gubbio after the form of a republic was introduced in the city, in the eleventh century, as I believe. From that time, the rural counts and other noble men—who had built castles, fortresses, towers, and fortifications on their lands and estates, or had occupied those built in ancient times—began to move into the city and be counted among the citizens, after the surrender of their castles and fortresses was made under fair conditions. If any, however, resisted more obstinately, they were subdued by arms; the castles and rights of many were also purchased by the commune at a just price. The same process was followed with the bishop and the abbots, who, after serious disagreements, were forced to renounce their lordship over the castles they possessed in the Gubbio countryside and concede them to the commune of Gubbio; some things regarding this matter will be said in their proper place in the chronological list of bishops, and even more in the second book of the antiquities of Fonte Avellana.

There, he said, "We saw two rocks from which a huge force of the river fell out." Whether those are the head or an addition to the Nile, or whether it is born there, or returns into the lands after being received from a prior course—do you not believe that whatever it is, it rises from a great lake of the earth? For it must have moisture scattered in many places and collected in the depths so that it can erupt with such force.

Some judge that fire is the cause of the motion of the earth, while others do not for the same reason. Foremost is <term>Anaxagoras</term> <gloss>a Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</gloss>, who thinks the earth is shaken by almost the same cause as the air. When, in the lower part, <term>spiritus</term> <gloss>breath or moving air</gloss> breaks through thick air that has been gathered into clouds by the same path through which clouds are also accustomed to be broken among us, fire flashes forth from this collision of clouds and the course of the forced air. This fire itself runs into obstacles while seeking an exit and tears apart whatever resists until it either finds a way of escaping to the sky through narrow spaces or makes a way by force or injury. Others judge that there is indeed a cause in fire, but not for this reason; rather, because it burns in many places and consumes everything nearby. If these burned areas ever collapse, a motion follows in those parts which, deprived of their underlying supports, give way until they fall, since nothing meets them to take up the weight. Then comes the calm; then vast chasms.

### VIII.

Therefore, the human body, being constituted and formed by natural things, is preserved not only through the expulsion of excrements <note>waste products or bodily discharges</note> which have been gathered through concoction <note>the process of digestion or the "cooking" of food within the body</note>, but also (because the body is in a state of continuous flux) through the restoration of that which has flowed away.

### IX.

Who indeed doubts that something is always flowing out from the human body? For if nothing flowed out from our bodies, but an equal mass of substance were always maintained, there would be no necessity for nourishment.

### X.

Since it is therefore true that the entire mass of living beings is in perpetual flux, unless a similar substance is restored in place of that which has flowed away, the whole will surely evaporate and be dissipated.

### XI.

To prevent this from happening prematurely, it is necessary for us to eat and drink.

On Lettuce. Chapter XXII.
Lettuce, as <term>Isidorus</term> <gloss>Isidore of Seville</gloss> says, is so named from the abundance of its milky juice <note>Latin: "lactei humoris"</note>, or because it fills nursing women with milk. In men, it restrains the movements of Venus <note>sexual desire</note>. Of this there are two species: namely, the domestic and the wild, which we call "feral," because its back has hard prickles like iron, as Isidore says in Book 17, the last chapter. Concerning this, <term>Plinius</term> <gloss>Pliny the Elder</gloss> says in his dietary writings: wild lettuce is similar in form to the domestic, but it has longer leaves, which are thinner, rougher, and less green due to the smallness of its moisture. Therefore, it has much bitterness and sharpness compared to the domestic kind, because it is of greater heat and dryness. Many say it provokes the menses and expels raw humors. As <term>Dyascorides</term> <gloss>Dioscorides</gloss> says: domestic lettuce is cold and humid in the second degree, and in neither quality does it exceed measure. Therefore, its use is significant in medicine, especially for delicate people and especially when it is fresh. Thus it is quickly digested and soothes the burning and gnawing of the stomach and red choler. It cools the boiling of the blood and calms sleeplessness. It heals headache and choleric fumes. It increases milk in women and generates and augments seed in men; this happens because of the goodness of the blood which it creates in perfect quantity and at a perfect age. But when it grows old and hardens, its moisture is diminished and it becomes bitter, and from its use the worst blood is generated. The power of sight fails and is weakened by it; the cause of this is the mortification of the animal sense, because with its sharpness it suffocates the natural heat. Therefore, such lettuce is most harmful to those wishing to procreate, for the matter freezes and coagulates the seminal fluid, especially its seed if it is frequently taken in food or drink, according to <term>Isaacus</term> <gloss>Isaac Israeli</gloss> in his dietary writings. 

Pliny, however, in Book 20, Chapter 8, says of lettuce: There is a species of lettuce growing spontaneously which they call goat-lettuce, which, when thrown into the sea, immediately kills the fishes that are nearby. With its stalk and leaves bruised and sprinkled with salt, it heals cut nerves. There is another species of lettuce that grows in the fields, whose leaves, crushed and smeared on with pearl barley, heal ulcers; the Greeks call this <term>ysopon</term>. A third species is that which grows in the woods, which they call <term>steraton</term>, whose crushed leaves heal festering wounds; with the root and leaves they mitigate <term>ignis sacer</term> <gloss>holy fire or erysipelas</gloss>. There is also another species of lettuce with round and short leaves which many call <term>beratia</term>; hawks, by scratching this herb, draw out its juice 

<column-break/>

and by wetting their eyes therewith, they shake off obscurity and darkness when they grow old. The juice of this herb heals the pains of the eyes, and especially when woman's milk is mixed with it. It cures the bites of serpents and the stings of scorpions if its juice is drunk with wine and the crushed leaves are applied over the wound as a plaster. It also discusses and restrains all swelling. Furthermore, the seed of lettuce, both wild and domestic, restrains the imaginations of lust in dreams and does not permit the body to be polluted <note>nocturnal emission</note> if it is frequently taken in food. However, frequent and excessive use of it causes dimness of the eyes. Pliny attributes many other praises to it in the same chapter, but let these suffice.

On the Burdock. Chapter XXIII.
The <term>lappa</term> <gloss>burdock</gloss> is an herb having broad and thick leaves near the ground, having at the tops of its stalks certain small heads that are prickly and aculeate but hooked, which are accustomed to cling to the clothes of passersby. Whence Isidore says in Book 17: it is called <term>lappa</term> because it has a stalk spread out on the ground, and by the Greeks it is called <term>philanthropos</term> <gloss>man-loving</gloss> because it clings to the clothes of men on account of its roughness. It grows near walls. It is called <term>philanthropos</term>, that is, loving man, because by a certain affection it seems to cling to a man's clothes. There are two species of burdock: the sharp and the round, arranged in the likeness of a horse's foot, which is called <term>ungula caballina</term> <gloss>colt's foot</gloss> by many. The leaves of both are of a foul and horrible odor and taste alike, as Dioscorides says. But Pliny says in Book 26: there are many species of burdock and all are medicinal. For they heal the stings of scorpions, nor do they strike a man if he has been anointed with its juice. A decoction of its root helps the teeth and even strengthens them if held warm in the mouth. Its seed cures the incurable vices of the stomach. To those spitting blood it is profitable and it assists in dysentery, for its root with wine stops the bowels. But given alone, it helps those with stones. The whole herb crushed with swine's grease is good for <term>struma</term> <gloss>scrofula or goiter</gloss>. According to <term>Platea</term> <gloss>Matthaeus Platearius</gloss>, the <term>lappa</term> or <term>lappacium</term> is a hot and dry herb having the power of dissolving, relaxing, opening, and thinning; therefore it is effective against the itch, pruritus, ringworm, and impetigo. It consumes humors under the skin and dissolves the hardness and swelling of abscesses. It is effective against cold dropsy and obstruction of the spleen. Its juice mixed with rue purges the brain of rheumatic superfluity if taken in a small quantity.

The prologue of the first book, and many other things, prove that Phaedrus did not write these fables for a few people, but for everyone, and not so much to soothe private grief as to seek public fame. For why those anxious <margin>ears</margin> <note>referring to the ears of the audience or reader</note> addressed to the reader, not only at the beginning and the end, but also in the middle of the books, which are not needed for friends? What of it? Since in the Prologue of Book III he complains with disdain that he is excluded from the assembly, and in the prologue of Book V he declares his desire to go toward literary applause, and says of Particulo that it is a
> *name that will live through his papers,*
> *as long as value remains for Latin letters.*

Do we think he hoped for this immortality of glory from the silent praises of friends, or from the public votes of the most learned men? And indeed, when he names the "assembly," he surely defines it as that which we have heard existed in Rome among those men whose writings were approved by the calculations of the Critics. Furthermore, how do those things fit, unless we believe these little books of Phaedrus were handled by the hands of everyone, from the Prologue of Book III:
> *If anyone wanders off through his own suspicion*
> *and seizes for himself what is common to all,*
> *he will foolishly bare the conscience of his mind.*
> *I would nonetheless wish myself excused to him.*
> *For it is not my intention to mark individuals,*
> *but to show life itself and the customs of men.*

It is tiresome to bring forward more, for there is no Prologue, no epilogue at the end of the books, that does not show he published the fables publicly. Moreover, I wonder how those who feel differently from us were led to the opinion that Phaedrus shows a fear of Sejanus in the prologue of Book III, as if Aelius Sejanus <note>The powerful commander of the Praetorian Guard under Tiberius</note> himself were understood by this name, and not rather a man not unlike him in character. For if you understand Sejanus himself, how, I ask, did a man who was a freedman dare to graze him so sharply in a public poem while he was ruling cruelly under a most savage Prince? For we perceive it was public from those things we just tasted from this Prologue. Or if he did dare, then Phaedrus was prodigal with his own life; how, I ask, did it happen that he bore such license of the tongue unpunished? THAT THIS MIND was in Plato—that God was the Creator of the heaven and the earth and all celestial and earthly things which previously did not exist, just as he had heard from his elders—is declared by other testimonies shining like stars throughout his entire philosophy, as he had confessed so clearly in the *Timaeus* and in the tenth book of the *Republic*. ### §. 665.

<margin></margin>
How dissent is inferred from an act.
</margin>
*If someone does that which he could not do unless he willed that something else not be done, he dissents in regard to that very thing.* This is evident in a manner not unlike that which we previously showed (§. 663.), that if someone does that which he could not do unless he willed that something else be done, he consents to that very thing.

The truth of this proposition is so manifest through the definition of <term>dissensus</term> <gloss>dissent</gloss> provided (§. 659.), that it is rightly numbered among the axioms (§. 273. *Logic*), and thus we ought to be little concerned with demonstrating it (§. 267. *Logic*). An example is a seller who, when a price is offered by a buyer, takes the merchandise away and puts it back. For indeed, if he did not will to hand over the merchandise for that price, he could not take it away and put it back, provided he still intends to sell the merchandise <note>original: "cum mercem vendere velit"</note>. By this very act he sufficiently indicates that he does not will to hand over the merchandise for that price; indeed, he declares his dissent more strongly than if he had said in open words that he could not hand it over for that price. For he indicates at the same time, quite clearly, that he despairs of a just price being given by the buyer, or even that he is annoyed that a higher price was not offered.

### §. 666.

<margin></margin>
How dissent is inferred from a non-act <note>that is, an omission</note>.
</margin>
*If someone does not do that which he ought to do unless he willed that something not be done, he dissents in regard to that very thing.* This is evident in a manner not unlike what we showed a little while ago (§. 664.), that if someone does not do what he ought to do unless he willed that something else be done, he consents.

What we just noted regarding the preceding proposition must also be held regarding the present one. The truth of the proposition becomes manifest by an example. If a buyer, who had already seen the merchandise before, returns and offers a price a little higher than he offered before, but the seller does not bring out the merchandise, the fact that he does not do this is abundantly understood to mean that he does not will to hand over the merchandise for that price. Consequently, he still dissents in the same matter (§. 659.), even if he does not say a single word.
