**S**omething must be argued, however, regarding the nature of gold, which according to **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note> is the only metal in which no defect appears. For neither part of its matter is corrupted or out of balance. Although it is composed of sulfur and quicksilver <note>mercury</note> like the others, its sulfur is most bright and pure, brought to a purity through the strongest washings so that it possesses no combustible oiliness at all, nor any phlegmatic, watery moisture that might evaporate. Perhaps in hollow places where the solid surface is frequently sublimated and digested by a tempered heat, it undergoes a ripening process called <term>pepansis</term> <gloss>ripening or complete digestion</gloss>. The earthy substance incorporated into the sulfur is pure, most subtle, and suspended like a vapor throughout the whole substance of the sulfur's radical moisture. For this reason, it remains that the heat of that sulfur is constitutional, departing in no way from a balanced temperament; and this is like the masculine power in the composition of gold. Similarly, its quicksilver has its two substances purified to the extreme. For the third part which is in the heat itself is thinned out—not just divided materially, but most subtle like a vapor. It is perhaps frequently sublimated in the cavities of the earth by the life-giving heat of the sun and stars. Likewise, the watery part is thinned out by the same method of repeated refinement; and since it contains "glassiness," it is thinned most subtly. It is certain that when these are mixed together by the heat and the layout of the place—which chokes and reflects the vapor back into itself—they are bound together by the strongest bond of mixture. Sulfur, however, does not enter the composition of gold merely through its quality, but through its substance; and since it is of a subtle substance, it will penetrate everywhere through the quicksilver and color it by coagulating it. Since both have been led by sublimation to the form of the superior elements—which agree with the eternal body in the nature of transparency—both will have much purity. When many parts of the matter are thickened, they will stand together; for it is a property of a subtle substance that, when standing firm through coagulation, it will hold many parts in a very small space. Therefore, contracted transparency produces a lemon-yellow color; subtlety produces the greatest solidification; and the standing together of many parts in a small space and position produces weight, as is proven by those things reasonably demonstrated in the book *On the Heavens and the World* <note>original: "de celo et mundo"; a reference to Aristotle's work</note>. Furthermore, it follows from the solidification and temperament together that gold is little prone to evaporation, or not at all; therefore it has almost no smell. While a smell is not essentially a smoky evaporation, a strong smell frequently occurs with smoky evaporation; for this reason, it also follows that gold is more incorruptible than any other metal and better withstands fire because of the very strong mixing of its blend. For smoky evaporation indicates a certain corruption of bodies, which is less in silver and more in copper. From these things we have the reason why things like sulfur and arsenic and certain others burn silver but do not burn gold. For the cause of this—

Because of its solidity, it does not stain the bodies it touches except with difficulty; and therefore it is worn in rings and other ornaments. The great purity of the matter means it is very rarely found mixed with another body, but almost always pure, because when mixed with others it cannot retain such great purity; and therefore it degenerates into copper. On the other hand, it is very rarely found unless incorporated in stones. Those things that purify gold are sharp and very dry, such as salts—especially sea salts—and the soot of oily but dry bodies, and ground brick. When gold is to be purified, a clay vessel is made in the manner of a gourd or a small dish; and over that vessel another similar one is made and glued at the points of contact with a tenacious clay which the alchemists call the **clay of wisdom** <note>term: "lutum sapientie"</note>. arguments against us in this matter. In order that their barking against the mother of the Messiah may be silenced, I desire you to respond to them through their own scriptures.

<margin>First argument of the Jews.</margin>
First, therefore, they argue thus: This sign (they say) which the prophet gave, was a sign of the future liberation of King Ahaz from the two kings who had come against him. But your Christ was born more than five hundred years after Ahaz. Therefore, this could not have been a sign of his conception from a virgin.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
GALATINUS: It will be easy for us to respond to this argument if we first briefly note the history for the understanding of prophetic truth. In the time when Ahaz reigned in Judah, when two powerful kings, namely of Syria and Israel, had besieged Jerusalem with a great army, as is written in Isaiah chapter 7 and 2 Kings 16, then the Lord God sent Isaiah to Ahaz to warn him not to fear the army of those kings. But he, being wicked and unbelieving (for he was a worshiper of idols), would not believe the words of the prophet. For this reason, the prophet warned him that,

since he did not believe him, he should ask for some sign of his liberation to be performed, saying: *Ask for yourself a sign or a miracle from the Lord your God. Ask it in the depth, or in the height above.* That is: Ask for a sign of your liberation to take place, either from the depth of hell through the resurrection of some dead person, or from heaven through the standing still of the sun, as was done in the time of Joshua. But he, since he was impious, not wishing to ask a sign from God, brought forth an excuse that this would be tempting God. Whence he said: *I will not ask, and I will not tempt.*

Since Isaiah knew that Ahaz had not said this in good faith, but rather because he did not fear God at all, judging him unworthy of such a sign, he did not wish to give the sign to him, but gave it to the house of David, saying: *Hear then, O house of David; Is it a small thing for you to weary men, that you weary my God also? Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and she shall call his name Emmanuel.*

From these things it is clear that the sign of the virgin’s conception and birth was not given to Ahaz himself, but to the house of David, from whose seed the Messiah was to be born according to the flesh. Therefore, it must be denied—as is claimed in the argument—that this sign was given to Ahaz himself. To that which is said, however—that since Christ was born more than five hundred years after Ahaz, his conception from a virgin could not be a sign of the predicted liberation from those two kings—we say that a twofold sign is found in Holy Scripture: one prognostic, the other commemorative.

<margin>The two types of signs: prognostic and commemorative.</margin>
A prognostic sign is one in respect to a future event. Of this sort was that which (as is said in Judges chapter 6) was given to Gideon in the fleece as an indication of a future victory. A commemorative sign is in respect to the past. Of this sort was that which the Lord gave to Moses in Exodus chapter 3, saying:
וזה לך האות כי אנכי שלחתיך בהוציאך את העם ממצרים תעבדון את האלהים על ההר הזה
<note>original: Exodus 3:12</note> This is: *And this shall be a sign unto thee, that I have sent thee: When thou hast brought forth the people out of Egypt, ye shall serve God upon this mountain*, namely, giving thanks to me for this mission which is imposed upon you. Therefore, the sign of the virgin’s conception and birth was commemorative, not prognostic. Nor does the great distance of time stand in the way...

actively, or by any thing which they do; yet they may be useful in what they may suffer; just as a barren tree, which is

*Hamzah’s Precepts:—* The first precept of <term>Ḥamzah</term> enjoins veracity in speech; the second, protection and mutual aid to the brethren in faith; the third, renunciation of all forms of former worship and false belief; the fourth, repudiation of the devil (<term>Iblīs</term>) and all forces of evil; the fifth, confession of the unity of the <term>Ḥākim</term>-God; the sixth, acquiescence in his acts no matter what they be; and the seventh, absolute submission and resignation to his divine will in both secret and public.¹

*Sources and Operation:—* The first two precepts enunciated by the founder of <term>Druzism</term> are ethical in their nature and therefore difficult to trace back to their origin. The genealogy of the third and fourth is likewise difficult to ascertain. The fifth is the dogma we treated before, and the rest are corollaries from that dogma. The operation of the first precept is, of course, circumscribed by the already established law of <term>dissimulation</term>.

Of these principles the second has perhaps been the most potent force in the life and history of the <term>Druze</term> people. It has made of the <term>Druze</term> community one compact social body, presenting more the aspects of a religious fraternal order than a sect. This fraternal feature is one of the distinctive characteristics of the <term>Druze</term> people and has, in a large measure, contributed to their survival to the present day. It has enabled them at the time of crisis to act in unison and as one body moved primarily by motives of self-interest and by the instinct of self-preservation.

The first, beginning at the bottom of the series, is Aesar.* He is called God; or fire intelligent, Dia or Logh: Mr. Vallencey says, the word Logh means the spiritual flame, and identifies itself with the Λογος of the Greeks. In a vast number of languages the word Logh, standing for some idea relating to fire, is to be found. The word Aesar, in Irish, literally means to kindle a fire. In Chaldean, אזה aza, to illuminate, אשא asa, fire. Sanskrit Osch,† fire or heat. By many of the ancient philosophers fire was considered as the primitive element, and it is unnecessary to say anything of the fire of the Magi, or of the numerous examples of the appearance of God as a fire to Moses, the sacred fire of the Israelites, &c.

Mr. Selden says, “Although you may truly say with Origen that, before our Saviour’s time, Britain acknowledged not one true God, yet it came as near to what they should have done, or rather nearer than most of others, either Greek or Roman, as by notions in Cæsar, Strabo, Lucan, and the like discoursing of them, you may be satisfied. For although Apollo, Mars, Mercury, were worshiped among the vulgar Gauls, yet it appears that the Druids’ invocation was to one all-healing or all-saving Power.”‡ <margin>the Sun.</margin>

As fire was supposed to be the first principle of all things, it was also supposed, by a peculiar refinement, to be the destroyer, whence, probably, first arose the idea of the Creator and the Destroyer being identified. The primitive fire was supposed to have an insatiable appetite for devouring all things. According to Maximus Tyrius, the ancient Persians threw into the fire combustible matters, crying, Devour, O Lord!§ It is remarkable, that in Irish, easam or asam signifies to make or create. Aesar, then, would be the creator. Aesar was also connected with the power of magic, and he was called a magician. The word אָסַר asr, in Hebrew, has the meaning of ligavit, obligavit, with the signification of incantare. According to Schelling,|| the Eastern words which have the signification of binding, have generally the signification of incantation. He attempts to explain the meaning of the word Osiris by אָסַר asr, ais, ¶ incantator ignis. He founds this interpretation on the Samaritan text of the 18th chapter and 11th verse of Deuteronomy, which renders חבר חבר hbr, hbr, ligans, ligationem, by אָסַר asr, asr, which puts out of doubt the signification of magic. The world loves the person who will sympathize with its ailments, but those sympathetic ones have never done the world any good. Sympathy breeds into the soul self-pity and the world is filled with people who are sorry for themselves and who feel that for some unknown reason that they are having a hard time which they do not deserve. This is a false concept and those who breed it in the minds of others breed falseness.

Man must be inspired in his efforts instead of being sympathized with in his ailments. The philosopher of old never sympathized with the crying child but sought to teach him the lesson of his fall. There is seldom if ever a time when sympathy really answers the question. It is a false narcotic, which, while it eases the pain for the moment, leaves the ultimate as far off as before.

Occult students want to learn to stop sympathizing with people for into the sympathetic ears of the world are poured all its woes by individuals who live only to tell their troubles to a sympathetic listener, said listener in turn consoling them and saying how sorry he is that it is so, how sad it must be to suffer so, and so forth and on and on into nothingness. This brings into the mind of the other person the belief that they really are terribly abused, badly off, and hopelessly mistreated. This course of procedure destroys the work of the Wisdom-Religion which is seeking to prove to man that he is responsible for his own troubles and suffering and that he must labor himself for the repair of his own temple, digging out of the debris the ruins of his own dreams. But he will never attain with the assistance of those who sympathize with him for they build in nothing but negative and willy-nilly things. The one who is truly the friend is not the one who says he is sorry and how terrible it must be but is the one who instructs and enlightens and takes the suffering of a life to show the workings of the divine powers.

There are two kinds of people in the world: one is the kind who are always bewailing, the other is the group that is eternally trying to find a real reason for the ever-changing conditions of life. The first group sympathize with everyone and everything, telling the

They are the strong characters and man will never grow strong while he seeks to justify his mistakes and soothe his conscience with the sympathetic words of others. The greatest mercy in the world is to tell the truth for while it may hurt today, in eternity it brings its blessing. While today it may be harsh, tomorrow it will be appreciated. Those who spend their lives trying to justify the thing that is not as it should be and who weep with you in your infirmities go down forgotten in history's pages. The friend who raises you is the true friend; the one who weeps with you is just another fool. The more sympathy we get the more we want until all the uncertainty and unbalance of the ages rests upon our shoulders, placed there by our friends whose sympathizing kills out our own incentive to do better. Our worst enemies weep with us while our true friends weep for us as they see us nursing our meanest temperaments and greatest weaknesses with friends around to weep and wail with us.

When a great prince of Egypt died they hired mourners to weep at the tombs and great processions of white-clad figures howled and wailed behind the funeral cortege for so many pieces of silver a day. You will further see that this idea of self is a delusive one. Almost every great writer on Vedāntic philosophy, as also both Buddha and Shaṅkarāchārya, have distinctly alleged that it is a delusive idea. You must not suppose that these great men said that the idea of self was delusive for the same reason which led John Stuart Mill to suppose that the idea of self is manufactured from a concatenation or series of mental states. It is not a manufactured idea, as it were, not a secondary idea which has arisen from any series of mental states. It is said to be delusive, as I have been trying to explain, because the real Self is the Logos itself, and what is generally considered as the ego is but its reflection. #### THE MONASTERY ARCHITECTURALLY CONSIDERED

The disposition of the monastic buildings naturally varies according as the site is an open or a restricted one, but certain governing principles are constant. The notable difference between the Eastern and Western monastery plans is the position of the church. Whereas our monastic churches usually occupy one side of a court, the Orthodox make it, where conditions allow, the central building of the whole: it normally stands free in the court, and in a cramped site it is always the court, never the church, which is curtailed, though the actual size of the church is small by Gothic standards. The liberal mind naturally experiences a difficulty in disbelieving where, a possibility being granted, the testimony in support of a matter is fair and honourable. And though sensible evidence and more than this sometimes is required to silence negative assertion; yet reason, supported by her witnesses, may enervate it, and induce that strict investigation and thought which should always precede experiment, but which the multitude have never yet been found willing to undertake; and are consequently led astray in progress, and learn as it were by chance. It is said that Lord Bacon instituted certain experiments with a view to the discovery of the philosopher's stone, and in the *Advancement of Learning* he faithfully recognises the possibility, as does also Sir Isaac Newton in his works; while Leibnitz devoted his early life to the pursuit: nor did either of these great men, though they were practically unsuccessful themselves, condemn the ancient tradition or deny its validity. Yet it would seem to be more ordinarily natural to the human mind to reject those things, which it has neither been early imbued in the belief of, nor instructed to understand; besides individual research into mere possibilities, and because facts only are alleged, is too hopeless and arduous for this short life, which requires a definite assurance of success, and fruit even from the smallest labour.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta> One notices this clearly on both the violin and the cello, at least for the lowest <term>Eigenton</term> <gloss>natural resonance tone</gloss>, when the corresponding notes are produced on the strings. They sound particularly full, and the fundamental of these sounds emerges with particular strength. To a lesser degree, I believe I have also heard the same for the a' of the violin, which corresponds to its higher natural tone.

Since the lowest note of the violin is g, only the higher octaves of its three lowest notes can be somewhat reinforced by the resonance of the higher natural tone of its air space. In general, however, the fundamental tones, especially of its higher notes, must be favored over the overtones, because these fundamentals lie closer to the natural tones of the air mass than the overtones do. This produces an effect similar to that on the piano, where the construction of the hammers likewise favors the overtones of the deep notes while those of the higher notes are weakened. In the case of the cello, whose lowest string provides C, the stronger natural tone of the air mass lies, just as with the violin, a fourth to a fifth higher than that of the lowest string. This creates a similar relationship between favored and unfavored tones, but everything is a twelfth lower. In the viola, however, the most favored tones, corresponding approximately to b', do not lie between those of the first and second strings, but between the second and third, which seems to be connected with the different <term>Klangfarbe</term> <gloss>tone color or timbre</gloss> of this instrument. Unfortunately, this influence cannot yet be expressed in figures. The resonance maximum for the natural tones of the air mass is not very sharply defined; otherwise, it would cause a much greater lack of uniformity in the scale of these string instruments as soon as one passed the part of the scale in which the natural tones of their air masses lie. Accordingly, it is to be suspected that the influence on the relative strength of the individual <term>Partialtöne</term> <gloss>partial tones</gloss> of the sounds of these instruments is also not very prominent.

# CHAPTER IV.

### Recognition of Stabs, Arrow-shots, Falls, and Bruises.

<margin>A</margin>Now further concerning other kinds of wounds, such as from stabbing, arrow-shots, falls, and the like. Between these and common wounds there is no difference in their essence, except only in this: that such a stab or arrow-shot, because of its narrowness, cannot give way to the <term>Anfall</term> <gloss>the sudden onset of inflammation or swelling</gloss>; therefore it penetrates further into the flesh and veins than a wound does. For it is the nature of every <term>Anfall</term> that it desires much cavity and width around itself. Therefore, open wounds that are not stitched are burdened with less <term>Anfall</term> and worry than those that are stitched up. And the more a wound is pressed together at the top, the more dangerous it is at the bottom. Thus it is with stabs and arrow-shots: as they swell on the outside, the <term>Anfall</term> presses inward, following the <term>Lacerten</term> <gloss>muscles/fibers</gloss>, <term>meatibus</term> <gloss>passageways</gloss>, and veins. For this reason, they are more deadly and worrisome than open wounds which are wide on the outside.

It is also to be noted in such cases that a stab or arrow should be pulled out immediately, before the swelling and <term>Anfall</term> close in. But where this does not happen, it leads more toward death than toward life. And where such danger is apparent through sufficient signs, then the instrument should remain inside and be allowed to come out through the power of the <term>Mumia</term> <gloss>the body's internal healing balm</gloss>. For its healing requires a different handle, and that in two ways: one, that a wound be cut next to the arrow; or that it be pulled out by the <term>Mumia</term> when mixed with <term>attractiva</term> <gloss>drawing medicines</gloss>, and not by the hand. Whatever the medicine draws out in this way is not detrimental to life. So it is also with bruises or falls: wounds should be made at that same place so that the <term>Anfall</term> has an exit and does not move inward toward the life-centers; or it should be stilled and driven away from the outside by the <term>Mumia</term>. For in every blow or bruise, no matter how hard or severe it may be, blue or black, the <term>Mumia</term> is able to bring it back to its original state without cutting or suppuration. For such <term>Inflationes</term> <gloss>swellings</gloss> are not ruptures or from a broken nature, but a swelling in good things; <margin>B</margin> therefore they pass away without further complication.

But should it happen that a fall, stab, or the like has gone into the internal <term>regiones</term> <gloss>regions of the body</gloss> and broken veins or something else whereby a "foreign guest" <note>meaning a foreign object like a shard or arrowhead</note> fell into the regions: in that place you shall be diligent to drive such things away, as is written concerning complications. But if such an iron is barbed or hooked, know that it does not come out backward, but should be pushed through: or else brought into an ulcer and filed out, provided that place is not detrimental to life. But if this is undertaken, let it be bound with <term>Mumia attractiva</term> <gloss>drawing balm</gloss>, which lays down the swelling and takes away the <term>Anfall</term> in such a way that the hook goes back the way it came. You should also be warned that you should in no way attempt to do anything with pliers or instruments. For you would only mock the limb: unless it were so close to the skin or in a flat place where it could be taken without worry. Although without <term>Mumia</term> it is seldom possible. Similarly, it often happens that bullets are shot into the body and are drawn out again by the <term>Mumia attractiva</term> through its kind and nature: unless it happens that the bullet falls into another region. Note therein that the <term>Mumia</term> has no power in foreign regions: therefore if a bullet is shot into the body and falls down between the <term>Intestina</term> <gloss>intestines</gloss>, or comes outside or beneath the <term>Diaphragma</term> <gloss>diaphragm</gloss>, it is not possible to draw it out from that place. Likewise, if one is shot in a "tube" <note>likely referring to a long bone or a deep sinus tract</note> and the bullet sinks downward in the tube, that is also another region. And even if the <term>Mumia</term> were strong enough to draw the bullets out, the "remorse" <note>original: "Rewe", likely referring to the physical resistance or contraction of the internal passage</note> inside the tube would not allow it. Therefore, in such matters, one must take good care of how one proceeds.

# CHAPTER V.

### On the Healing of the Aforementioned, and What Belongs to It.

<margin>C</margin>Now the healing of such wounds is similar to the process for common wounds: it differs only in that the <term>Mumia</term> should be fed with <term>attractiva</term>. These drawing agents should be those that do not draw humors or liquids to themselves, but only take up metals, wood, or bone, etc. For if common drawing agents were used, flows of fluid would persist.

Although it also sometimes happens that a bullet or such an iron heals within the <term>lacertis</term> <gloss>muscles</gloss> because of a good <term>Mumia</term> that has not fallen into <term>Anfall</term> or been strongly provoked. Sometimes after many years, with time, it changes and falls out again: this is permitted by Nature and should not be interfered with. For if Nature heals it, who would want to take it away from her again?

To speak of the <term>attractivis</term>, there are some that draw wood, fibers, and such things, like <term>Asphaltum</term> <gloss>bitumen</gloss> and <term>Carabae</term> <gloss>amber</gloss>. Some draw iron, such as <term>Magnes</term> <gloss>magnet/lodestone</gloss>. Some draw copper and tin, such as colored amethysts. Some draw lead and stone, such as alabaster. Some draw scraps of flesh and bone-chips, such as gums, turpentine, and <term>Asphaltum</term>. Some draw all things, such as <term>Serpentina</term> <gloss>serpentine stone</gloss>. How all such powers are constituted should not be unknown to a physician. For in the working of Nature, when they are laid over the wounds, they all draw equally: thus, what draws a heap of straw and wood will, in a wound, draw iron, lead, stone, and bone. Conversely, what draws only iron will draw whatever lies loose in the wound. Therefore, a physician should not follow external powers, but the internal ones, as they unite with Nature.

### To heal the eyes and eyelids.
Take one cup of the best wine you can have, if it were <term>Malvasia</term> <gloss>Malmsey wine</gloss> it would be better, and let it be white wine. Then take a quarter of an ounce of <term>tucia alexandrina</term> <gloss>Alexandrian tutty, a medicinal zinc oxide powder</gloss> and extinguish the said tutty in the said wine at least ten times and allow it to settle for an hour. Then pour out the clear liquid into another glass. Then take the said tutty, namely the fourth part, and grind it very finely and put it in the said wine and with it the sick person should wash his eyes often. And if he is not healed by this: Take a little of the gall of a pig and put it into the said wine and likewise let him wash himself often as before. And if the redness still does not recede by this: then take the white of an egg and put it into a bowl, beating it well so that it becomes clear like water. And note well that the sick person should lay himself upon a bed stretched out for three hours at least: first bathing the eyes with the above-mentioned water or wine. Then he should have a linen cloth or <term>stoppa</term> <gloss>tow or oakum fiber</gloss> and moisten it in the egg white and place it over the eyes and thus lie for three hours. Then he should rise and go about the chamber, often bathing his eyes with the said wine. And you should do this for three or four days or more: and without fail he will be healed.

### For a blow to the eye if any cloudiness should occur through a blow, whether to a person or a horse.
Take the juice of ivy and a little of the best <term>Malvasia</term> <gloss>Malmsey wine</gloss>, mix them together, and with a feather put it into the eye twice a day and he will be healed immediately.

### To make silver wax for seals.
Take one part of wax and two of mercury and heat it at the fire, rubbing it with the fingers until it is equally and totally waxed and <term>mortified</term> <gloss>chemically altered or fixed</gloss>. And afterward you shall seal with the heated wax itself.

->Witnesses.<-

We, then, having suffered these things at the hands of Leochares, and having him as a surety for us, did not cast him into prison even though we had convicted him of false testimony and he faced disenfranchisement. Instead, it was enough for us to recover our property and be done with it. But despite being lenient toward Leochares and Dicaeogenes, we were deceived by them, men. For neither did Dicaeogenes hand over the two portions of the estate to us as he agreed in court, nor does Leochares admit that he stood as surety for him then. Yet he stood as surety in the presence of five hundred judges. If he did this in front of all those bystanders, I do not know what else he could have done. To prove they are lying openly, I provide you with witnesses who were present when Dicaeogenes withdrew from the two portions of the estate and promised to hand them over to Dicaeogenes' sisters free of dispute, and when Leochares stood surety that he would perform what he promised. We also think that if any of you, men, happened to be present then, you will remember that what we say is true and will come to our aid. 

For, men, if Dicaeogenes is telling the truth, what did we gain by winning, or what did he lose by being defeated? If he only withdrew from two portions of the estate, as he says, but did not agree to hand them over free of dispute, what did he lose by withdrawing from things he did not even possess? For even before losing the case, he did not possess the things we were claiming, but rather those who had bought or taken them as security from him, to whom he ought to have returned the price so that he could restore the portions to us. This is exactly why we took a surety from him: because we did not trust him to do what he promised. For of two houses outside the wall and about sixty <term>plethra</term> <gloss>roughly 15 acres</gloss> of land, we have recovered nothing. Instead, those who took them as security or bought them from him hold them. We do not evict them, for we fear we might lose the resulting lawsuits. For when we tried to evict them from the bathhouse at the order of Dicaeogenes—who then claimed he would not guarantee the title—we were fined forty <term>minae</term> because of Dicaeogenes, men. 

Because we believed he would guarantee nothing of what he surrendered to us in court, he made an agreement with Micion in the presence of the judges, declaring he was willing to suffer any penalty if Dicaeogenes did not guarantee the bathhouse for him. We never thought he would act contrary to what he agreed, for no other reason than that the sureties had been established for us. But Dicaeogenes, after withdrawing from these portions which he even now admits to surrendering to us, instead guaranteed the bathhouse for Micion. And I, wretched as I am, not only have I received nothing from the estate, but I have lost an additional forty <term>minae</term> and depart insulted by Dicaeogenes; and I will provide you with witnesses of these facts.

The book was full of such calamities. Recognizing them from the very first titles and themes, we immediately wished to proceed no further. However, since it was absolutely necessary that such a work be destroyed, it seemed just to us to grant the author, as if he were present, the favor of not condemning the book in its absence <note>original: "by default"</note>. Instead, we chose to appoint the Reason within us from God and the conscience of truth as judges over the man's intent and his zeal, to follow wherever they might lead and to act as they might vote. For it was perhaps likely that he, coming after all others who have been zealous about such matters, had found some better defense of religion, and having encountered arguments both newer and more worthy, had been persuaded by them—arguments which one should certainly not overlook. At the very least, he would be not far from forgiveness if he had yielded to stronger arguments which had not yet been examined by the teachers of the Church, but which had completely overcome him since he had no means of contradiction. Indeed, we were aware from the beginning that he had entertained this wicked preconception. But it was necessary to seat the court in an impartial manner. It would not escape us whether the things that had captured his soul were the same as, or even worse than, those discovered by others, or whether they were better and newer. For of sacred theology <note>original: "theologia"</note>, which has been our greatest concern throughout our entire life, we would yield to no one now living anywhere in the claim to know as much as we do; and of the Greek <note>original: "Hellenic"</note> books and arguments to which he refers himself, nothing has been neglected by us, so that we were reasonably able to pass judgment on them for being what they are, even before arriving at such a disposition.

But first he thinks it right to have us attend to the diagram of propositions that has been set out, to see how the propositions of the impossible are ordered and how those of the necessary are, so that we may also be able to perceive whatever it is in this that is incorrect; for which reason he also introduces these words:

> "Now the impossible and the not impossible follow the contingent and possible and the not contingent and not possible, in a contradictory but reversed way. For the negation of the impossible follows the possible to be, namely, the not impossible to be. But the affirmation follows the negation; for the impossible to be follows the not possible to be. For 'impossible to be' is an affirmation, while 'not impossible to be' is a negation. But we must see how it stands with the necessary. It is clear that it does not stand in the same way. Instead, the contraries follow, while the contradictions follow separately. For the negation of the necessary not to be is not 'not necessary to be.' For it is possible for both to be true of the same thing; for that which is necessary not to be is not necessary to be."

Through these words he says that the propositions of the <term>impossible</term> <gloss>adunaton</gloss>, both affirmative and negative, are set out in sequence and subordinated to the affirmative and negative propositions of the <term>possible</term> <gloss>dynaton</gloss> and the <term>contingent</term> <gloss>endechomenon</gloss>, with the negations being diagrammed in a straight line with their own affirmations. The entire simple contradiction of the impossible is ordered under the simple contradictions of those others, and the entire set by transposition <note>referring to propositions with a negative predicate, such as "possible not to be"</note> is under those by transposition. But, as he says, this happens in a reversed way, with the inversion being observed only regarding the order of quality; because the negations of the impossible follow the affirmations of those others.

### ON THE SAME DAY, THE MEMORY OF THE HOLY WOMEN
### XANTHIPPE AND POLYXENE:

The holy Xanthippe lived during the time of Claudius Caesar <note>reigned 41 to 54 AD</note>, emperor of the Romans. She was the wife of Probus, the governor of Spain. She had a sister who was a virgin, named Polyxene. When the holy Apostle Paul arrived in the land of Spain and preached Christ, Xanthippe approached him and was instructed by him, having been initiated into the faith of Christ by him. Afterward, she also brought her husband Probus to become a Christian. Likewise, her sister Polyxene was also taught by the same apostle at that time. 

After his departure, having heard that the blessed Apostle Andrew was preaching the truth of the faith in Patras of Achaia <note>a region in Greece</note>, she went to him. Having learned the matters of the religion more perfectly, she was baptized. Returning again to her own country, she found her sister Xanthippe shining with all virtues. Receiving her with joy, they both taught many to believe in Christ, and then they died <note>original: "ἐτελεύτησαν", meaning they died peacefully rather than by martyrdom</note>.

Thus, having been delivered from shivering and delivered from evils, with one mind, one judgment, and one impulse, our path toward salvation might be achieved. For there is no other way to be delivered from evils except by being of one mind toward the same goal.

And that it is necessary to do these things as one should, regarding both present and future things, and in the face of misfortunes and the hope of salvation, we are taught not only by words but by the very facts themselves. This is not hidden, but manifest among all nations and places, wherever one might wish—not only now, but for a long time past, and it has not yet reached its peak and ceased. For to flee misfortunes and seek salvation are not fleeting and fabricated things, but true and certain, coming from the words of God. Who does not know that most evils are the inventions of our own lack of ambition? For we have hastened to come not only toward nothing regarding salvation, but toward that which is evil and difficult; like a certain golden chain—not that of Homer <note>A reference to the 'Catena Aurea' or Golden Chain in the Iliad, often interpreted allegorically in Byzantine thought.</note>, but that of the devil, through which he promises a golden hope but a bitter enjoyment. He does not stop before declaring all our abundance with Macedonian praises <note>Likely a reference to flattery or empty political rhetoric</note>, and toward the honor of friends, the goods of the many, those things belonging to them and to us, to those near and those far, and whatever one might say, he draws all things to himself—not in doing well, but in doing ill, and in making the things of others his own, and the things of others foreign. 

Instead of images he offers words, instead of truth, idols, and instead of glory, he brings about dishonor; because he not only carries the <term>glōssokomon</term> <gloss>money-box/casket</gloss> and deceives with what is collected there, but he also draws and compels their bodies, like certain instruments, toward his own vainglory. Thus, there are many dramas of evil, some upon the earth, some in the sea, and some in the air. Nothing seems to be marvelous to those in the world, nor to those in this life; if indeed we the pious, who have Christ within ourselves and the light of truth, undergo not less or smaller trials, but more and greater than the nations. We are examined in nothing else but in evils, and we introduce a notable but evil and unholy reputation. We are in nothing else but the paths of some enemy and wicked one, in sea-passages, in the loss of lands and the men within them, in the expenditures at sea and the falls upon the land, in the sufferings in the air and the evils in life, in the dangers in death and those hoped for thereafter, in the enemies of the present and the punishments of the future. Nothing of evil is lacking, but all come together, and all come upon us. 

We lose nothing else but the hope which we had before our eyes, as in a mirror and a riddle, and we draw upon ourselves nothing else but destruction, like a paternal inheritance. We draw a slow but wicked hope, one that is neither good nor saving, and every future expectation with fear and trembling. We seek hopes of future things for the sake of cheer in present and following things; and after the despair which we know to be against nature, we turn toward apparent glory and the delight in present things, the evils in them, the passions in them, the abundance in them, the wicked and unrestrained desire, the pleasures in them, the lusts in them, the debauchery in them, and the evils in them. These occur not only in the cities, but in the deserts, in the roads, in the houses, in the places, in the lands, in the harbors, in the seas, in the mountains, in the glens, in the caves, in the caverns, in the plains—in all things, in all things, in all things.

If you are not conscious of any such failing in yourself, you must sharply rebuke those who err, both in writing and in speech. Become much more fearsome when the objects of your anger fall within your aim. Use your authority without sparing the injustice, but rather even going beyond the measure of the sins themselves; for this is how those in charge ought to bring their subjects to the point of committing no wrong. 

But when, on the other hand, time has passed and you yourself feel, through your conscience, that you have suffered some ill as if you had sinned, or when another of those under your authority has acted rightly as was required, it would not be out of place to admire their change of heart <term>metanoia</term> <gloss>repentance or turning of the mind</gloss>. 

Indeed, one must respond to individual commands, yet without exceeding bounds. Regarding matters of anger <term>thymos</term> <gloss>spirited passion or wrath</gloss>, it is beneficial to recognize that there is no place where one who wishes to rule should rebuke excessively, nor should one demand a penalty from everyone harshly. For they will not grant forgiveness in the same way to those who are self-controlled <term>sophrosi</term> <gloss>temperate or of sound mind</gloss> and rational, and generally to those who have caused no grief, when they happen to err. 

Because they seek nothing and do nothing out of place, it is a mark of the irrational and the foolish to maintain this attitude toward their conscience. If they should seem to signal things not in harmony with the law <term>nomos</term> <gloss>custom or divine law</gloss>, the laws do not treat such people with horses and splendor as a leading private citizen. For it is a habit, as if by a theatrical machine <note>original: "apo mechanes," likely referring to a deus ex machina</note>, to present both the bearing and the restraining of oneself; hence one should not easily incline toward being angry. 

If hardships are according to nature, they arise from a different nature. These things, then, seem to me to pertain to the cultivation of self-control <term>sophrosyne</term> <gloss>temperance and moral excellence</gloss>. Therefore, those who punish wrongdoers must do so not with some spirited anger or by being harshly indignant; for such as these must admit they stumble as if before God. 

For a transgression <term>plemmelema</term> <gloss>error or fault</gloss> is a wicked thing for all. After these things, one must realize that it would be the act of an irrational person to proceed based on one's own sins. Instead, one must calculate the sins of one's neighbors, so that while living, they are not ignored. Do not become a law unto your own self-control and then take vengeance beyond what is necessary. 

Through this, one might escape being harsh to another; otherwise, one becomes such a person. For such a man might not wish for it, but for whomever it happens, it is better. But this is not achieved by greatness, nor by wishing for one's servants to be foolish. Rather, one should apply these efforts to all laws and according to the mind. Thus, one would not wish to act without self-control, nor irrationally, nor through sin <term>hamartia</term> <gloss>missing the mark or error</gloss>. For it is through such a wondrous law that one serves, while it is the act of the irrational and the foolish to do otherwise.

Most recently, G. Koertius undertook a detailed study concerning that part of the *Cynegeticus* <note>On Hunting</note> which is called the technical section, but he was cut off by death before he could bring it to completion. First, he explained that not only is the arrangement inconvenient, but the teaching itself is so defective and obscure that it could hardly be of use to hunters. And it must be admitted that he argued this with justice; but it confirms our conjecture about the origin of this little book. For Xenophon’s heir—a man certainly not unacquainted with rhetorical studies, but clumsy in writing—preserved the sequence of subjects exactly as he had found them written in the volume handed down to him, nor did he dare to add anything from his own knowledge to the rules that might clarify them or reduce them to a proper order.

But many of the instructions in this part of the work, says Koertius, are so false that they could in no way have been written by a man truly skilled in hunting. He was prevented by fate from explaining and establishing this opinion with a full number of examples. But I would say that at least some of the things he criticized, or was going to criticize, are controversial rather than false. For the author of the *Cynegeticus* advises that the hunter should hand over a hare to the hounds to be torn to pieces once it has been caught. Koertius rebukes this advice as plainly absurd. Yet Blanius, a man no less knowledgeable in the art of hunting than Koertius, commends that very practice. What of it? In the book *On Horsemanship* <note>original: "De Re Equestri"</note>, Xenophon praises Simon for teaching that the goodness of a horse's feet is revealed by the sound they make: a thing which Bourgelatus and Berenger declare to be patently false. **Law-writers** <term>nomographoi</term>. Among the Romans, in the three hundred and first year after the founding of the city, the office of the consuls having been suspended, ten law-writers <note>the Decemviri</note> were entrusted with the leadership of public affairs. For a certain time, by interpreting things for the benefit and pleasure of the citizens, they seemed moderate and most fit to rule of all men. These men, having recorded laws—both local and Greek—on ten tablets, set them up on the so-called <term>kyrbeis</term> <gloss>turning pillars/display boards</gloss>. But in the second year of their leadership, having incurred the charge of tyrannical cruelty, they were dissolved. Appius especially moved the multitude to hatred of the Decemvirate; he intended to ruin Virginia, the virgin daughter of a man not undistinguished in war, having been seized by a burning passion for the girl. Her father killed her with his own hand, fearing the power of Appius, who was determined to shame the girl by force. At this, the entire military was moved and stripped the Ten of their authority, forcing them to pay the penalty for the wrongs committed during their rule.

First of all, we do not have this saying in the four Gospels handed down to us, but in the Gospel according to the Egyptians. Furthermore, he seems to me to be ignorant that he <note>the author of that Gospel</note> is speaking in riddles: the "male" refers to anger <note>original: <term>thymon</term></gloss> and the "female" to desire <note>original: <term>epithymian</term></gloss>. When these are active, repentance and shame follow. When, therefore, we do not indulge in either anger or desire—which, having increased through habit and bad upbringing, overshadow and veil the reasoning mind—but having stripped off the mist arising from these, being put to shame by repentance, let us unite spirit and soul in obedience to the Word <note>original: <term>Logos</term></gloss>. Then, as Paul says, there is among you neither male nor female. For when the soul departs from this outward form by which it distinguishes male and female, the soul is transformed into unity, being neither one nor the other. But this noble fellow <note>Cassianus</note> thinks more like a Platonist: that the soul, being divine from above, having been made female by desire, has come down here into birth and destruction. Immediately he forces Paul to say that birth consists of deception, through these words: "For I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve, your thoughts should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ."

But indeed, the Lord confessedly came for those who had wandered; yet they had not wandered from above down into this birth here; for birth is a creation of the Almighty, who would never lead a soul down from better things to worse. Rather, the Savior came to us, who are called the "wandering ones"; we who were corrupted through disobedience to the commandments because we became lovers of pleasure. Perhaps the time of the first-formed humans encompassed us, and we reached for the grace of marriage before the proper hour and went astray; because "everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her," not having waited for the time of the divine will. The same Lord was present then as now, judging the desire that encompassed marriage. So, when the Apostle says, "Put on the new man, created according to God," he is speaking to us, who were formed by the will of the Almighty as we have been formed. And when he speaks of the "old man," he does not refer to birth <note>original: <term>genesin</term></gloss>, but to the life led in disobedience before the time of obedience. Cassianus thinks the "garments of skin" <note>Genesis 3:21</note> are the bodies. Later, concerning these things and those who dogmatize like him, we shall prove they are in error when we take up the explanation concerning the birth of man in a systematic way for those who need to be answered. Since, he says, "those who are ruled by earthly things both marry and are given in marriage; but our citizenship is in heaven, from which also we expect a Savior." We also know these things were well said; for we ought to live our lives as strangers and sojourners: those who marry as though they did not marry; those who acquire as though they did not acquire; those who procreate children as though begetting mortals, as though they will leave behind their possessions, as though they will live even without a wife if necessary; using their possessions without being distracted by them, with thanksgiving through all things, and with greatness of soul. And again, when he says: "It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of sexual immorality, let each man have his own wife"; as if explaining himself, he says again, "Lest Satan tempt you." It is clear, therefore, from what has been said, that being altered and the process of alteration occur in perceptible things and in the sensitive part of the soul, but in no other part except accidentally.

One might raise the question whether every motion is comparable with every other or not. If indeed they are all comparable, and things that move an equal distance in an equal time are of equal speed, then some circular line will be equal to a straight line, and also greater or less. Furthermore, an alteration and a locomotion would be equal when one thing is altered and another is moved in an equal time. Therefore, an affection <note>a quality or state</note> will be equal to a length. But this is impossible. However, is it the case that whenever something moves an equal amount in an equal time, it is then of equal speed? But an affection is not equal to a length. Consequently, an alteration is neither equal to nor less than a locomotion. Thus, not every motion is comparable. But how will this turn out in the case of the circle and the straight line? For it would be absurd if it were not possible for this thing to move in a circle and that thing to move on a straight line in a similar way, but instead it were immediately necessary for one to be either faster or slower, just as if one were moving downhill and the other uphill. Furthermore, it makes no difference even in the argument if someone should say it is immediately necessary to move either faster or slower; for then the circular line will be greater or less than the straight line, so it could also be equal. For if in time A one thing

<column-break/>

traversed distance B and the other distance C, then B would be greater than C; for that was what was meant by "faster." It is also faster if it traverses an equal distance in less time; so there will be some part of time A in which the object on the circle traverses distance B, and the object on distance C traverses its path in the whole of time A. Yet if they are comparable, the result just mentioned follows: that a straight line is equal to a circle. But they are not comparable; therefore, neither are the motions. However, all things that are not <term>homonymous</term> <gloss>having the same name but different definitions</gloss> are comparable. For instance, why is it not comparable whether a stylus, wine, or the highest note <note>the <term>nete</term> in the Greek musical scale</note> is "sharper"? Because they are homonymous, they are not comparable; but the highest note is comparable to the next-highest note <note>the <term>paranete</term></note>, because "sharp" signifies the same thing for both. Is "fast," then, not the same thing here and there? It is even less so in alteration and locomotion. Or is this first of all not true, that all things not homonymous are comparable? For "much" signifies the same thing in water and in air, and yet they are not comparable. If not "much," then at least "double" is the same (for it is two to one), yet they are not comparable. Or does the same reasoning apply to these? For "much" is also homonymous. In some cases, even the definitions are homonymous, as if one were to say that "much" is "this much and yet more." For "this much" and "equal" are homonymous, and "one" might also be immediately homonymous. If this is so, then "two" is also homonymous; for why would some things be comparable and others not, if there were a single nature? Is it because they exist in a different primary recipient? A horse and a dog are comparable as to which is whiter; for that in which the color primarily resides is the same, namely the surface; and they are likewise comparable in size. But water and a voice are not; for the quality resides in a different recipient. Or is it clear that in this way one would make everything one, by saying it is in a different recipient?

The organ of distress <note>original: lypē (λύπη); also translated as grief or pain.</note> is the mouth of the stomach. For it is this part that feels the biting sensation during times of distress. As Galen says in the sixth book of his On Demonstration <note>original: De Demonstratione (Ἀποδεικτική). A lost work of Galen.</note>:

> In those who are distressed, no small amount of yellow bile flows down into the stomach. This is what causes the biting sensation for them, and they do not cease being distressed and "bitten" until they have vomited the bile.

For the biting sensation occurs for them below the cartilage situated in the middle of the chest, which is named the xiphoid <note>original: xiphoeidēs (ξιφοειδής); the "sword-shaped" process at the base of the sternum.</note>. The heart, however, lies much higher up; for while the stomach is below the diaphragm, the heart is above it. It is customary for the ancients to call the mouth of the stomach "the heart" <note>original: kardia (καρδία). The term was used in antiquity for both the heart and the cardiac orifice of the stomach.</note>, as Hippocrates does, and Thucydides when speaking of the plague:

> And whenever it settled in the heart, it would turn it over and cause evacuations of bile. All those evacuations named by physicians came upon them.

For that which is "turned over" is the mouth of the stomach being forced to vomit, not the internal organ called the heart.

### CHAPTER 21. ON ANGER.

Anger <note>original: thymos (θυμός).</note> is a boiling of the blood around the heart, resulting from the evaporation of bile or its becoming clouded. For this reason it is also called <term>cholē</term> <gloss>bile</gloss> and <term>cholos</term> <gloss>wrath</gloss>. Sometimes anger is also the desire for retaliation. For when we are wronged, or think we are being wronged, we become angry; in that case, the passion is a mixture of desire and anger. There are three types of anger: wrath <note>original: orgē (ὀργή).</note>, which is also called <term>cholē</term> <gloss>bile</gloss> and <term>cholos</term> <gloss>gall</gloss>; rancor <note>original: mēnis (μῆνις)</note>; and resentment <note>original: kotos (κότος)</note>. The large Tower, marked **A** (Drawn on Page 61,) must be manufactured as its Figure demonstrates: It is necessary that its Bricks, (And those of the <term>Tournelle</term> <gloss>small tower or side-chamber</gloss>, where the <term>Coction</term> <gloss>the process of cooking or heating</gloss> of the Compound must be done,) be half a foot wide, but not of the same length; For this large Tower must not be wider in its cavity than half a foot and four fingers; And from the Grate, marked **C**, up to the Lid, marked **B**, (meaning up to the top of the Lid,) it should be more than four feet in height.

The Charcoal that will be placed in this large Tower must be made of Beechwood <note>original: "Bois de Fou," an archaic term for beech</note>; there should be no flaming or smoking pieces; and the said Charcoal must be broken into pieces to prevent it from hanging in the air <note>referring to pieces getting stuck or creating air pockets that disrupt the steady descent of fuel</note>.

Furthermore, it is necessary that the Pipe, marked **E**, (through which the heat from the large Charcoal Tower will pass into the <term>Tournelle</term>,) be made of iron, copper, or good fired potter's clay, and made all of one piece, one inch thick, and three feet long, and four inches wide in its cavity: It must not be entirely straight, but one must begin to curve it little by little from one end to the other, like the neck of a <term>Retort</term> <gloss>a glass vessel with a long downward-pointing neck used for distillation</gloss>, but not so much.

Of lines, some are straight and some are curved. The straight line is a sign drawn directly in length from one point to another. The curved line is that which will be drawn not directly from one point to another, but instead forming an arc. If many lines, like threads in a cloth, are joined together, they will form a <term>superficie</term> <gloss>surface</gloss>: because the surface is that outermost part of a body which is considered without any regard for depth, but only regarding its width and length, which are its proper qualities. Of these qualities, some are so inherent in the surface that, unless it is completely altered, they can in no way be moved or separated from it. Other qualities are such that, while the same face of the surface is maintained, they appear to the sight in such a way that the surface seems altered to those who look at it. The permanent qualities of surfaces are two: one is truly that which we come to know by means of that outer boundary by which the surface is enclosed, which boundary some call the <term>orizonte</term> <gloss>horizon</gloss>. We, if we may be permitted by way of a certain similarity, will call it by the Latin term <term>Ora</term> <gloss>edge or border</gloss>, or if it pleases us more, the <term>d’intorno</term> <gloss>outline</gloss>. And this outline will be terminated by one or by several lines. By one alone, such as a circular line; by several, such as one curved and one straight, or even by several straight lines, or several curved ones. The circular line is that which embraces and contains within itself the whole space of the circle. And the circle is a type of surface that is surrounded by a line, in the manner of a crown. In the middle of which, if there is a point, all the rays that depart in length from this point and go directly to the crown or circumference will be equal to each other.

### THE MAGICAL EXPERIMENTS OF THE INDEPENDENT GROUP FOR ESOTERIC STUDIES.

In 1889, we founded in Paris the <term>Groupe indépendant d'études ésotériques</term> <gloss>Independent Group for Esoteric Studies</gloss>, intended to verify experiments concerning the forces still unknown at work in man and in nature.

The first months were devoted to propaganda, and work could be fruitfully pursued from the beginning of the year 1891. Book VIII of the *Speculum naturale* speaks first of mineral matters, divided into four types, namely: fusible bodies or metals, stones, sulfurous matters, and salts. Precious stones and minerals properly so called are not described there, being reserved for book IX.

The history of each metal is presented separately, following a systematic course; the compiler first summarizes the ancient texts of Pliny, Isidore of Seville, and others; then for each body comes an alchemical chapter: *De operatione auri in alchimia* <gloss>On the operation of gold in alchemy</gloss>; *De operatione argenti, cupri, stanni, plumbi, ferri* <gloss>On the operation of silver, copper, tin, lead, iron</gloss>, etc., chapters where the author reproduces texts taken from the *Alchemist*, from the *Meteorology* of Aristotle and their pretended sequel, from Rhazes <note>original: "Rasès"</note>, from Avicenna, etc., in accordance with what was said above.

Just as a second ray of the sun
is seen to issue from the first and rise back up,
just like a pilgrim who wishes to return;
So from her act, infused through my eyes
into my imagination, my own act was formed,
and I fixed my eyes on the sun beyond our custom.
Much is permitted there which is not permitted here
to our faculties, thanks to the place
made as the proper home for the human species.
I did not endure it for long, nor so little
that I did not see it sparking all around,
as boiling iron comes out of the fire.
And suddenly it seemed to me that day to day
had been added, as if He who is able
had adorned the heaven with another sun.

Just as a ray of the sun, by reflecting, returns up to where it came from—resembling a man who returns home from a pilgrimage—so the fixed act of Beatrice, of looking fixedly into the sun, entered into my imagination and disposed me to look similarly into the sun. Because when the rays of the divine sun are reflected in theological doctrine—which alone can sustain their sight—it illuminates us, and it strengthens and corroborates our eyes so that we too can look at the sun. Therefore Augustine rightly writes: <term>Bonum dei cognoscitur per theologiam quae perficit intellectum & dirigit affectum</term> <gloss>The goodness of God is known through theology, which perfects the intellect and directs the affection</gloss>. And so that we do not marvel that he could look fixedly into the sun beyond our custom, he adds: that the power of that place is such that we can do many things there that we cannot do here. For that place is made as the proper home of the human species; and the terrestrial paradise was created by God so that man might dwell there a long time in a state of innocence, and then, when it pleased Him, he would be taken up to his beatitude. Therefore, since through the purgatorial virtues we have returned to the state of innocence, it is no wonder if in that place—that is, in such a state—it is permitted to us to look into the sun, which is not permitted to us here—that is, in the state of sin. **I DID NOT ENDURE** it for long, nor so little: The poet's meaning is that, once the sun rose, he began to rise toward heaven—that is, to contemplate; for contemplation is the free looking of the mind into the speculation of wisdom with suspended admiration. And regarding the looking into the sun: this is nothing other than that, being illuminated by divine grace, he is able to look into the sun—that is, at the speculation of the divinity. Nevertheless, he did not endure it long, because if the eyes—that is, the light of the intellect—had endured the light for a longer time, he would have been able to discern the entire solar body—that is, he would have had true knowledge of the divine essence. But he did not have such a powerful eye. Nevertheless, for the little that he endured, he saw the sparks and flashes that were born from the solar body, in the same form that they are born from a red-hot iron. The allegorical sense is that the purified soul can contemplate God, but not in a way that it knows His essence; rather, it has knowledge of the sparks that come from the sun—that is, of the effects that proceed from God, since we know the cause through the effects, and not the effects through the cause. And that the sun had so much greater light that it seemed doubled signifies that theological contemplation illuminates the intellect much more than philosophy, because it is not without the infusion of the Spirit, as you will see a little further down.

Beatrice was standing with her eyes
fixed entirely upon the eternal wheels, and I on her,
with my sight fixed, remote from those things above.
In her aspect I became such within
as Glaucus became upon tasting the herb
that made him a companion to the other gods in the sea.
To signify "transhumanizing" through words
would be impossible; therefore let the example suffice
for him for whom grace preserves the experience.

If I was only that part of me which You created
most recently, O Love who governs the heavens,
You know it, You who lifted me with Your light.
When the wheel that You make sempiternal
through being desired, made me attentive to You
with the harmony that You temper and discern,
so much of the heaven then seemed kindled to me
by the flame of the sun, that no rain or river
ever made a lake so widely spread.
The novelty of the sound and the great light
kindled in me a desire for their cause,

He wishes to express something else here, showing that Beatrice held her eyes fixed on heaven, and he his on the eyes of Beatrice. This means nothing else than that sacred theology contemplates nothing but divine things; and whoever wishes to understand them must place his entire mind into theology and into its doctors. And certainly, through contemplation of the divinity, we become divine and gods, as Boethius shows at length. **GLAUCUS**, the son of Anthedon, was a fisherman. Placing the fish he had caught on the meadow so that the nets might dry, it happened that some of them, tasting a certain herb, regained their strength and jumped back into the water. Glaucus was amazed by the event and tasted that same herb himself; seized by a sudden fury, he threw himself into the sea, and there from a man he became a sea god. **TRANSHUMANIZING**: that is, transcending from human nature to divine.

The poet shows himself to have been enraptured by the Holy Spirit, and by the sweetness of the song that he heard, and by the greatest light that was shining. Therefore, he was filled with ineffable joy in both sight and taste. Turning then to the Holy Spirit, he speaks like a man now returned to the world: "O Holy Spirit, who are Love and govern the heavens, You alone know if, when I was in such meditation, I was only that soul which You created in me anew when You transformed me. **XL.** Virtue possesses the property of being of divine origin <margin>Chapter III.</margin>; for these three parts of it taken together constitute true virtue, and each of them is always found joined with the other two. Indeed, in prudence there is also fortitude, in that the mind labors and endures toil in searching for the truth, and does not rest until it finds it; there is also temperance, since it is a wise thing to be ignorant of certain matters. In temperance, one then finds prudence, which counsels us not to neglect things useful to life, lest we suffer detriment; for this reason Medicine is of divine origin, because it is dictated by this eternal truth: there is also fortitude, so that one may know how to keep away from pleasures. Finally, in fortitude there is also prudence to defend what is honorable; and there is temperance, so that the victors do not wish to destroy the vanquished, whom they can keep alive without harm.

**THE NATURAL THIRST.** He showed above that there can be an innate thirst and desire in man for knowledge. And because the knowledge of divine things is that through which we are blessed, and we cannot have this perfectly through our own industry nor through natural means unless we are illuminated by the Holy Spirit. Christ denoted this in the Gospel of Saint John, chapter four, when asking for a drink from the Samaritan woman at the well of Jacob; and she denying it to him, alleging that the Jews do not use things belonging to Samaritans. He added: if you knew who it is that asks you for a drink, you would ask him, and he would give you to drink of a water from a fountain that springs up into eternal life. The young woman then, after many words, asked him for the grace, and Christ filled her with the Holy Spirit. Therefore, most wisely at present, the poet shows that the natural thirst, i.e., the natural desire for learning and knowing, is never quenched except with the water for which the young Samaritan woman asked the grace, i.e., the grace of the Holy Spirit. **TROUBLED ME.** <note>original: "mitravagliava"</note> This is a metaphor from grain already threshed, which, so that it remains purged and clean, is "troubled," i.e., passed from sieve to sieve; thus our soul, wanting to find the truth, goes about purging itself from time to time. **AND THE HASTE GOADED ME** shows that at the same time the soul was eager to investigate the cause of the shaking of the mountain and of the song of the souls, and the body had to hasten in following its journey. But <term>Statius</term> <gloss>Publius Papinius Statius, a Roman poet of the 1st century AD</gloss>, arriving, declares that which neither Dante, i.e., sensuality, nor Virgil, i.e., human intellect—although illuminated by much learning—could understand by themselves. But Statius, who is accustomed to such things, declares them. And he represents Statius as the human intellect which extends itself to comprehend that which cannot be comprehended by way of reason. And by comparison, he shows according to what Luke writes in the twenty-fourth chapter <note>The text incorrectly cites chapter 23.</note>.

For the <term>Dorian</term> <gloss>Doria</gloss> harmony was named after the Dorians, who were its inventors; the <term>Phrygian</term> <gloss>Frigia</gloss> after the peoples who inhabited Phrygia; and the <term>Lydian</term> <gloss>Lidia</gloss> from those of Lydia; and so on for the others in order. It is indeed true that, as each of these had something unique in its song and was accompanied by different <term>Numbers</term> <gloss>rhythmic meters</gloss>, they called some of them grave and severe; some bacchanalian and furious; some honest and religious; and others they named lascivious and warlike. Thus, in this regard, they took great care in accompanying such Harmonies with the proper Rhythms, together with a purpose suited to the subject matter expressed in the Oration or Speech, according to their nature.

Having then considered all these things, they named their compositions according to the nature of the composition itself: for example, <term>Mournful Modes</term> <gloss>Modi flebili</gloss>, which are the Elegies. For these contain sad and mournful subjects, as can be seen expressly in those two volumes (among nearly infinite others by other authors) which Ovid wrote after he was sent into exile by Augustus; and also from what he writes in the *Epistle of Sappho to Phaon*, wishing to show that amorous things are mournful subjects and suitable for the Elegy, saying:

> Perhaps you also ask why my verses are in alternating lines,
> Since I am more suited to lyric modes.
> My love is to be wept for. Elegy is a mournful song.
> No lyre is made for my tears. <note>original: "Forsitan & quare mea sint alterna requiris / Carmina, cùm lyricis sim magis apta modis. / Flendus amor meus est. Elegia flebile carmen. / Non facit ad lacrymas barbitos ulla meos."</note>

Horace made mention of these Modes, saying:

> You always pursue in mournful modes
> Mystes, who was taken away. <note>original: "Tu semper urges flebilibus modis / Mysten ademptum."</note>

And also Boethius in the third book of *The Consolation of Philosophy*:

> Once, mourning the death of his wife,
> The Thracian poet, 
> After he had, with mournful modes,
> Compelled the forests to run and the moving
> Rivers to stand still; <note>original: "Quondam funera coniugis / Vates thraicius gemens, / Postquàm flebilibus modis, / Syluas currere, mobiles / Amnes stare coegerat;"</note>

Just as Cicero also commemorated them in the *Tusculan Disputations*, when (making mention of the humble and depressed together) he said: *These are sung together with pressed and mournful modes, which bring sadness to entire theaters.* <note>original: "Hæc cum pressis & flebilibus modis, qui totis theatris moestitiam inferant, concinuntur."</note> And in another place, making mention of slow modes: *The same Roscius used to say that the more age came upon him, the slower he would make the modes of the flute player, and the more relaxed the songs.* <note>original: "Solet idem Roscius dicere, se quo plus ætatis sibi accederet, eo tardiores tibicinis modos, & cantus remissiores esse facturum."</note>

Others they named <term>Lamenting Modes</term> <gloss>Modi lamenteuoli</gloss>, as can be seen in Apuleius when he says: *And the sound of the wedding flute is changed into the plaintive Lydian mode.* <note>original: "Et sonus Tibiæ Zigiæ mutatur in quærulum Lydij modum."</note> Some then called them <term>Sweet Modes</term> <gloss>Modi dolci</gloss>; as the same Horace shows us in another place, when he says:

> Now Thracian Chloe rules me,
> Learned in sweet modes, and 
> Skilled in the cithara. <note>original: "Me nunc Tressa Chloe regit, / Dulces docta modos, & / Citharæ sciens."</note>

And Seneca also: *Let the flute pour forth sweet sacrificial modes.* <note>original: "Sacrificas dulces tibia effundat modos."</note> They also named some others <term>Sad Modes</term> <gloss>Modi mesti</gloss>; as can be seen from the authority of Boethius:

> I who once composed songs with flourishing zeal,
> Am now forced, alas, to enter into sad, mournful modes; <note>original: "Carmina qui quondam studio florente peregi, / Flebilis heu mæstos cogor inire modos;"</note>

And some <term>Unchaste Modes</term> <gloss>Modi impudici</gloss>, which Quintilian commemorates saying: *Yet I think it must be more openly confessed, that this music is not taught by me, which is now on the stages, effeminate and broken by unchaste modes.* <note>original: "Apertius tamen profitendum puto, non hanc a me præcipi, quæ nunc in scenis effæminata, & impu dicis modis fracta."</note> Others called them <term>Rough</term> <gloss>rudi</gloss> or <term>Coarse Modes</term> <gloss>grossi</gloss>, as Ovid demonstrates:

> And while, with the Tuscan flute player providing a rough mode,
> The Lydian dancer strikes the leveled ground three times with his foot; <note>original: "Dumq; rudem præbente modum tibicine Tusco, / Lydius æquatam ter pede pulsat humum;"</note>

And others <term>Discordant Modes</term> <gloss>Modi discordanti</gloss>; and of these Statius makes mention:

> Discordant modes and sobbing words
> I labor at. <note>original: "Discordesq; modos, & singultantia uerba / Molior."</note>

Lastly (leaving out many others for brevity), they universally called some compositions <term>Lyric Modes</term> <gloss>Modi lirici</gloss>, as can be understood from the authority of Ovid cited above. Such subjects were not expressed with the voice alone, but were accompanied by the Harmony arising from some instrument, whether it were the <term>Cittern</term> <gloss>Cetera</gloss>, or <term>Lyre</term> <gloss>Lira</gloss>, or else the <term>Pipe</term> <gloss>Piffero</gloss>, or of any other sort. A great difference was nevertheless found between these Modes: since the people of one province used one kind of Verse and one Instrument, and those of another used another Instrument and another kind. And they were not different only in these, but in the Harmonies as well: for one kind of harmony was used by one people and another by another; so that they were also different in the Rhythms found in the verses. # CHAPTER THIRTY-ONE.

## *Chirotheca marina. Sarong tangan laut.*

This is also a spongy plant, extending itself from a narrow beginning far out into many fingers, which are narrow and joined together at the bottom, but broad at the top and hollowed out with a hole; furthermore, it is hollow inside and of two forms.

The first has many round fingers, some no thicker than a thumb, bearing a narrow and round little hole at the top.

*Others are as thick as an infant’s arm and wide open like an intestine. Furthermore, they are hollow inside like a small cup, or like the cut-off fingers of woolen gloves; smoother on the inside than the outside, with a substance like wool and sponge mixed together, of a pale-gray color like other sponges.*

It sits upon all kinds of cliffs without any visible roots, and in the cavities of the fingers live small fish and shrimp, swimming in and out of them.

*The second form has longer and sharper fingers at the top, very prickly on the outside, though the thorns are not hard; it is of a coarser and broader weave than the preceding one, leaning more toward a spongy than a woody nature. Inside, the fingers are also hollow and smooth, in which similar small fish and shrimp play. They are clusters over a foot high, with many fingers grown together, standing on a poor root.*

*Name.* In Latin <term>Chirotheca marina</term> <gloss>Sea Glove</gloss>; in Malay <term>Sarong tangan laut</term> <gloss>Sea glove-sheath</gloss>.

*Place and Use.* These plants serve no use, but like the previous ones, they are kept as rarities.

In this <term>Chirotheca marina</term> lives another small fish of a peculiar nature and shape, a kind of <term>Ican batu</term> <gloss>Stone fish</gloss>, flat and thin in shape, red in color with blackish rings, which is also found under hollow stones; it inhabits these fingers, but it is not known whether it forms them; it pecks at people like a hen if they come too close, though without causing pain.
