# CHAPTER THIRTY-TWO.

## *Barba marina.*

Finally, there follow two rare marine plants which also have commonalities with the <term>Zoophyta</term> <gloss>animal-plants</gloss>, but they lean even closer to a stony nature, and therefore belong in this Book.

*1. <term>Barba marina</term> <gloss>Sea Beard</gloss> seems to be a bundle of white or gray, stiff bristles, in the shape of a brush or a coarse paintbrush. At the bottom, they stand on a knotty root, formed almost like a scrotum, made of small and stony grit. The bristles are stuck into this, the entire brush being over a span long, tapering to a point at the top like a cone, smooth on the outside and somewhat angular, covered with a fine substance like the linen called <term>Tshjavoni</term> <note>A type of fine cloth or gauze</note>, under which many small eyes or holes are seen. When this stony linen is pulled away, the white or gray bristles first appear, having the thickness of horsehairs, rough and sharp, especially around the lower part, where they also cut somewhat. Then the hairs of the cone open up and form a tangled beard, breaking easily when touched, and the pieces stick to the skin with a slight itching. The rest of the cone still clings together like a lock of hair that hangs together through filth and nits. Under water, it seems to show some sensation through its slimy skin, but above water, no sign of life or movement can be detected in it, except for a slight itching on the skin.*

*Name.* In Latin <term>Barba marina</term>; in Malay one may call it <term>Djangot</term> or <term>Barba laut</term> <gloss>Sea beard</gloss>. By others it is also called <term>Penicillus marinus</term> <gloss>Marine paintbrush</gloss>, for a form of it is also found in the Mediterranean Sea. In these lands, it rarely comes to light, being only occasionally pulled up by fishermen's hooks that are let down quite deep into the sea. It also has no known use to this day, for the fishermen consider it a harmful growth, throwing it immediately back into the sea.*

It is sufficient then to know that the Gospel which bears the name of Mark, as well as the three others, is a product of the Holy Spirit, who guided the hand and pen of this Evangelist. This alone is what constitutes the excellence of the Holy Books, and gives them the authority they possess to subject our faith to them, and not the names of their authors, however famous they may have been in the Church. Regarding the language in which Mark wrote, earliest antiquity has never doubted, nor said otherwise, than that it was Greek. In later centuries there were some who wished to award that honor to Latin; and since the heart often holds tender interests that involve the mind in its cause, there have been found people following that pleasant dream who wished to make a history of it and present it as truth.

Since it is likely that Mark did not write his Gospel until after that of Matthew, and probably that of Luke, had already seen the light, he did not, like the first two, recount the genealogy of Jesus Christ: what they had written was sufficient to show that Jesus, the son of Mary, was truly descended from David, according to the prophecies seen in the Prophets. Therefore, Mark began the History of the Gospel differently than the first two Evangelists, and he chose to have it follow immediately upon the prophecy of Malachi, which closes the gate of the Old

<column-break/>

Testament, as if to link the same to the book of that Prophet. Malachi had ended his prophecy thus:
> *Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD. And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, lest I come and smite the earth with a curse.*

These words clearly signify John the Baptist; thereupon Mark comes five hundred years after Malachi, and linking the fulfillment to the prophecy, he makes that the beginning of his Gospel.
> *The beginning, he says, of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God; as it is written in the Prophets: Behold, I send my messenger before your face.*

He continues by speaking briefly of John the Baptist, and then passes over, like Matthew and Luke, to the baptism of Jesus Christ. Furthermore, until the end he maintains nearly the same order as the first, and it seems as if he did nothing but abridge him, whether such was indeed his intention in many places—to expand somewhat more on others—or whether the Holy Spirit, who enlightened him with the same understanding as Matthew, often caused him to agree with him, as Micah formerly did with Isaiah. But one should not therefore view Mark as an abridger of Matthew, since such does not seem exalted enough for an inspired writer who is himself an original narrator; besides, this opinion is clearly contradicted by a careful comparison of one Gospel with the other.

When examining the history of this art, those in the Tang Dynasty who excelled at flower painting first began with the "feathers and fur" <note>bird and animal painting</note> tradition started by Xue Ji and Bian Luan. This was followed by the emergence of Liang Guang, Yu Xi, Diao Guang, Zhou Huang, Guo Qianhui, and Guo Qianyou. These artists were all famous for their depictions of flowers and birds. 

During the Five Dynasties period, Teng Changyou, Zhong Yin, and the father and son Huang Quan and Huang Jucai rose to prominence one after another. In the case of Changyou, his artistic mind and brushwork did not rely on the help of any teacher. Zhong Yin followed the traditions of the Guo brothers. Huang Quan was skilled at gathering the strengths of various masters: he took Changyou as his teacher for flowers, Diao Guang for birds, and he had his own specific methods for dragons, cranes, trees, and rocks. His sons, Huang Jubao and Huang Jucai, were able to carry on the family traditions. For this reason, their names were esteemed in their time, and their methods have been passed down through a thousand ages; this is truly no empty claim. Therefore, the painting methods of the early Song Dynasty were entirely based on the standards set by the Huang father and son.

In the Song Dynasty, Xu Xi appeared and uniquely changed the old methods. He was truly without equal among those who came before or after him. Although he existed chronologically between Huang Quan and Zhao Chang, his divine mystery was uniquely superior. He passed this down to his descendants, Xu Chongsi and Xu Chongju; their family school was maintained through generations, and they were truly able to follow in their ancestor’s footsteps. 

When Zhao Chang applied color, it was extremely exquisite. He did not merely capture the likeness of the form, but was also able to directly transmit the spirit. Some say that Xu Xi, Huang Quan, and Zhao Chang followed one another in succession. However, it is said that Quan’s paintings were spiritual but not marvelous <note>original: "shen er bu miao"</note>, while Chang’s paintings were marvelous but lacked the spirit <note>original: "miao er bu shen"</note>. Perhaps this is an accurate assessment. 

For this reason, when Yi Yuanji first studied the art of painting and saw the work of Zhao Chang, he said: "The world does not lack talented people. But one must cast off old habits and surpass the ancients to truly reach the height of excellence." Qiu Qingyu initially took Zhao Chang as his teacher, but in his later years, he surpassed him and directly followed the style of Xu Xi. Cui Bai and Cui Que, along with Ai Xuan, Ding Kuang, Ge Shouchang, and Wu Yuanyu, were all summoned into the Imperial Painting Academy <term>huayuan</term>, and their reputations were great.

If the sun has a yellow **Straight Pillar** <term>Zhi</term> <gloss>a vertical solar pillar</gloss>, it indicates the ruler will appoint a minister. If there are blue or red **Straight Pillars**, it means a minister will attempt to establish himself independently.

If a **Straight Pillar** is red in the center and blue on the outside, a minister who attempts to establish himself will not succeed. If the pillar is yellow or white and appears moist and lustrous, his attempt will succeed.

When blue and red vapors take the shape of two crossing lines located above, below, or to the left and right of the sun, this is called **Intercrossing** <term>Jiao</term>. This is a vapor of **Excessive Licentiousness** <term>Yin</term> <gloss>referring to unbridled or deviant behavior</gloss>. It primarily indicates that those in power will engage in licentious conduct. If there are intercrossing red clouds beside the sun, there will be military conflict beneath them.

If there are two vapors beside the sun that cross each other, pierce through one another, or face away from each other, these all signify that great military conflicts will arise throughout the world. They also portend internal rebellion and a lack of harmony within the army. Another interpretation states that if there is an **Intercrossing** beside the sun, the side that launches an attack from the direction of the crossing will be victorious.

Various vapors may form a shape like the character for **Mouth** <note>original: kou (口); a square or rectangular shape</note> beside the sun; this is called a **Solar Mouth**. If there are one or two such **Mouths**, it indicates that treacherous and evil people are causing harm. If there are three, four, or five such **Mouths**, it signifies that princes and marquises are plotting to establish a new ruler.

# Records of Military Preparations, Volume 179

### Gates <gloss>In the context of the Eight Gates of Qimen Dunjia divination</gloss>

When a Gate is <term>Pressed</term> <gloss>original: Beipo; a state where the elemental energy of a Gate is restricted by the Palace it occupies</gloss>, then auspicious matters will not reach completion. If a <term>Malefic Gate</term> is pressed, then the disasters and calamities will be even more severe.

For example, if the <term>Open Gate</term> <note>Kai Men, associated with Metal</note> <gloss>Metal</gloss> arrives at the Third Palace <gloss>Wood</gloss> or the Fourth Palace <gloss>Wood</gloss>; or the <term>Rest Gate</term> <note>Xiu Men, associated with Water</note> <gloss>Water</gloss> arrives at the Ninth Palace <gloss>Fire</gloss>; or the <term>Life Gate</term> <note>Sheng Men, associated with Earth</note> <gloss>Earth</gloss> arrives at the First Palace <gloss>Water</gloss>; or the <term>Scenery Gate</term> <note>Jing Men, associated with Fire</note> <gloss>Fire</gloss> arrives at the Sixth Palace <gloss>Metal</gloss> or the Seventh Palace <gloss>Metal</gloss>: these are instances of <term>Auspicious Gates</term> being pressed, and thus auspicious matters will not succeed.

For example, if the <term>Injury Gate</term> <note>Shang Men, associated with Wood</note> <gloss>Wood</gloss> arrives at the Eighth Palace <gloss>Earth</gloss> or the Second Palace <gloss>Earth</gloss>; or the <term>Death Gate</term> <note>Si Men, associated with Earth</note> <gloss>Earth</gloss> arrives at the First Palace <gloss>Water</gloss>; or the <term>Fear Gate</term> <note>Jing Men, associated with Metal</note> <gloss>Metal</gloss> arrives at the Third Palace <gloss>Wood</gloss>: these are instances of <term>Malefic Gates</term> being pressed, and the disastrous calamities will be even more extreme.

<summary>This page explains the theory of the Pressed Gate, where the elemental conflict between a divination Gate and its occupying Palace negates positive outcomes or intensifies negative ones. After determining whether a figure is **Outgoing** <term>Kharij</term> <gloss>Moving outward</gloss> or of another nature, the practitioner should definitively explain the specific distinctions of departure to the querent, describing the result as auspicious or inauspicious, and whether it will be achieved through ease or through great labor. ॥ १७ ॥

Having considered all the questions regarding departure and other matters in this manner before the querent, if the practitioner's mental state <term>Chitta-vritti</term> is steady, if they have faith in the science of geomancy <term>Ramal-shastra</term> and their teacher <term>Guru</term>, and if their heart is pure, then the success of the question <term>Prashna-siddhi</term> <note>meaning the accuracy and fulfillment of the prediction</note> is achieved. ॥ १८ ॥

-> This concludes the method for questions on departure and related matters. <-

-> Now, the purpose of **Inversion** <term>Inkilab</term>. <-

Now I shall speak of the results arising from questions involving **Inversion** <term>Inkilab</term> <note>a technical term in Ramal where figures are transformed or reversed</note>. If the figure **Congregation** <term>Jamaat</term> <note>a specific geomantic figure consisting of four points in each row</note> appears in the fifteenth house, one should declare the result based on its origins in the thirteenth and fourteenth houses. ॥ १९ ॥

If the figures in the thirteenth and fourteenth houses are **Outgoing** <term>Kharij</term> such as **The Great Joy** <term>Vishwa</term> <note>original: "Vishwa-shakra-akhye"</note> and are auspicious, they grant success in questions regarding departure. If they are **Incoming** <term>Dakhil</term> <gloss>Entering</gloss> and auspicious, they grant success in questions regarding arrival. ॥ २० ॥

Similarly, if the figures are **Fixed** <term>Sabit</term> and auspicious, they grant success in matters requiring stability. If they are of **Medium** <term>Madhyama</term> strength and powerful, there is success; if they are weak, there is little success. ॥ २१ ॥

If the conditions are reversed, success will not be achieved. One should judge the auspicious or inauspicious nature as previously described. All segments of the question should be considered and spoken of in the same manner as before. ॥ २२ ॥

Questions regarding what is held in the fist <term>Mushti</term>, questions from a silent querent <term>Muka</term>, or questions concerning time, letters, or limits <note>original: "Mushthimukasharutpatravadhiprashnaharahidha"</note> are settled without the use of **Inversion** <term>Inkilab</term>; therefore, Inversion should not be applied to these. ॥ २३ ॥

In this way, the general determination for all houses has been stated. I shall now describe the specific characteristics pertaining to each individual house. ॥ २४ ॥

**Commentary**—Now the purpose of **Inversion** <term>Inkilab</term> is explained. If a question arises involving Inversion, and the figure **Congregation** <term>Jamaat</term> appears in the 15th house, the result must be interpreted from its roots in the 13th and 14th houses. ॥ १९ ॥ It is like this: if the figures from the 13th and 14th houses are **Outgoing** <term>Kharij</term> and auspicious, they grant success to a question about departure. If they are **Incoming** <term>Dakhil</term> and auspicious, they grant success to a question about arrival.

Just as light is the cause of the perception of form, so is the cause of knowledge of form; it is the cause of modification when the mind is directed toward another object. Just as fire is to the food being cooked. Knowledge of smoke is the cause of cognition for the knowledge of fire. The practice of the limbs of Yoga is the cause of attainment for discriminative realization.

The same practice is the cause of separation from impurity. It is the cause of distinctness, just as a goldsmith is for gold. In the same way, regarding a single perception of a woman, ignorance <note>original: <term>avidyā</term></note> is the cause of delusion, while aversion is the cause of the perception as painful.

<column-break/>

Refinement or manifestation of an object, whether through the senses or by itself, has its cause illustrated by how light relates to form. The cause of modification is the mind turning to another object. For example, consider someone like <term>Kandu</term> <note>A sage famous in the Puranas for being distracted by an Apsara</note> whose mind was steady until, upon hearing the fifth note played on a lute and opening his eyes <margin>1. Some manuscripts read "the sage Mrikandu"</margin>, he beheld the celestial nymph <term>Pramlocā</term>, endowed with beauty and youth. Abandoning his meditative absorption <note>original: <term>samādhi</term></note>, his mind became attached to her <margin>2. Alternative reading: his mind was placed</margin> <margin>3. Alternative reading: became bound</margin>. 

He provides an example of this very point: **"Just as fire is for the food being cooked,"** <note>original: <term>pākya</term></note> such as rice. Fire is the cause of the modification of the hard arrangement of parts into the characteristic loosened combination of parts. 

Regarding an existing object, the cause of cognition is illustrated by how the knowledge of smoke leads to the knowledge of fire. Knowledge refers to that which is known; the fire is the knowledge, thus "fire-knowledge." This is what is meant: since the fire already exists and is to be known, the cognition of smoke acts as the cause of its perception. 

The attainment of the result of causes occurs naturally and independently; "non-attainment" is an exception caused by some obstruction. Just as the natural downward flow of water is blocked by a dam, so too the sattvic mind-stuff, which has the nature of happiness and illumination, has a natural capacity to attain the production of discriminative realization. That attainment does not happen because of some obstruction from <term>tamas</term> <gloss>darkness/inertia</gloss> or demerit. When that obstruction is removed through demerit or the practice of the limbs of Yoga, the capacity to produce that realization is attained purely by its own nature, as its activity is no longer blocked. As he will say later: **"The incidental cause does not move the natural tendencies into action; it merely pierces the veil, like a farmer."** <note>Reference to Yoga Sutra 4.3 regarding how nature flows when obstacles are removed</note>

Thus, the cause of attainment has been explained in relation to the effect called discriminative realization. He now explains that, in relation to a secondary effect, the very same thing is the cause of separation: **"Cause of separation."** 

He explains the cause of distinctness: **"The cause of distinctness is like a goldsmith for gold."** Gold can be viewed as either different or non-different from bracelets, earrings, or armlets. When one intends to distinguish them, the gold is different from the bracelet; when one intends to see the unity, it is non-different. Thus, the goldsmith, by making a bracelet, creates a distinction by making the gold something other than an earring, even though the gold itself is non-different. Although fire is also a cause of distinctness for the food being cooked, because we do not intend to distinguish between the substrate and its qualities—such as being raw grain versus cooked rice—the substrate persists even as qualities arise or vanish. Therefore, it is not strictly called a cause of distinctness, but rather a cause of modification; thus, there is no confusion of terms. One should not interpret this as meaning that a change in shape is the cause of the distinctness of the substrate itself, as the example of the goldsmith would then be inconsistent. 

Having presented an external cause of distinctness, he now illustrates an internal <note>spiritual or psychological</note> one: **"In the same way, regarding a single,"** etc. Ignorance <note>original: <term>avidyā</term></note> is the cognition that "this girl is beautiful," etc. <margin>4. Some manuscripts read: even in the absence of ignorance</margin>. Due to the connection with that delusion, the very same perception of a woman <margin>5. Text is interrupted here</margin>...

<summary>Vācaspati Miśra clarifies the nine types of causes mentioned in the Vyāsa Bhāṣya, using examples like the goldsmith and the sage Kandu to explain how the mind undergoes modification and how Yoga practice removes obstructions to realization.</summary>

A target sixteen fingers wide, with a base made of mustard seeds, should be constructed of solid iron and made to resemble the body of an elephant. <note>verse 44</note>

These firm targets should be bound between two pillar branches. One should strike them three times at the height of a man's chest. <note>verse 45</note>

An expert in the practice should shoot so that the arrow, having pierced through and come out the other side, pierces the ground with its tip and stands upright. <note>verse 46</note>

When the arrow is held between the side of the thumb and the index finger, with the bow-grip and the nock of the arrow level, it is called <term>sama-sandhāna</term> <gloss>level aiming</gloss>. <note>verse 47</note>

When the nock is lower than the level of the bowstring, it is <term>adhaḥ-sandhāna</term> <gloss>low aiming</gloss>. When the nock is higher than the level of the string, it is considered <term>ūrdhva-sandhāna</term> <gloss>high aiming</gloss>. <note>verse 48</note>

When the target is high and far away, one uses low aiming. For a low target, one uses high aiming, and for a level target, one uses level aiming. <note>verse 49</note>

A target with a sixteen-finger circumference is called a large target. A small target is two fingers wide, and a target made of hair is five fingers wide. <note>verse 50</note>

A target inferred only by sound is called <term>parāpara</term> <gloss>the distant and the near</gloss>. Thus, one should demonstrate these five types of targets for piercing. <note>verse 51</note>

The positions for these targets are described as running horizontally, moving away, spinning, or leaping up, whether in the sky, on the ground, or in water. <note>verse 52</note>

In terms of distance on the ground, two hundred <term>dhanus</term> <gloss>bow-lengths, approximately 4 yards each</gloss> is called excellent, one hundred and fifty is medium, and one hundred and twenty is the lowest distance. <note>verse 53</note>

The king should strike at an excellent distance slowly using four types of arrows: those with equal feathers, those that are thick or thin, those without feathers, and those called <term>nāgara</term> <gloss>city-style or specialized arrows</gloss>. <note>verse 54</note>

The king should display his dexterity by shooting one arrow at a falling object, one into the hand, and five arrows into the sky to pierce the target. <note>verse 55</note>

Below, this is superior for it comes from the Master <note>the Creator</note> to the Zohar. He preserves His mercies for those who distance themselves from the side of harsh judgment. Just as in Understanding <term>Binah</term>, there is a drop of a dream <note>referring to a spiritual vision or flow</note> for the righteous. He provides for her as a day of eight <note>likely referring to the eighth gate or the number eight in kabbalistic symbolism</note>. In her place, she alone receives and does not provide. To absorb the heat of existence, they were needed to ascend to them and provide for them, and they are like a well and a pit. 

The secret of the Kingdom <term>Malchut</term> illuminates from the source of the holy signs <note>original: "otot kodesh"</note>. They are drawn from the strength and splendor alone. The symbol is Foundation <term>Yesod</term>, for they do not receive influence except through the power of the soul <term>nefesh</term>. The navel is appointed from their joints, and they descend into the pit. For she is the one who fills from Her Eye, may He be blessed. The foundation of the voice is not perceived as a screen that departs from the one above. Therefore, he said that the vessels and the humble ones of the spirit are drawn to the righteous. 

Returning to the light as we explained regarding the secret of the surrounding hands. It is like the garment of a pit. He wrapped himself in the light of day. He decrees from the mouth of the well. The King of the vessels explores within the purity in the middle. In the way of fear, he turns toward the right. He uncovers the gathering of the waters. He turned to dig for them there, a vessel from the depths of the Philistines. From here, the entire Chariot <term>Merkabah</term> is found to be focused on this secret for the sake of the Supernal Sefirot. There is a secret of the eye here that looks toward the Holy One, Blessed be He, along with the souls of the righteous that ascend with their actions above. 

When the lower waters are from the rest, this is through the secret of the double falling. Therefore, the blessing of the water is upon every vessel that pours in the secret of the appearance of the gaze. He established himself as an embrace. In the drop of the soul of a woman, in order to be included in the secret of the ancient one <term>kadmon</term>, the influences and their purifications are from above. In the secret of the masculine for the sake of the one above who draws to the Kingdom <term>Malchut</term> masculine waters. From the right, he pours downward forever. 

Behold, the children of the Shekhinah are in the righteous ones, and the pouring is for the sake of the answer of the roses <note>original: "shoshannim"</note>. The image of Jacob <term>diuqna de-Yaakov</term> below was established. Even though he is small, it is like the image that entered the Kingdom. Its light is upon the image of the windows. Furthermore, all the righteous who reside within it are not because of the merit of anything else. The teachings within them are the light of the Sun. This means not to diminish from the good species to examine them. For the sake of the upper one, they were not sunken in their goodness. 

Regarding the righteous: King David, the King of Israel, and his son, and the Greatness of the Great ones <term>Rav-Ravin</term>, and the Master of the generation. Jacob is superior to all of them because he is in the place of the existing power and not in the branches. There is another reason for the connection of the Holy One, Blessed be He, with the souls of the righteous. Whether it is during their life in this world or their life in the world to come, they are all requested by the Holy One, Blessed be He, for His glory. This is as it is written in the portion of Lech-Lecha <note>Genesis 12-17</note>, page 82. For every righteous person whose soul departs from the punishment of the grave, it is because with the soul that ascends above, there is a unification and a union. She is designated to receive her portion as the ancient Master of the World. He provides abundance and blessing. 

The Torah in the upper worlds is not like the lower ones. Our time and our designated season at the end of time is to assist. This is the secret of the small chapter concerning the small finger of a day-old child. There is always a reason for the bread of faces <term>Lechem ha-Panim</term> and the arrangement of the table for the meal. For who is it? For his Father at the start of the meal. Three pieces of bread for the Blessing after Meals <term>Birkat ha-Mazon</term> in the power of the morning, our teachers said: three, three, until one hundred. This is also the case for the daily offerings as in the order of the Mishnah that we learned.

I have found written in books that the angel appointed over dreams is Gabriel. He is in charge of all matters concerning dreams and everything a person sees in his dream. Therefore, a person must be very careful not to see vain dreams and should not engage in idle matters before sleeping, so that evil thoughts do not come to him in his dream. A person must also recite the <term>Kiriath Shema</term> <gloss>the Shema prayer recited before bed</gloss> with great intention, so that the angels may protect him from every evil occurrence, every bad dream, and every evil thought. 

I also found written that whoever wishes to know something in his dream must fast for one day, immerse in pure waters <note>a ritual bath or mikvah</note>, wear clean clothes, and pray a pure and clear prayer. He should request from the Name, may He be blessed <note>the Hebrew term Ha-Shem, a respectful way to refer to God</note>, that He reveal to him the matter he desires to know. Then he should go to sleep in purity and holiness, and with the help of the Name, may He be blessed, he will see what he seeks in his dream. 

Furthermore, a person must be careful not to tell his dream to just anyone, but only to a faithful friend or a wise person who knows how to interpret dreams properly. This is so the dream does not manifest for evil, God forbid, for the dream follows the mouth <note>a Talmudic principle suggesting that the interpretation of a dream influences its realization</note>. Therefore, a person must be very careful with his words and his thoughts. 

I also found written that there are dreams that come from the Name, may He be blessed, and there are dreams that come from the Satan <note>the Accuser or the impulse toward evil</note>, and there are dreams that come from the thoughts of the person himself. Therefore, a person must be wise and distinguish between one dream and another. One who wishes to know if a dream is from the Name, may He be blessed, should check if the dream concerns a good matter and if it is something that leads the person toward <term>Yirat Shamayim</term> <gloss>fear of Heaven/reverence</gloss> and toward the service of the Name, may He be blessed. If it is so, then it is a good dream and from the Name, may He be blessed. But if it is an evil matter or something that leads the person toward transgression or toward sadness, then it is a dream from the Satan, and the person must distance himself from it and pay it no heed at all. 

A person must also always pray to the Name, may He be blessed, that He protect him from every bad dream and every evil thought, and grant him the merit to see good dreams that herald good tidings for him and for all of Israel, Amen and Amen.

# Portion of Toldot: The Written Torah
## This is the name by which he shall be called: The Source of Blessings

### The Lamp of Commandment

<margin></margin>
And Isaac sowed in that land and found in that year a hundredfold <note>literally: "a hundred gates"</note>, and the Lord blessed him. They said in Genesis Rabbah, and Rashi brought it in his commentary: "a hundred gates" means they estimated how much the field was fit to produce, and it produced one hundred times the estimate. Our Rabbis of blessed memory said this estimation was for the sake of tithes.
</margin>

Behold, the Patriarchs fulfilled the entire Torah, and the Torah specified this attribute in the details of the commandments that were practiced, as we find with our father Abraham, who gave a tithe of everything. Here too with Isaac, and likewise with Jacob, who said, "and of all that You give me, I will surely give a tenth to You." Our father Jacob gave a tithe even of souls, as our Sages of blessed memory said: there were fourteen tribes with Ephraim and Manasseh, subtract four mothers <note>Rachel, Leah, Bilhah, and Zilpah</note> who are themselves holy, ten remained, and Levi was separated to be holy—thus Levi was the tithe. Thus the Patriarchs fulfilled the commandment of tithing with all their heart, all their soul, and all their might. "With all their might" is taken literally: a tithe of everything, even a tithe of money. "With all their soul" refers to Jacob tithing the souls of his sons. "With all their heart" pertains to the Great Offering <term>Terumah Gedolah</term> <gloss>the first gift of grain given to the Priest</gloss>, which has no fixed measure except according to the generosity of one's heart. Regarding the Offering to God, our Sages of blessed memory said: a generous eye gives one-fortieth; an average eye gives one-fiftieth; a stingy eye gives one-sixtieth. All of this is hinted at in the verse "And he gave him a tithe of all." It would have sufficed to say "he gave a tithe"; rather, "of all" hints at the Great Offering, for the Tithe of the Tithe is included within the Tithe, as I will explain later. For he gave Melchizedek the Tithe and also the Tithe-Offering. Behold, the numerical value of "all" <note>Hebrew: "Kol", Gematria 50</note> is fifty, which is the average eye of one who gives one-fiftieth. However, Abraham was a pietist <note>Hebrew: "Chassid"</note> and gave ten out of fifty so that he might give the Great Offering from them; for by removing ten from fifty, forty remain, meaning he gave one part out of forty for the Great Offering. Even though the average way is "of all" <note>one-fiftieth</note>, when he took the offering as mentioned, he removed ten from fifty and then separated one for the Great Offering because he was generous of heart.

Regarding the Great Offering, it seems possible to resolve what was said: "this estimation was for the sake of tithes." This is difficult, for we have learned in the Mishnah: "Do not increase tithing by estimation." Rather, Isaac our father would measure and tithe, but the estimation was for the Great Offering, as we learned in Tractate Terumot, Chapter 1: "One does not give the offering by measure, nor by weight, nor by count." Even though the Sages gave a proportion—such as the generous eye—it is still called "by estimation." We learn this from the verse: "And your offering shall be reckoned <note>Hebrew: "venechshav", implying thought or estimation</note> for you," meaning like an estimation. And even though this is written regarding the Tithe-Offering <term>Terumat Ma'aser</term>, since it is not relevant there—as the Torah gave a fixed measure <note>one tenth of a tenth</note> and it must be measured—apply it to the matter of the Great Offering.

However, if you examine it closely, it implies the estimation was for all tithes, for this estimation occurred before the growth, as they said: "How much is the field fit to produce?" It certainly seems that at the time of separating the tithe he would measure it, but the estimation that occurred before the crop grew was an act of personal piety. The law is that one is not obligated until the work is completed and it "sees the face of the house" <note>is brought indoors</note>. Whatever he ate before then was an act of pure piety regarding the tithe. Isaac wished to be stringent and would say... to separate even from what was eaten in the field. Regarding the rule "Do not tithe by estimation," this was only said concerning the legal obligation of tithing, but this was a stringency beyond the law by Isaac our father. Since this verse speaks of the commandment of tithing, it therefore says, "And the Lord blessed him," as it is written in Malachi: "Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse... and test Me now in this... if I will not pour out for you a blessing until there is no more room." As for what I wrote that they gave the offerings and tithes to Melchizedek—even though tithes belong only to Levites—know that Melchizedek was Shem the son of Noah, and he possessed the power of a Levite according to what we received from our Sages. Aaron the Priest comes from the kingdom of Melchizedek, for Melchizedek represents Supernal Righteousness <note>Hebrew: "Tzedek"</note>, and Samuel the Prophet, who was a Levite, came from the soul of Aaron. This is hinted at in the verse: "And his exports and your brother the Levite." Melchizedek is Shem the son of Noah; you will see that Shem and Eber sat there, and the name "Salem" <note>Peace/Completeness</note> rested upon him. Therefore, Melchizedek's voice is in the power of his soul.

Three days later <note>the text likely refers to three distinct time-markers or a specific duration</note> they went to the Blessed One and asked, "Who is it that creates this brilliant light?" 

The Buddha explained how the buffalo had been reborn as a god and so forth. The herders were filled with wonder and thought, "If even one born in an animal state can achieve such a result, why should we not also attain something special?" They satisfied the Blessed One and the monastic community with excellent food and then renounced their worldly lives. Through great diligence, they directly realized the state of an <term>Arhat</term> <gloss>one who has overcome all inner enemies</gloss>.

Once, while the Blessed One was staying in the Jeta Grove, King Prasenajit was preparing to pay his respects. The King of Panchala had sent five hundred geese as a gift to King Prasenajit of Kosala, and these geese were brought to the Jeta Grove. Whenever the Buddha and the monastic community were taking their meal and resting, the geese would go toward the Blessed One. The Blessed One and the great disciples gave them scraps of food. Having eaten and been satisfied, the geese stayed there, their faculties becoming clear. They became weary of the world through the power of the Buddha's Dharma.

Then, <term>Utpala</term> bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and made this request: "Please teach me the Dharma so that I may be completely liberated from this karmic, foul-smelling body through even a small amount of merit." Regarding the distinction between virtuous phenomena <note>Tibetan: <term>chos</term> <gloss>Dharma/phenomena</gloss></note>, these are the teachings and qualities that give rise to benefit and happiness within the mind. They consist of the three roots of virtue <note>non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion</note>, the six perfections <note>Tibetan: <term>phar-phyin</term> <gloss>paramitas</gloss></note>, the eight branches of the noble path, and the phenomena associated with primordial wisdom and the two accumulations <note>the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of wisdom</note>.

Phenomena other than these are those that give rise to harm and suffering within the mind. These include the three roots of non-virtue <note>attachment, hatred, and ignorance</note>, the six root afflictions <note>Tibetan: <term>nyon-mongs</term> <gloss>kleshas</gloss></note>, the twenty secondary afflictions, and all those phenomena that cause one to wander in cyclic existence <note>Tibetan: <term>’khor-ba</term> <gloss>samsara</gloss></note> through the power of karma and mental afflictions.

The poetic education of the Eastern Country <note>Korea</note> differs from that of the Central State <note>China</note>. In the Central State, they follow modern trends, and the atmosphere daily drifts toward over-refinement, craftiness, and extravagance. The Eastern Country still values ancient methods. Although there are times when the tones do not harmonize or words are used forcefully, the innocent and overflowing naturalness does not diminish their excellence. In the year of Gyeongja <note>1780</note>, I met with the brothers Yi Sun-gye and Nyom-jae and composed a book to discuss this. Now, Buyon <note>the author Choe Hyang-won</note> has brought this collection to show me. The thoughts and feelings are vast and transcendent. It is what one might call a spirit emerging from the ancient and strange to achieve a singular excellence. At times, it reveals a crisp and refreshing appearance that startles the eyes. One can tell that what he holds within him is such that he might look down upon the whole world. How could one not be moved? Buyon’s rise is different from the ordinary. As it is said, "If there were no men of virtue in Lu, where could this man have acquired his character?" <note>A quote from the Analects of Confucius, praising the presence of noble scholars in a region.</note> Truly, the Eastern Country has many worthies. Having opened this volume, I cannot bear to let it out of my hands. It is truly as the saying goes: when one finishes reading these new poems, the blue mountains have already turned to dusk. However, lines such as "The colors of the trees like floating clouds," or "The sound of the river in the setting sun at Jialing," do not quite reach the distant spirit of Master Yu <note>Yu Ji, a famous Yuan dynasty poet</note>. Other lines like "The frost of the fifth watch enters one's clothes," "Autumn arises in the garden of Yu," "The chickens return when few guests have arrived," or "Many butterflies speak to the high tower," are not at all inferior to the works of Du Fu, Han Yu, Gao Shi, or Cen Shen.

# The Ministers of Song Congratulate the Appointment of Zhang Jun and Zhao Ding as Chancellors and the Recruitment of Worthy Talents, Hailed as the "Lesser Yuanyou"

<margin>Looking back at the ancestors, they were never idle; they looked up and carried out the great work of revitalization. When the Chancellors act on behalf of the Emperor to find the right people, the name of the "Lesser Yuanyou" <note>referring to the Yuanyou era (1086–1094) of Emperor Zhezong, known for the governance of virtuous ministers</note> is spread abroad.</note>
The most distinguished scholars all assemble, and the great fortune of the state opens once more. Respectfully, the Zhou nation is made to flourish again; the ten generations of Han's misfortune are overcome.
<margin>We remember the achievements of the former Emperor Zhezong in reaching Great Peace, though he had few worthy chancellors to help him support the virtuous classes.</margin>
Within the <term>Yanlang</term> <gloss>the corridors of the imperial court</gloss>, eight out of nine seats were filled <note>meaning most positions were vacant or held by the wrong people</note>, yet now the old corruptions of the Xining and Yuanfeng eras are reformed. In the bright court, the most talented of the age are listed, capable of restoring the grand standards of the Jiayou era <note>the reign of Emperor Renzong, considered a golden age</note>.
<margin>Unfortunately, a single mistake led to the promotion of the wrong man, yet the governance of those nine years is quickly restored.</margin>
Through the successive generations, the pivot of history has turned toward the great transformation of the "Three Ascensions" <note>a state of ideal peace and prosperity</note>. When the national destiny was in danger and stopped, we mourned that the prosperous times would not return.
<margin>Fortunately, in these days of reconstruction from the ruins, there is the excellence of seeking out worthy men through <term>Meibu</term> <gloss>divination for a chancellor</gloss>.</margin>
The two men <note>Zhang Jun and Zhao Ding</note> are joined in common integrity, not shaming the long-standing reputation of the imperial kin. They lead the various worthies to stand by their side; are these not the remaining talents refined by the standards of Tao, Han, and Wei? <note>referring to famous virtuous officials of the past</note>.
<margin>Indeed, the sincere admiration of the people of this time is comparable to the governance of the early years of Emperor Zhezong.</margin>
We rejoice that the group of worthies assists in harmony, all saying that the fragrance of the past will increase. We celebrate the peaceful harmony of the new transformation; everyone calls it the return of the glorious destiny.
<margin>This is what is called being on the same path toward good governance. Who can say that the Heavens have made the timing different?</margin>
Because virtuous chancellors are at court, many scholars have the joy of "dusting off their caps" <note>an idiom meaning preparing to enter government service together</note>. Therefore, the public sentiment looks up to the transformation, saying it is like the time when Empress Xuanren presided over the court.
<margin>We sigh that after the decline during the Jingkang era, the old forms and appearances were lost. Who would have thought that in these days of the new founding of the Jianyan era, we would see the Great Peace of the former dynasty again?</margin>
How can our congratulations end? We realize that today is just like the old days.

<column-break/>

<margin>The ban on the <term>Yichuan</term> <gloss>the school of Cheng Yi</gloss> learning is lifted, and worthy scholars flourish like a forest. The historical slanders of Cai Jing are washed away, and the brilliant achievements of the ancestors shine again.</margin>
Relying on the generation of distinguished men who emerge from hiding, they still speak of the virtuous character of the late Empress. They establish the governance of Yao and Shun for a thousand years; this is the most prosperous period of our Song dynasty.
<margin>The gentlemen find their timing to act, unlike the atmosphere of the Jingguo era. The clear court relies on the transformation of the "harmonizing of the candles" <note>the chancellor's role in balancing the state</note>, which follows the scale and standards of the Shaosheng era.</margin>
The figures of the Eastern Capital <note>Kaifeng</note> do not yield to the high officials of the Western Han. The governance of the Yuanyou and Zhiping eras flourished with the style and color of the Zhenguan era <note>the golden age of the Tang dynasty</note>.
<margin>Following the fragrance of the previous cultivation of the talented, it is not just the business of the chancellorship held in common. Treading in the footsteps of the former kings who employed the worthy, all look up to the same sign of the sage's transformation.</margin>

<summary>The ministers of the Southern Song dynasty celebrate the appointment of Zhang Jun and Zhao Ding as chancellors. They view this as a restoration of the virtuous governance seen in the Yuanyou era of the Northern Song.</summary>

At the foot of Mount Xiangbai <note>Ivory Elephant Mountain</note>, there was a man named Lei Yuanzi. He was cautious in his speech and temperate in his eating and drinking. He had no schemes for wealth or high status. He happened to practice the method of <term>Najia</term> <gloss>a system matching celestial stems and branches to hexagram lines</gloss>. After the ninth month, it is said he distributed much of his wealth.

Everyone said that Lei Yuanzi viewed children with great desire. Though danger may arise, he sustained them. He lost his own house but remained and gained the support of his village. Therefore, people of the time said that while others may be corrupt, he remained steadfast. Some are greedy and lowly; they are greedy but survive. Generally, those who do little are excessive, and those who calculate small gains lack righteousness. If a poor man dwells with such a scholar, he will surely encounter calamity. When the family fortune encounters the number one, those in official service will suffer loss. Whenever one seeks a scholar of the "left," they find them living in desolate, diminishing places. Local custom says this involves rebelling against the Way and fighting over wealth. Generally, only a presiding official can maintain this state. If such a scholar advances, whether he is greedy or honest depends on the individual's aspirations regarding their granary.

<insert>Standing Flowers</insert>

**Six in the Second Line:** This desire brushes against the classic principles of the self. Persistence brings misfortune <note>original: "Zhen Xiong"</note>. This is the basis of the text. It is very difficult to maintain one's health <note>original: "Yang-sheng"</note>. The land is like something vomited out. If the presiding official is not diligent, he cannot protect or nourish his nature. He lacks patience. If he does not commit to the long duration of the "brush and moon" <note>scholarly study</note>, he becomes too influenced by habits. His learning is not focused. He puts the low before the high and the wonderful before the intimate. He sees what he suffers from. Things are mixed and upside down, forced and rhythmic. When military luck encounters the number one in official life, one visits and reads with scholars. In common customs, when conducting affairs, there is the error of moving forward and backward. It does not result in disaster, but many are said to fall ill and die.

**Six in the Third Line:** Brushing away desires. Persistence. For ten years, do not use it. The arrow fails. In this text, the omen of nourishment is very dangerous. Those who take misfortune as a way to correct their faults do so in their private rooms. If one acts with urgency, there is much blame. Like a scholar, one must seek brilliance. If one obtains it with few others, the thought will not persist to the extreme. Therefore, the rebellion of the <term>Kulu</term> <note>possibly a reference to a specific rebellious group or state of disorder</note> arises from being unrestrained. Disaster follows. Later, the direction flourishes, but the clan's core is broken. When the family fortune encounters the number one, there is mourning. If one is immediately blocked, a scholar may have ability in compensating and measuring. When it leaves, the customs become desolate, and the dwelling comes first. The situation is such that it must be expressed. It is an omen. It is the custom.

For in truth, whoever takes it does not fail to lose credit, unless they are very well established in their <term>hazienda</term> <gloss>estate or property</gloss>. But certainly, these sellers do not have the same license as others to buy it back. This appears quite clearly in the fact that even to the common people—without much <term>philosophia</term> <gloss>philosophy</gloss> and with only the light of natural reason—it seems very wrong for the seller to take it back themselves. They hold such people in poor opinion, while they do not condemn or reproach anyone else who might buy it. This should be an argument for them that it is not lawful for everyone. Such a negotiation is offensive to the face; it has a very bad appearance and, perhaps, bad substance. I mean to say that, inside and out, it has nothing healthy about it, nor anything that looks right.

Also (as we said above), one of the things that makes <term>baratas</term> <gloss>deceptive credit-sale transactions</gloss> more legitimate is when the goods are sold in public, and many people know about it, so that more buyers attend and the goods can be sold for better prices, rather than only the <term>corredor</term> <gloss>broker</gloss> and the <term>regaton</term> <gloss>huckster or retail reseller</gloss> knowing of it. Thus, I say in resolution that this business is very shameful because it is generally prohibited for the same person who gives the clothing to take it back. Especially without having actually delivered it, so that everything passes by word of mouth; this is not a real sale, but rather a real and manifest <term>usura</term> <gloss>usury</gloss>, and condemned as such. 

If it should happen that, having sold his clothing, a man later sees it in a shop or exposed at an <term>almoneda</term> <gloss>public auction</gloss> to be sold, and there is no secret agreement in the matter, nor any fear of infamy, he may certainly buy it just like any other person from the town for the price that others are paying. He will not be at fault, unless he was at fault in the sale he originally made by charging more than it was worth because it was on credit. All of this being established, it is easy to satisfy what is asked in the problem. Thus, responding in order, I say that the trees of this land <note>referring to the New World</note> never lose their leaves because none of the causes we mentioned above are sufficient to dry them and make them fall. 

Firstly, they cannot fall in winter time because, as we are located and living within the <term>torrid zone</term> <gloss>the tropics</gloss>, the sun moves very little away from us during the winter. Therefore, we cannot call such a time winter, but rather a perpetual summer, since the sun always travels near us. Furthermore, as these trees of the land are always raised in hot lands, they are never abandoned by the heat, which is what vivifies and preserves the plant. 

The <term>Indian</term> <gloss>referring to the West Indies/Americas</gloss> trees lose their leaves and dry out even less due to a lack of moisture. In the summer <note>original: estio</note>, there is an abundance of moisture from the rains, and in winter, there is the moisture that descends and flows down from the mountains to water the said hot lands where we have stated the fruit trees of the Indies grow. 

Even the burning heat of the summer is less able to dry the leaves of the trees, because since the rains occur in summer, their moisture blunts and restrains the great force of the heat. Thus, we can truly say that in the Indies, more heat reigns in the spring than in the summer, because the rains that temper the summer heat have not yet begun in the spring. 

As for the extreme cold that might scorch the leaves of the trees, such a thing was never seen in the very hot lands of the Indies. For all the aforementioned reasons, the trees of this land do not lose their leaves at any time. All of this is aided by the fact that the trees of this land are <term>wild</term> <gloss>original: salvages</gloss> and <term>rustic</term> <gloss>original: agrestes</gloss>, and consequently <term>sturdy</term> <gloss>original: rezios</gloss> and very hard. Thus, they powerfully resist every contrary force of cold and heat which, as I have said, are not very strong in the hot lands of the Indies.
